meta.title: judges_2025-2026 [Enriched + Top 10 Judges]
meta.scope: Top 10 judges by substantive (final_merits, >=2000 words) case count across 2025-2026 decisions.
meta.deep_pass: LLM extraction over full judgment text (pdfs/<year>/raw). Each case.deep holds facts, issues, legal_test, evidence_weighing, reasoning, a verified outcome, and real award (from the Remedy section; null when remedy was deferred).
meta.notes: summary_statistical = original heuristic counts over ALL the judge cases. summary_verified = recomputed from LLM-verified outcomes over the substantive cases only. Awards in case.deep.award_gbp are REAL (extracted), not synthetic.

reasoning_profile.disposition_summary: Alliott is a thorough, fact-intensive judge handling a heavy disability-discrimination and time-limit caseload, who dismisses most discrimination claims for failure to shift the burden (often via hypothetical-comparator analysis) while readily making favourable disability-status findings and upholding discrete, well-evidenced discrimination or deduction heads. He balances prejudice carefully on time extensions, granting short, understandable delays but refusing long unexplained ones. He is even-handed, candid about claimants' shortcomings (including exaggeration), and decides each pleaded issue separately.
reasoning_profile.procedural_vs_substantive: balanced - he decides disability status and many discrimination merits substantively, but a large body of his work turns on reasonably-practicable and just-and-equitable time-limit gateways and employee-status thresholds.
reasoning_profile.evidence_approach: He relies on contemporaneous medical records over exaggerated impact statements when assessing disability, and on detailed issue-by-issue comparator analysis for discrimination; he is candid about poor credibility on both sides (backdated documents, 'cavalier' attitudes) and finds many alleged facts simply 'not proved', while crediting specific, supported acts.
recurring_themes: hypothetical/actual comparator analysis - same treatment defeats inference (Zafar)
disability status decided on contemporaneous medical evidence, discounting exaggeration
just-and-equitable / reasonably-practicable extension turns on length and explanation of delay
issue-by-issue findings - many allegations 'not proved'
burden does not shift without facts beyond unreasonable conduct
redundancy/capability fairness and Polkey/contributory reductions
common_legal_tests: s.13/s.23 EqA comparator and s.136 burden (Igen, Barton); Zafar
s.6 and Schedule 1 EqA disability definition (effect-focused, deduced effects)
s.15 EqA, ss.20/21 reasonable adjustments, s.26 harassment, s.27 victimisation
s.98 ERA band of reasonable responses (Burchell); Polkey; s.123(6)
reasonably-practicable (Palmer, Dedman) and s.123 just-and-equitable extension (Robertson)
constructive dismissal s.95(1)(c) (Western Excavating) and affirmation
reasoning_profile.deliberation_guidance: Decide each pleaded issue separately and resist global conclusions. On disability status, prefer contemporaneous medical records over the claimant's impact statement and be willing to find disability even where the claimant exaggerates. On discrimination, construct the relevant comparator (real or hypothetical) and ask whether they would have been treated the same; remember unreasonable or unexplained conduct alone is not enough to shift the burden - the claimant needs facts pointing to the protected characteristic. On time limits, weigh the precise length and explanation of the delay and the balance of prejudice, extending short understandable delays but refusing long unexplained ones. Apply Polkey and contributory fault on remedy.

deep.facts: The claimant, Commercial Manager (formerly Deputy Managing Director) of a UK property company managing Libyan-owned real estate, was employed from 1987 and summarily dismissed for alleged gross misconduct on 18 March 2024. The respondent alleged misconduct including renting properties to a company linked to his sons without disclosure, failing to secure OFSI sanctions licences causing financial loss, and failing to defend a legal claim resulting in default judgment. The claimant brought claims for unfair dismissal, holiday pay, failure to provide written reasons, redundancy pay, notice pay, a contractual inflation pay adjustment, and expenses; he conceded or had been paid the redundancy, notice and inflation claims, and withdrew the expenses claim.
issues: What was the reason or principal reason for dismissal, and was it the claimant's conduct?
Did the respondent genuinely and reasonably believe the claimant was guilty of misconduct after a reasonable investigation?
Was dismissal within the range of reasonable responses, including whether the lack of an appeal was reasonable given the claimant's seniority?
Did the respondent fail to provide written reasons for dismissal on request, entitling the claimant to two weeks' pay under s.93(2) ERA 1996?
Was the holiday pay claim out of time and how many days of untaken holiday accrued in the relevant period?
deep.legal_test: Unfair dismissal under s.98 ERA 1996 applying British Home Stores Ltd v Burchell (genuine belief on reasonable grounds after reasonable investigation) and the band/range of reasonable responses, with Polkey and contributory conduct considerations
deep.evidence_weighing: The tribunal found the dismissal unfair (procedurally and/or substantively) and that holiday entitlement had not been paid; on the written-reasons claim it found against the claimant. The detailed liability reasoning on the conduct allegations is largely in the trimmed gaps, but the tribunal accepted the holiday-accrual evidence, calculating 827.25 untaken days.
deep.reasoning: Applying s.98 and Burchell, the tribunal concluded the claimant was unfairly dismissed and ordered payment of accrued but unpaid holiday. It dismissed the written-reasons claim, and dismissed the redundancy, notice and contractual inflation claims because the claimant conceded redundancy was not the reason and had already been paid notice and the inflation adjustment. In the remedy reasons it calculated a compensatory award of £91,489.73 and holiday pay of £391,942.77.
deep.award_basis: compensatory award for unfair dismissal (£91,489.73) plus accrued untaken holiday pay (£391,942.77, gross, subject to tax/NI)

cases.respondent: The Real Greek Food Company Ltd

deep.facts: The claimant, a chef, brought age and disability discrimination claims and at a preliminary hearing the tribunal had to decide whether he was disabled within the Equality Act 2010 by reason of a right-knee injury after falls in February and April 2022. He repeatedly failed to provide a proper impact statement or complete medical records despite multiple orders. A later hearing dealt with the substantive claim.
issues: Was the claimant a disabled person within s.6 Equality Act 2010 during the material period by reason of his knee impairment?
Whether the impairment had a substantial and long-term adverse effect on normal day-to-day activities
(At the final hearing) whether the claim should proceed given the claimant's non-attendance
deep.legal_test: Definition of disability under s.6 and Schedule 1 Equality Act 2010 (physical/mental impairment with substantial and long-term adverse effect); at the final hearing, dismissal for non-attendance under Rule 47 of the Employment Tribunal Procedure Rules 2024
deep.evidence_weighing: On the limited medical evidence (orthopaedic letters confirming a February 2022 fall, an osteochondral defect and Grade 4 patellofemoral changes), the judge accepted the claimant was disabled for the period 17 May to 24 November 2022, while noting his oral evidence might later be shown incorrect. At the final hearing the claimant did not attend.
deep.reasoning: Despite the claimant's procedural failings, the judge tried the disability issue on the available medical evidence and found a physical impairment to the right knee that met the s.6 test for the material period, while expressly reserving the right to reconsider if the claimant's oral evidence proved manifestly incorrect. The substantive claim was then dismissed by Employment Judge Young under Rule 47 because the claimant failed to attend the February 2026 final hearing.

cases.respondent: North Star Community Trust Ltd and others

deep.facts: The claimant, a teacher employed from September 2019, was dismissed on 30 April 2023 on capability grounds (long-term sickness absence). He had physical (knee osteoarthritis) and mental (anxiety/depression) impairments and brought five consolidated claims of discrimination arising from disability, failure to make reasonable adjustments, harassment related to disability, and unfair dismissal against the Trust and three individuals. The respondent admitted disability for the knee from March 2020 and for the mental impairment from December 2021.
issues: Were the discrimination acts in time, part of conduct extending over a period, or should time be extended on a just and equitable basis?
Was the dismissal for capability (long-term absence) fair under s.98 ERA, including adequate consultation, investigation and whether the employer could reasonably wait longer?
Did the respondent discriminate arising from disability (s.15) by warning and dismissing the claimant, and was any unfavourable treatment justified?
Did the respondent fail to make reasonable adjustments (s.20/21) and harass the claimant (s.26)?
deep.legal_test: Unfair dismissal under s.98 ERA 1996 (capability, range of reasonable responses for long-term ill-health); discrimination arising from disability under s.15, reasonable adjustments under s.20/21, and harassment under s.26 Equality Act 2010; time limits under s.123 EqA
deep.evidence_weighing: The tribunal reviewed medical evidence including a psychiatric report and found the s.15, reasonable-adjustments and harassment complaints made out only on three specific issues (failure to share departmental equipment and a grievance-outcome statement that there was no disability evidence on file), finding other treatment related to a racism allegation rather than disability.
deep.reasoning: The tribunal upheld three discrete claims against the first respondent (discrimination arising from disability and failure to make adjustments over departmental equipment, and harassment via the 22 October 2021 'no evidence of disability' statement), extending time as just and equitable, while dismissing all other discrimination claims and the unfair dismissal claim. It found no causative link between the discrimination found and the claimant's loss of earnings, awarding £3,000 (injury to feelings) plus interest and £1,500 for treatment.
deep.award_basis: injury to feelings (£3,000) plus interest at 34.87% (£1,046.10) plus £1,500 cost of treatment for the discrimination found

deep.facts: The claimant, a tax solicitor employed from February 2020 as Chief Commercial Officer and Chief Legal Officer (and an early investor/shareholder), was told on 31 March 2023 he was potentially redundant, then resigned with immediate effect on 10 May 2023. He claimed constructive unfair dismissal, breach of contract and unauthorised deduction of wages, relying on alleged misleading correspondence, failure to consult on redundancy, blocking of his share options, and non-payment of contractual salary. A central dispute was whether his agreed salary was £120,000 p.a. or £2,000 per month rising later.
issues: Was the implied term of mutual trust and confidence breached such that the claimant was constructively dismissed under s.95(1)(c) ERA 1996?
Did the claimant resign in response to any breach, or had he affirmed the contract?
What salary did the parties agree, and did the respondent make unauthorised deductions from wages and/or breach the contract?
deep.legal_test: Constructive dismissal under s.95(1)(c) ERA 1996 applying the four Western Excavating/Harvey conditions (repudiatory breach, sufficiently serious, resignation in response, no affirmation); unauthorised deduction from wages under ERA Part II
deep.evidence_weighing: The judge questioned the probity and credibility of both the claimant (over a backdated employment contract, on which the claimant invoked the privilege against self-incrimination) and Brett Riley (over prevaricating on the share options), finding both had a cavalier attitude to document dating.
deep.reasoning: The judge found the redundancy/consultation process and surrounding conduct did not breach the implied term of trust and confidence and rejected the claimant's late attempt to argue the redundancy was a sham as it was not in his claim or resignation letter, so the constructive unfair dismissal claim failed. He upheld that unauthorised deductions had been made (sum to be confirmed) and left the breach-of-contract claim and quantum to a remedy hearing, including what trigger event should be implied for the share options.
deep.award_basis: unauthorised deduction from wages (sum to be confirmed); breach of contract to be determined

cases.respondent: Metropolitan Housing Trust Ltd and Thames Valley Housing Association Ltd

deep.facts: The claimant, a Care and Support Worker employed from November 2021, says she was assaulted by a service user on 7 March 2023 (bitten and hit with a walking stick), was hospitalised for eight days, and subsequently suffered PTSD, hypertension, a right shoulder injury and migraine. At a preliminary hearing the tribunal had to decide whether she was disabled within the Equality Act 2010. The judge found her oral evidence unsatisfactory and exaggerated but accepted she had genuine impairments shown in contemporaneous medical records.
issues: Was the claimant a disabled person within s.6 Equality Act 2010 at the material times by reason of her physical and mental impairments?
When did the substantial adverse effects of those impairments manifest and were they long-term?
deep.legal_test: Definition of disability under s.6 and Schedule 1 Equality Act 2010 (substantial and long-term adverse effect on normal day-to-day activities, including the long-term and medical-treatment provisions)
deep.evidence_weighing: The judge discounted the claimant's exaggerated impact statement and oral evidence (noting an Occupational Health report on 26 April 2023 found her fit for a phased return) and relied instead on contemporaneous medical records, including discharge notes, an MRI showing a supraspinatus tear, and counselling/CBT referrals.
deep.reasoning: Despite finding the claimant exaggerated, the judge held the contemporaneous medical evidence established genuine physical and mental impairments and that from the second half of 2023 she was clearly unfit for any employment, with substantial and long-term effects. He therefore found her disabled by reason of PTSD, hypertension, right shoulder injury and migraine at all material times after 15 January 2024, and made case management orders.

deep.facts: The claimant, a Senior Consultant at a fast-growing cyber-security firm employed from 26 June 2023 and neurodivergent (ADHD and ASC), was dismissed with immediate effect on 17 October 2023 during his probationary period (paid one week's notice in lieu). The respondent's concern was that he had not been logging on/off for the requisite hours and had submitted timesheets in excess of probable hours worked. He brought claims of direct disability discrimination, discrimination arising from disability, indirect discrimination, failure to make reasonable adjustments, harassment, victimisation and wrongful dismissal.
issues: Were the discrimination and victimisation complaints brought in time under s.123 Equality Act 2010 or part of conduct extending over a period?
Was the claimant disabled by reason of ADHD/ASC and/or trauma/PTSD?
Did the respondent commit direct discrimination, discrimination arising from disability, indirect discrimination, harassment, victimisation, or fail to make reasonable adjustments?
Was the claimant wrongfully dismissed / entitled to more notice pay?
deep.legal_test: Equality Act 2010 ss.13 (direct), 15 (arising from disability), 19 (indirect), 20/21 (reasonable adjustments), 26 (harassment) and 27 (victimisation), with the burden-shifting approach; wrongful dismissal assessed against the contract and gross misconduct
deep.evidence_weighing: The tribunal found the claimant was disabled by ADHD and ASC but not by trauma/PTSD, and that the respondent had actively engaged with and tried to assist him (KPIs devised collaboratively). Working from incomplete and inaccurate AI-transcribed meeting evidence, it concluded the dismissal concern was about logged hours/timesheets, unrelated to his disabilities.
deep.reasoning: On the contractual claim the tribunal found the probation extension and one-week notice were contractual and paid, and that the claimant had in fact committed gross misconduct, so wrongful dismissal failed. On discrimination, it found his concerns were not ignored and that the treatment (including the dismissal) was driven by genuine concerns about his hours logged and timesheets rather than his disability, leading it to dismiss all the discrimination, harassment and victimisation claims.

deep.facts: The claimant brought claims of detriment/automatically unfair dismissal for whistleblowing and for trade union membership/activities, breach of contract/unlawful deduction/holiday pay, and disability discrimination against her employer. The preliminary hearing concerned whether the claims were in time, including the effect of a second ACAS Early Conciliation certificate. The claimant had used skilled advisers in respect of the non-discrimination claims.
issues: Was it reasonably practicable for the whistleblowing, trade-union and contract/wages/holiday pay claims to be presented in time under the ERA 1996?
Did a second ACAS EC certificate extend the limitation period (was the dismissal part of the same 'matter' as the first certificate)?
Were the disability discrimination claims in time, and if not was it just and equitable to extend time under s.123 Equality Act 2010?
deep.legal_test: Reasonably practicable test for ERA time limits (Palmer v Southend, Dedman principle on use of skilled advisers); just and equitable extension under s.123 Equality Act 2010 (Robertson v Bexley); effect of a second EC certificate (Serra Garau, Compass Group v Morgan)
deep.evidence_weighing: The judge weighed the prejudice to each side: for the discrimination claims the claimant was only 23 days late for understandable reasons and would lose her claim entirely, whereas the respondent only lost a limitation defence; the non-discrimination claims were barred because it had been reasonably practicable to bring them in time.
deep.reasoning: Applying the reasonably-practicable test and the Dedman principle, the judge held it had been reasonably practicable to present the whistleblowing, trade-union and contract/wages/holiday claims in time, so there was no jurisdiction and they were dismissed/struck out. For the disability discrimination claims, applying the wider just-and-equitable discretion and balancing prejudice, he extended time to 24 January 2024 because the delay was short (23 days) and understandable.

deep.facts: The claimant, a Sterile Services Technician employed by an NHS Trust from June 2014, was dismissed with immediate effect on 25 August 2023 (paid 12 weeks in lieu) on capability grounds for persistent sickness absence measured by the Bradford Score, following ten Occupational Health referrals and five Stage 2 meetings over about four and a half years. He brought claims of unfair dismissal, disability and race discrimination and victimisation; he withdrew the race discrimination claim at the hearing.
issues: Was the reason for dismissal capability (repeated absence) and was the dismissal fair under s.98 ERA, including genuine belief, consultation, investigation, and whether the employer could reasonably wait longer?

Did the respondent discriminate arising from disability under s.15 Equality Act by dismissing him because of disability-related sickness absence, and was the treatment a proportionate means of achieving a legitimate aim?
Was the dismissal/rejection of appeal an act of victimisation for a protected act?
deep.legal_test: Unfair dismissal under s.98 ERA 1996 (capability for ill-health absence, range of reasonable responses); discrimination arising from disability under s.15 Equality Act 2010 (proportionate means of achieving a legitimate aim); victimisation under s.27 Equality Act 2010
deep.evidence_weighing: The tribunal accepted the respondent's evidence of extensive process (10 OH referrals, 5 Stage 2 meetings) and that only a small proportion of the claimant's absence was disability-related (in 2022, 6 of 54 absence days), plus cost evidence that absences had cost £7,814.63 and replacement would cost £15-20,000.
deep.reasoning: The tribunal found the dismissal reason was genuinely capability, that the respondent had more than adequately consulted and investigated the up-to-date medical position, could not reasonably be expected to wait longer, and that dismissal was within the range of reasonable responses, so the unfair dismissal claim failed. It found the s.15 treatment was a proportionate means of achieving legitimate aims given the limited disability-related portion of absence and the costs, and that the dismissal/appeal rejection was not because of any protected act, so all claims were dismissed (race discrimination dismissed on withdrawal).

deep.facts: The claimant, who began work for the London Borough of Barnet on 31 May 2022, brought disability discrimination claims and at a preliminary hearing the tribunal had to determine whether she was disabled within the Equality Act 2010 across a range of conditions. She had a long and complex medical history (529 pages of medical documents, ten road traffic accidents from 1996) including Ehlers-Danlos/hypermobility, disc/back problems, head trauma with light/noise sensitivity, chronic fatigue syndrome, low blood pressure/anaemia and stress.
issues: Did the claimant's medical conditions have substantial adverse effects on her ability to carry out normal day-to-day activities?
Were the effects long-term (lasting or likely to last 12 months, or likely to recur), taking account of the effect of medical treatment?
deep.legal_test: Definition of disability under s.6 and Schedule 1 Equality Act 2010, applying the EHRC Code of Practice on Employment (2011) and statutory Guidance (focus on effect not cause, deduced effects, avoidance strategies)
deep.evidence_weighing: On the extensive medical record and the claimant's lengthy impact and disability statements, the judge found each of the six conditions had a significant adverse effect on her day-to-day activities (e.g. inability to do repetitive movements or walk long periods, exhaustion from every task, inability to work in bright/noisy environments, dizziness and fatigue).
deep.reasoning: Working through each condition against the s.6 test and the statutory Guidance, the judge concluded that all six impairments had a substantial adverse effect on the claimant's ability to undertake normal day-to-day activities and were long-term, and therefore that she was disabled at all material times between 31 May 2022 and 3 May 2024 by reason of all six conditions. He noted (as an observation, not a finding) that the severity might call into question whether she could ever work even with adjustments.

cases.respondent: Eastwood v Central London Community Healthcare NHS Trust

deep.facts: The claimant, a Band 6 Diabetes Specialist Dietician with ADHD (admitted disability) employed from 16 May 2022, resigned with immediate effect on 4 November 2022. She claimed discriminatory constructive dismissal and wrongful dismissal, plus discrimination arising from disability, failure to make reasonable adjustments (relating to Needs Assessment recommendations), harassment and victimisation; her ordinary unfair dismissal claim was withdrawn. She complained she was required to work beyond her contracted hours to complete administration and that a critical Occupational Health referral was made on 9 September 2022.
issues: Did the respondent have actual or constructive knowledge of the claimant's ADHD at the relevant time?
Did the respondent fail to make reasonable adjustments (s.20/21) by requiring her to work without the Needs Assessment recommendations?
Did the respondent discriminate arising from disability (s.15), harass (s.26) and victimise (s.27) the claimant?
Were the proven acts in time, and was the claimant wrongfully (constructively) dismissed?
deep.legal_test: Reasonable adjustments under ss.20/21, discrimination arising from disability under s.15, harassment under s.26 and victimisation under s.27 Equality Act 2010 (with burden of proof); constructive/wrongful dismissal via breach of the implied term of mutual trust and confidence and affirmation
deep.evidence_weighing: The tribunal relied on the claimant's diagnostic and cognitive assessments and found specific proven acts: being required to work excess hours to complete admin (s.15 discrimination), and Ms Botha's unfairly critical Occupational Health referral of 9 September 2022 (both harassment and victimisation); it rejected the broader reasonable-adjustments and other claims.
deep.reasoning: The tribunal upheld a limited set of claims: discrimination arising from disability (excess hours), and harassment and victimisation arising from the unfairly critical 9 September 2022 OH referral, finding those proven acts were in time. However, it found that by the time she resigned the claimant had affirmed the contract, so the discriminatory constructive/wrongful dismissal claim failed, and it dismissed the reasonable-adjustments claims and the remaining discrimination, harassment and victimisation allegations.

deep.facts: The claimant was engaged by the respondent from 15 July 2020 under a document titled 'Consultancy Agreement' (sending invoices, paid gross, responsible for her own tax/NI, free to take days off), and was then engaged on a contract of employment from 18 September 2022, resigning on 16 May 2024. She claimed constructive unfair dismissal and disability discrimination (dyslexia). At a preliminary hearing the tribunal had to decide her disability status and whether she was an employee during the consultancy period, which determined whether she had two years' qualifying service.
issues: Was the claimant disabled within the Equality Act 2010 by reason of dyslexia?
Was the claimant an employee under s.230 ERA 1996 between 15 July 2020 and 17 September 2022?
Did the claimant have sufficient continuity of service to bring a constructive unfair dismissal claim?
deep.legal_test: Employee status under s.230 ERA 1996 applying the Ready Mixed Concrete three-part test (personal service, mutuality of obligation, control and consistency of terms) as endorsed in Autoclenz and Atholl House; disability under s.6 Equality Act 2010
deep.evidence_weighing: The judge found personal service (the substitution clause was not genuine) and mutuality of obligation (a contractual duty to work two six-hour sessions weekly), but weighed counter-indicators heavily: the agreement's wording, the claimant invoicing, being paid gross, handling her own tax/NI, and taking holidays at will, showing the parties did not intend an employment relationship.
deep.reasoning: Although the first two Ready Mixed Concrete conditions (personal service and mutuality) were satisfied, on the third stage the judge made an overall assessment that the surrounding factors and the parties' conduct showed they did not intend to create an employment relationship during the consultancy period. He therefore found she was not an employee from 15 July 2020 to 17 September 2022, so she lacked two years' qualifying service and the unfair dismissal claim was dismissed (while accepting, by concession, she was disabled by dyslexia).

cases.respondent: Impact Recruitment Services Ltd and Howden Joinery Ltd

deep.facts: The claimant, an agency worker supplied by the first respondent to work at the second respondent (Howden Joinery) from January 2018, brought claims of unfair dismissal and wrongful (notice pay) dismissal against the agency and age discrimination against both respondents. There was a dispute over whether she was dismissed or resigned around the start of the COVID-19 pandemic, with the agency asserting any termination was by reason of redundancy/some other substantial reason caused by the pandemic. The age discrimination claim relied on allegations including not being given a permanent contract, being asked to lift heavy items, and an alleged comment that she was 'too slow and too old'.
issues: Was the claimant dismissed or did she resign, and what was the effective date and reason for dismissal?
Was the dismissal fair under s.98 ERA 1996, and what Polkey adjustment (if any) applied?
Was the claimant subjected to less favourable treatment because of age (s.13 Equality Act 2010), and were the discrimination complaints in time?
deep.legal_test: Unfair dismissal under s.98 ERA 1996 (with Polkey/Software 2000 on compensation); direct age discrimination under s.13 Equality Act 2010 applying the burden of proof (Barton/Igen guidelines) and 'reason why' analysis; breach of contract for notice pay
deep.evidence_weighing: By a majority the tribunal found the claimant was unfairly dismissed by the first respondent and entitled to notice pay; unanimously it found the age discrimination claims not made out, the burden of proof not shifting on the comparator and 'too old' allegations.
deep.reasoning: The majority concluded the claimant was dismissed (not a resignation) and that the dismissal was unfair, and that the breach-of-contract notice-pay claim was well founded against the first respondent. Unanimously, applying the discrimination burden of proof, the tribunal found no facts from which age discrimination could be inferred and dismissed those claims. On remedy it assessed loss of earnings net of mitigation, awarding £6,935.13 for loss of earnings plus £500 for loss of statutory rights, a compensatory award totalling £7,435.13.
deep.award_basis: compensatory award for unfair dismissal: loss of earnings (£6,935.13) plus loss of statutory rights (£500), with notice pay (breach of contract) also well founded

deep.facts: Mr Kendall, a pilot employed since 1979 (later TUPE-transferred to TUI Airways), faced mandatory retirement at age 65 under aviation regulations, with his employment ending the day before his 65th birthday. He claimed entitlement to permanent health insurance (PHI) benefits and continued employer pension contributions until state pension age (66), said to arise from handbooks and a 2017 settlement agreement, and brought claims of unlawful deduction of wages, age discrimination, unfair and wrongful dismissal. The disability discrimination claims were withdrawn at the outset.
issues: Did the claimant have a contractual right to PHI benefits and/or continued employer pension contributions until state pension age of 66?
Did the 2015/2018 handbooks or the 2017 settlement agreement create such contractual rights?
Did the respondent make an unlawful deduction from wages contrary to s.13 ERA 1996?
Did the alleged acts amount to direct age discrimination?
Was the claimant unfairly and/or wrongfully dismissed?
deep.legal_test: s.13/s.27 ERA 1996 for unauthorised deduction from wages (whether sums were contractually due 'wages'); direct age discrimination under the Equality Act 2010; unfair dismissal under s.98 ERA 1996
deep.evidence_weighing: The tribunal found the 2015/2018 handbooks were non-contractual and the 2017 settlement agreement did not create a contractual right to PHI; PHI benefit was in any event contingent on continued employment, which ceased the day before his 65th birthday. However, because the claimant had opted out of the pension scheme so contributions were paid to him directly, those contributions were treated as 'wages', and the settlement agreement was found to give a contractual right to continued employer pension contributions on 100% of basic salary.
deep.reasoning: Applying contract construction, the tribunal held PHI eligibility/benefit was non-contractual and contingent on employment, so no PHI entitlement survived his enforced retirement; the age-related dismissal flowed from a lawful regulatory age limit the claimant always knew about, so the age discrimination, unfair and wrongful dismissal claims were dismissed. On the deduction claim, the settlement agreement did secure continued employer pension contributions treated as wages, and a later consent judgment ordered the respondent to pay £14,972.01 for unauthorised deductions.
deep.award_basis: unauthorised deductions from wages (employer pension contributions), by consent judgment

deep.facts: Mrs Osborn, a Technical & CSR Manager at Mothercare since 2016, was dismissed on 3 December 2021, the respondent citing redundancy. She had been on additional maternity leave and contended her dismissal and the failure to offer her the more senior Head of Technical role were connected to her maternity. She brought claims of automatically unfair dismissal, ordinary unfair dismissal, maternity (pregnancy) discrimination and direct sex discrimination.
issues: Was the principal reason for dismissal a prescribed maternity reason (automatic unfair dismissal under s.99 ERA / reg.20 MAPLE) or redundancy?
Was the dismissal fair under s.98(4) ERA, applying the Williams v Compair Maxam redundancy fairness factors?
Was Regulation 10 MAPLE engaged given the timing of the redundancy and the maternity leave period?
Was the claimant treated unfavourably because she was exercising the right to additional maternity leave (s.18 Equality Act 2010)?
Was there direct sex discrimination?
deep.legal_test: s.98(4) ERA 1996 reasonableness applying Williams v Compair Maxam redundancy factors; automatic unfair dismissal under s.99 ERA / reg.20 MAPLE; pregnancy/maternity discrimination under s.18 Equality Act 2010
deep.evidence_weighing: The tribunal found the redundancy process was a sham and that the unfavourable treatment was connected to the claimant exercising additional maternity leave; the dismissal did not end her maternity leave period, so the automatic unfair dismissal route under reg.20(1)(b)/(3)(b) MAPLE did not apply.
deep.reasoning: Because the dismissal did not end the maternity leave period, the prescribed-reason automatic unfair dismissal claim failed, but the tribunal found ordinary unfair dismissal and maternity discrimination made out, treating the redundancy as a sham linked to her additional maternity leave. At the remedy hearing it assessed loss, applied mitigation principles and awarded injury to feelings of £20,000 plus interest, with the total grossed up for tax to £67,801.88; the direct sex discrimination and automatic unfair dismissal claims were dismissed.
deep.award_basis: unfair dismissal and maternity discrimination remedy: loss of earnings/pension, loss of statutory rights (£500), injury to feelings (£20,000) plus interest (£6,123.86), grossed up for tax

deep.facts: Ms Cap, a Polish national employed by Socks World International as a Wholesale and Shipping Administrator from 2017, was dismissed for redundancy effective 1 April 2022. She was never given a written statement of particulars and brought claims of unfair and automatically unfair dismissal, detriment for taking time off for dependents, race harassment, direct race discrimination, indirect sex discrimination, equal pay and failure to provide written particulars.
issues: Was the dismissal for redundancy fair under s.98 ERA, including warning, consultation, selection pool and search for alternatives?
Was the principal reason for dismissal/selection that she took time off for dependents (s.99 ERA / s.57A)?
Were the discrimination, harassment, detriment and equal pay claims made out and in time?
Did the respondent fail to provide a written statement of particulars under s.1 ERA?
deep.legal_test: s.98 ERA 1996 reasonableness / band of reasonable responses in redundancy (warning, consultation, fair selection pool, alternative employment); s.99 ERA automatic unfair dismissal; s.123 Equality Act time limits; s.1/s.38 ERA written particulars
deep.evidence_weighing: The tribunal found the reason was genuinely redundancy and the principal reason was not the time off she took on 1 March 2022; but the respondent failed to warn/consult adequately and chose a pool of one when it should have included Paige Smyth. The discrimination claims were found not proved and were also some 20 months out of time.
deep.reasoning: The tribunal accepted redundancy as the genuine reason but held the procedure (no proper warning/consultation and an unreasonable pool of one) fell outside the band of reasonable responses, so the dismissal was unfair, while the automatic unfair dismissal, detriment and discrimination claims failed on the facts and/or time. It also found a breach of the s.1 duty to provide written particulars. Remedy was assessed with a 50% reduction applied to loss of earnings, pension and statutory rights, plus 4 weeks' pay (£2,176) for the written particulars failure.
deep.award_basis: unfair dismissal remedy (50% reduced): loss of earnings £10,591.90, job-seeking expenses £40, loss of pension £762.30, loss of statutory rights £250, plus 4 weeks' pay £2,176 for failure to provide written particulars

deep.facts: Ms Aldine John, an overseas-trained teacher employed by Oasis Community Learning Trust as a Cover Supervisor/Associate Teacher since 2014 and in her 50s, alleged she was treated less favourably because of her age - not being put forward for QTS, not receiving formal observations, feedback or appraisals, and being timetabled as main teacher without support. She brought claims of direct age discrimination and breach of contract; she remained employed when she presented her claim but later resigned.
issues: Did the alleged acts/omissions amount to less favourable treatment because of age under s.13 Equality Act 2010?
Were appropriate comparators in materially the same circumstances, and would a hypothetical comparator have been treated the same?
Were the complaints in time under s.123 Equality Act 2010?
Could the breach of contract claim succeed given she was still employed when the claim was presented?
deep.legal_test: Direct age discrimination under s.13 Equality Act 2010 (with s.23 comparator and s.136 burden of proof), and the s.13(2) proportionate-means justification defence for age
deep.evidence_weighing: The tribunal found several alleged facts proved (she was not put forward for QTS, lacked formal appraisals, was timetabled as main teacher) but found all cover supervisors were treated the same, the comparators were in materially different circumstances, and there was no evidence linking the treatment to age; the claimant effectively said it was age discrimination because she was off work due to discrimination, which was not relevant.
deep.reasoning: Applying s.13/s.23, the tribunal held that even where the factual allegations were proved, there was no less favourable treatment because all cover supervisors were treated identically and any difference was not because of age, so the burden never shifted. The breach of contract claim necessarily failed because she was still employed when the claim was presented (the tribunal lacks jurisdiction over a breach of contract claim while employment continues). All claims were dismissed.

cases.respondent: West Hertfordshire Teaching Hospitals NHS Trust

deep.facts: Mr Mohamed Razick, of Sri Lankan race, employed by West Hertfordshire Teaching Hospitals NHS Trust from 2014 as an Endoscopy Decontamination Technician and later Production Lead, alleged he had been subjected to multiple disciplinary processes, race/religion comments by his manager Ms Bailey, and mishandled grievances, leading him to resign. He brought claims of direct race and religion/belief discrimination, harassment, and constructive unfair dismissal.
issues: Were the discrimination and harassment complaints presented in time, and if not, was it just and equitable to extend time under s.123 Equality Act 2010?

Was the claimant constructively dismissed - did the respondent commit a repudiatory breach of contract (e.g. unfair disciplinary investigations/multiple procedures) entitling him to resign under s.95(1)(c) ERA?
deep.legal_test: s.123 Equality Act 2010 'just and equitable' extension (per Robertson v Bexley and Miller v MoJ - extension is the exception not the rule); constructive dismissal under s.95(1)(c) ERA 1996 (repudiatory breach of contract)
deep.evidence_weighing: The tribunal noted the friendly history between the claimant and Ms Bailey (he attended her wedding party, she bought a present for his son, she has mixed-race family) and that her behaviour changed after a difficult period caring for her dying mother; it found the grievance was not dismissed out of hand. It declined to extend time, finding it not just and equitable.
deep.reasoning: The discrimination and harassment claims were out of time and, applying the Robertson/Miller principles that extension is the exception, the tribunal found it not just and equitable to extend, so there was no jurisdiction and they were dismissed. On the constructive dismissal claim, it found the disciplinary and grievance handling did not amount to a repudiatory breach (the grievance was investigated, not dismissed out of hand), so the s.95(1)(c) claim failed and was dismissed.

deep.facts: Ms Sylvia Constance, who describes herself as Black British and was aged 71/72, was employed by Harpenden Mencap (a learning-disability care charity) as a part-time support worker from 2016 and dismissed on 13 June 2023. The respondent's stated reason was an irrevocable breakdown in the working relationship (some other substantial reason). She brought claims of unfair dismissal, direct race and age discrimination and victimisation.
issues: What was the reason or principal reason for dismissal, and was it a substantial reason capable of justifying dismissal?
Was the dismissal fair under s.98(4) ERA / within the band of reasonable responses?
Was the dismissal or other treatment direct race or age discrimination (s.13 Equality Act 2010) or victimisation for protected acts?
Were the discrimination/victimisation complaints in time?
deep.legal_test: s.98 ERA 1996 (some other substantial reason - breakdown in relationship - and band of reasonable responses under s.98(4)); direct discrimination under s.13 Equality Act 2010 with comparator (s.23); victimisation
deep.evidence_weighing: The tribunal found the conclusion that the working relationship had irretrievably broken down was reasonable and within the band of reasonable responses, and that a younger, white comparator would have been treated in exactly the same way; the dismissal was found to be because of the breakdown, not because of protected acts.
deep.reasoning: Applying s.98(4) and the band of reasonable responses, the tribunal held the relationship-breakdown dismissal was fair. On discrimination it found no less favourable treatment, concluding a younger white comparator would have been treated identically, and that the dismissal was a detriment but not done because of the protected acts, so victimisation failed; given those findings it did not need to decide time issues, and all claims were dismissed.

cases.respondent: West London NHS Trust and Ms E Jefferson

deep.facts: Mrs Ilda Esteves, a bank-only healthcare assistant for West London NHS Trust working flexibly across psychiatric wards, brought numerous claims against the Trust and an individual (Ms Jefferson), including direct race/age/sex discrimination, harassment on grounds of race/sex/age, victimisation, detriment for protected disclosures and unauthorised deduction of wages. A central event involved emails of 1 August 2023 alleging she had inappropriately touched a service user, plus comments by Charles Oppong.
issues: Were the various discrimination, harassment, victimisation and protected-disclosure detriment claims well founded?
Did the comments of Charles Oppong amount to harassment related to age and sex under s.26 Equality Act 2010?
Were claims in time / part of a continuing act, and was it just and equitable to extend time?
Was there an unauthorised deduction of wages?
Should an anonymity order be granted?
deep.legal_test: ss.13, 23, 26, 27 and 136 Equality Act 2010 (direct discrimination, harassment, victimisation and burden of proof); s.123 time limits; ERA protected-disclosure detriment and unauthorised deduction provisions; Vento bands for injury to feelings
deep.evidence_weighing: The tribunal found the 1 August 2023 emails were accurate and true, which defeated most claims and the anonymity application; it accepted that Charles Oppong's comments (relating to Ghanaian heritage but against her wishes) caused some injury to feelings over a short period of about two and a third months, against a background of other unconnected stressors including a parallel claim against another Trust.
deep.reasoning: The tribunal upheld only the age/sex harassment claim based on Charles Oppong's comments, placing injury to feelings at the bottom of the lower Vento band (£1,200) plus interest (£225.12), total £1,425.12, while dismissing all other discrimination, harassment, victimisation, protected-disclosure and deduction claims (largely because the underlying email allegation was found true and the other claims not made out). The anonymity order was refused because the open-justice interest outweighed her rights given the email was true.
deep.award_basis: injury to feelings (£1,200, bottom of lower Vento band) plus interest (£225.12) for age/sex harassment

deep.facts: Mrs Janice Trustram, employed by EasyJet since 2005 and latterly a Crewing Officer at Luton, was summarily dismissed on 17 August 2023 for gross misconduct after the employer concluded she had intentionally manipulated a colleague's roster dishonestly. She denied responsibility, suggesting someone else used her account, and contended the real reasons related to a previous tribunal claim, a personal injury claim, her long-term sickness/disability and a redeployment request. She brought claims of unfair dismissal, wrongful dismissal, discrimination arising from disability and victimisation.
issues: Was the reason for dismissal conduct, and did the respondent genuinely believe she committed the misconduct?
Did the respondent have reasonable grounds and a reasonable investigation, and was dismissal within the band of reasonable responses (s.98 ERA / Burchell)?
Was the unfavourable treatment because of something arising from disability (s.15 Equality Act 2010)?
Were the detriments because she had done a protected act (victimisation)?
Was she wrongfully (summarily) dismissed?
deep.legal_test: s.98 ERA 1996 with British Home Stores v Burchell (genuine belief, reasonable grounds, reasonable investigation) and band of reasonable responses; discrimination arising from disability under s.15 Equality Act 2010; wrongful dismissal (fundamental breach)
deep.evidence_weighing: The tribunal accepted the dismissing manager genuinely believed the claimant had committed gross misconduct on reasonable grounds after a reasonable investigation; although the recorded times of the roster changes were incorrect, the dates were not, and on the balance of probabilities the claimant did make the changes. It found the unfavourable treatment was not because of her sickness absence and the detriments were not because of any protected act.
deep.reasoning: Applying Burchell and the band of reasonable responses, the tribunal held the conduct dismissal fair, and any defects (incorrect change times, not reconvening the appeal) did not render the process unfair because she was not prejudiced. It found on the balance of probabilities she did make the roster changes, so she was in fundamental breach justifying summary dismissal (defeating wrongful dismissal), and the disability/victimisation claims failed because the treatment was not because of disability or protected acts. All claims were dismissed.

deep.facts: Mr Mohammed Mudashiru brought unfair dismissal and disability discrimination (including failure to make reasonable adjustments and harassment) claims against Sainsbury's Supermarkets that were presented after the primary time limits. He had been advised by Haringey Law Centre in March 2024 to wait for his internal appeal to be exhausted, and there was a roughly seven-week delay in providing his appeal outcome; he issued his claim on the day his ACAS certificate was issued. This was a preliminary hearing solely on whether the claims were in time.
issues: Was it reasonably practicable to present the unfair dismissal claim within the three-month time limit (s.111 ERA 1996)?
If not, was it presented within a reasonable further period?
Was it just and equitable to extend time for the disability discrimination, reasonable adjustments and harassment claims (s.123 Equality Act 2010)?
deep.legal_test: s.111(2)(b) ERA 1996 'not reasonably practicable' test (Palmer 'reasonably feasible', Dedman, Porter v Bandridge, reasonable ignorance of rights); s.123 Equality Act 2010 'just and equitable' extension
deep.evidence_weighing: The judge accepted the claimant reasonably relied on advice from Haringey Law Centre to await the internal appeal outcome, that the advice was probably good given the timing, that his ignorance of the time limit was reasonable, and that an unexplained seven-week delay in the appeal outcome (not his fault) pushed him out of time; he then acted reasonably in going to ACAS and issuing on the day of the certificate.
deep.reasoning: The judge found it was not reasonably practicable to present the unfair dismissal claim in time because the claimant reasonably relied on advice to exhaust the internal appeal and his ignorance of the time limit was reasonable, and he presented within a reasonable further period; for the same reasons it was just and equitable to extend time for the discrimination claims to 16 July 2024. The tribunal therefore held it had jurisdiction to hear all the claims.

cases.respondent: Total Facilities Recruitment Ltd and Clipper Contracting Group Ltd

deep.facts: Mr Grenville Dias responded to a recruitment agency (Total Facilities Recruitment, first respondent) advert for a Catering Supervisor role and was paid via an umbrella payroll company (Clipper Contracting Group, second respondent). His engagement was very short (early October 2023) and he disputed the deductions made from his pay. He brought claims of unauthorised deduction of wages, breach of contract (notice pay), holiday pay, and (not pursued) 'discrimination' and a redundancy payment.
issues: Did either respondent make unauthorised deductions from the claimant's wages contrary to s.13 ERA 1996?
Was the claimant owed notice pay / breach of contract damages or accrued holiday pay?
Could the discrimination and redundancy payment claims proceed (the latter requiring two years' continuous service)?
deep.legal_test: s.13/s.27 ERA 1996 - whether a relevant deduction was made from wages without statutory or contractual authority or written consent
deep.evidence_weighing: The judge found the second respondent had deducted employer's NICs, an apprenticeship levy and a management margin from the claimant's gross pay on behalf of the first respondent, but there was no written agreement or assignment schedule authorising those deductions, so they were unauthorised; holiday pay at the agreed 12.07% rolled-up rate was included in the calculation.
deep.reasoning: Because no written authorisation for the deductions was shown, the judge found the first respondent had made unauthorised deductions and calculated the gross sum due as £538.84 (23.5 hours x £20.46 plus 12.07% holiday pay), against which the claimant had to credit £370.89 net already paid. The remaining breach of contract (notice), holiday pay and deduction claims against both respondents were dismissed, and the discrimination and redundancy claims were dismissed (the latter for lack of two years' service and the former being unparticularised).
deep.award_basis: unauthorised deductions from wages (gross, subject to tax/NI, including 12.07% rolled-up holiday pay), with credit for £370.89 net already paid

deep.facts: Mr S Moradi Mohades, a Trainee Store Advisor at Boots employed from 2022, took controlled ADHD drugs from the pharmacy on 9 March 2023 (ingesting some and pocketing the rest) and accepted a police caution for theft; he was summarily dismissed for gross misconduct on 17 March 2023. He said his judgment was compromised by withdrawal symptoms from a medication shortage and complained the dismissal and a 15 May 2023 communication to UCL and the General Pharmaceutical Council were disability discrimination. This was a preliminary hearing on time limits and strike-out.
issues: Were the disability discrimination claims presented within the s.123 Equality Act 2010 time limit?
If not, was it just and equitable to extend time?
(Not reached) the respondent's strike-out application that the claims had no reasonable prospect of success.
deep.legal_test: s.123 Equality Act 2010 'just and equitable' extension of time (Robertson v Bexley - extension is the exception not the rule; onus on claimant)
deep.evidence_weighing: The judge considered the claimant's medical conditions (ADHD, major depressive disorder, clinical depression, possible autism, PTSD) and a psychological report, but found that he had had the ability to initiate legal proceedings and take legal advice (he had a barrister and psychologist involved during his appeal), and was aware of the May 2023 communication by 23 July 2023.
deep.reasoning: Applying the Robertson principle that a just and equitable extension is the exception and the onus is on the claimant, the judge found the disability discrimination claims (covering both the dismissal and the May 2023 communication) were out of time and that, given the claimant's capacity to take legal advice and act, it was not just and equitable to extend. The claims were dismissed for want of jurisdiction; the strike-out application did not need to be decided, and a later reconsideration application was refused.

deep.facts: Mr R J Taylor, employed by Sainsbury's from 2020 and promoted to Trading Shift Manager in 2022, has ankylosing spondylitis (a conceded disability) causing fluctuating disability-related sickness absences. He complained the respondent applied its absence management policy to him, gave him a written warning, halved his bonus, paid SSP instead of company sick pay, and failed him on probation, and that he was required to work beyond his base hours; he resigned in July 2023 (EDT 17 August 2023). He brought claims of direct disability discrimination, s.15 discrimination, failure to make reasonable adjustments, constructive unfair dismissal and unauthorised deduction of wages.
issues: Did the respondent fail to make reasonable adjustments (e.g. adapting the absence policy and ensuring he worked only base hours)?
Did the respondent discriminate arising from disability under s.15 by applying the absence policy, paying SSP, issuing a warning, halving the bonus and failing his probation?
Was there direct disability discrimination?
Was the claimant constructively unfairly dismissed (repudiatory breach he resigned in response to)?
Were there unauthorised deductions / breach of contract regarding pay?
deep.legal_test: s.13 (direct), s.15 (discrimination arising from disability - unfavourable treatment because of something arising from disability, proportionate means defence), ss.20/21 (reasonable adjustments) Equality Act 2010; constructive unfair dismissal under s.95(1)(c)/s.98 ERA 1996; s.13 ERA unauthorised deductions
deep.evidence_weighing: The tribunal found all seven of the claimant's relevant absences were disability-related and that a reasonable adjustment would have been to disregard historic absences and apply higher attendance trigger thresholds (supported by the respondent's own later acknowledgment that doubling triggers to 6% or 6 occurrences was a reasonable adjustment); the WRAP recommendations had not been fully implemented.
deep.reasoning: The tribunal held the respondent failed to make reasonable adjustments and discriminated arising from disability by routing his disability-related absences through the absence policy, warning him, halving his bonus, paying SSP and failing his probation, and that these breaches led to his constructive unfair dismissal. Direct disability discrimination was dismissed. At the remedy hearing it awarded £2,403.82 unauthorised deductions (contractual sick pay £2,145.94 plus bonus £257.88) and a basic award of £1,636.47, with constructive unfair dismissal compensation also assessed.
deep.award_basis: unauthorised deductions £2,403.82 (contractual sick pay £2,145.94 + bonus £257.88) plus unfair dismissal basic award £1,636.47 (compensatory award also assessed at remedy hearing)

deep.facts: The claimant, a part-time weekend Catering Supervisor of Arab descent and black, was employed by OCS Group at St Bernard's Hospital from 5 June 2023 and summarily dismissed on 4 August 2023 with two weeks' pay in lieu of notice, having not passed her three-month probation. She brought direct race discrimination claims, alleging that colleagues of Indian heritage and a white security staff member raised false allegations against her (including a 'hoax' about putting a towel in an oven) to engineer her dismissal. The dismissal was upheld on appeal on 19 September 2023.
issues: Did the respondent (through named colleagues and managers) carry out the alleged acts, including raising complaints and false allegations and deciding to dismiss her?
Was any such treatment less favourable treatment compared to an appropriate comparator?
If so, was the less favourable treatment because of race?
Remedy for discrimination (only if liability established)
deep.legal_test: direct race discrimination under s.13 Equality Act 2010, with comparator analysis under s.23 and the burden of proof under s.136; unreasonable conduct alone is insufficient to infer discrimination (Glasgow City Council v Zafar)
deep.evidence_weighing: The tribunal found the claimant's own further-and-better-particulars revealed long-standing antipathy toward Asian/Indian people and that her comments were 'highly offensive and racist', undermining her conspiracy theory; her perception of Indian colleagues was found to have driven the claim rather than any provable discriminatory acts by the respondent.
deep.reasoning: Applying s.136, the tribunal concluded the claimant had not proved facts from which discrimination could be inferred, finding the alleged group conspiracy to fabricate allegations unlikely and unsupported by the evidence. The claimant's own documented antipathy toward Indian colleagues explained the friction, and the dismissal during probation was not shown to be because of race, so the burden never shifted to the respondent and the claims were dismissed. A later costs order was made against the claimant and a reconsideration application was refused.

deep.facts: The claimant, a black African man employed by Clarion Housing Group as a Customer Support Officer (later Customer Accounts Specialist) since October 2014 and still employed, brought a direct race discrimination claim. He alleged that from 2021 colleagues conspired to set him up to fail by routing an excessive number of calls to him, investigated him for call-avoidance, involved individuals connected to an earlier 2019 grievance, withheld a bonus, and recorded incomplete notes. The respondent defended the claims.
issues: Were the discrimination complaints brought within the s.123 Equality Act time limit, or was there conduct extending over a period, or was it just and equitable to extend time?
Did the respondent carry out the numerous alleged acts (call routing, investigation, involvement of certain individuals, bonus withholding, note-taking, etc.)?
If so, were those acts less favourable treatment by reference to a comparator?
Was any less favourable treatment because of race?
deep.legal_test: direct race discrimination under s.13 Equality Act 2010, using a hypothetical comparator under s.23 and the s.136 burden of proof
deep.evidence_weighing: On a detailed issue-by-issue analysis, the tribunal found many alleged acts simply 'not proved', and for those that occurred it found a non-black-African comparator in the same circumstances (e.g. high volume of short calls, not informing the manager of an accepted internal job, presenting covert recordings, the bonus policy) would have been treated identically.
deep.reasoning: Taking a hypothetical comparator for each proved issue, the tribunal held that none of the treatment was less favourable because a comparator in materially identical circumstances would have been treated the same way (driven by call-handling concerns and company policy, not race). Since neither less favourable treatment nor a racial basis was established, the s.136 burden did not shift and the claims were dismissed. A subsequent respondent application for costs was itself dismissed.

reasoning_profile.disposition_summary: Gumbiti-zimuto is a credibility-centred judge with a notably high dismissal rate, who repeatedly finds claimants to be unreliable historians or to have constructed unsustainable narratives and prefers consistent, contemporaneous respondent evidence and benign explanations. He applies Burchell and the band of reasonable responses faithfully and is comfortable upholding even an arguably flawed dismissal once the employer's belief and process are reasonable. Yet he is not reflexively pro-employer: where he prefers the claimant's account he makes clear constructive-dismissal and harassment findings, and even when criticising an employer's process he assesses whether the defect was actually critical.
reasoning_profile.procedural_vs_substantive: substance-focused - the bulk of his decisions turn on credibility, the reasonableness of the employer's belief/process and discrimination causation, with status and time-limit/jurisdiction gateways used only where decisive.
reasoning_profile.evidence_approach: Credibility is decisive: he treats claimants with caution where their accounts are inconsistent, mendacious or unsupported (misremembered dates, abandoned allegations, no witness statement) and accepts respondents' consistent, document-backed evidence and benign explanations; conversely he will prefer a claimant's account and infer harassment where the respondent's evidence is weaker or documents (e.g. deleted messages) suggest impropriety.
recurring_themes: claimant credibility / 'unreliable historian' findings drive dismissals
Burchell genuine-belief and band-of-reasonable-responses applied robustly
procedural defects assessed for whether they were actually critical
discrimination causation - benign non-discriminatory explanation accepted
knowledge requirement for disability discrimination (actual/constructive)
objective construction of resignation/dismissal words (Omar)
common_legal_tests: s.98 ERA / Burchell genuine belief, reasonable investigation, band of responses (Hitt, Iceland)
constructive dismissal s.95(1)(c) (Western Excavating, Omilaju)
s.13/s.15/s.19/ss.20-21/s.26/s.27 EqA with s.136 burden and s.123 time limits
disability discrimination knowledge requirement (actual/constructive)
TUPE service-provision-change (same client, continuing activities)
Polkey reduction and employee status (Ready Mixed Concrete)
reasoning_profile.deliberation_guidance: Begin by testing the claimant's reliability against the contemporaneous record and internal consistency - look for misremembered dates, abandoned or unsustainable allegations, and missing witness statements, and treat such accounts with caution while crediting consistent, document-backed respondent evidence and benign explanations. Apply Burchell and the band of reasonable responses without substituting your own view, and where you find a procedural defect, go on to ask whether it was actually critical to the outcome. For disability discrimination, confirm the respondent had actual or constructive knowledge before finding liability. But do not default to the employer: where the claimant's account is the more probable and documents suggest impropriety, make the constructive-dismissal or harassment finding and award accordingly.

cases.respondent: Smartsec Solutions Ltd and Karter Estates Ltd

deep.facts: The claimant worked in a security/concierge role at the Central Point building in Reading from 2008 under a succession of employers, transferring to the first respondent (Smartsec) in 2016 when Helix subcontracted the building's security and concierge function to it. In January 2024 the building was sold to the second respondent (Karter Estates), a special purpose vehicle that intended to buy only the asset, not an ongoing business. The preliminary issue was whether the claimant's employment transferred to the second respondent under TUPE around January 2024.
issues: Was there a relevant transfer under TUPE of the claimant's employment from the first respondent to the second respondent around January 2024?
Specifically, was there a service provision change, requiring the client to remain the same and the activities to continue after the purchase?
deep.legal_test: whether there was a 'relevant transfer' / service provision change under TUPE (Transfer of Undertakings (Protection of Employment) Regulations 2006), requiring the same client and continuation of the activities
deep.evidence_weighing: The claimant gave no evidence and provided no witness statement; the tribunal preferred Ranjit Dharwar's consistent evidence that the second respondent did not intend to continue security/concierge services, and read Peter Wilkinson's email as merely reviewing service charges rather than committing to continue the services.
deep.reasoning: The tribunal found that the client changed because Helix (acting for Al Adan) ceased to be the client from 7 February 2024 when notice took effect, and a service provision change requires the client to remain the same. It further found the activities did not continue and ceased after 2 February 2024, and that between 5 January and 7 February 2024 the claimant remained employed and paid by the first respondent. With no continuing activities and a changed client, there was no service provision change and therefore no relevant transfer.

deep.facts: The claimant, a Delivery Postman with Royal Mail since 2002 and a clear conduct record over 21 years, was dismissed on 29 December 2023 following a fraud investigation. His driving licence and Royal Mail ID had been used to open a Royal Mail Online Business Account (OBA) in October 2020 for a company, HN Enterprise, linked to a fraudster who had previously defaulted and been rejected; the address used was connected to the claimant. Royal Mail concluded he was 'somewhat involved' in a conspiracy to commit fraud and dismissed him for conduct; he also claimed wrongful dismissal over notice pay.
issues: Was the reason for dismissal conduct, and did the respondent act reasonably in treating it as sufficient reason to dismiss?
Did the respondent hold a genuine belief in misconduct on reasonable grounds after a reasonable investigation, and was dismissal within the band of reasonable responses with a fair procedure?
Wrongful dismissal: what was the notice period, was the claimant paid for it, and was he guilty of gross misconduct?
deep.legal_test: unfair dismissal under s.98 ERA with the Burchell test (genuine belief in misconduct, reasonable grounds, reasonable investigation) and the band of reasonable responses
deep.evidence_weighing: The tribunal rejected the claimant's allegation of bias against manager Mr O'Brien, finding him a straightforward witness whose statements could be explained without partiality; it accepted the respondent's investigators acted properly on the civil (balance of probabilities) standard rather than the criminal standard.
deep.reasoning: Despite criticising the respondent for effectively putting the onus on the claimant to prove his innocence and for not weighing his 21-year clean record at the culpability stage, the tribunal held this was not critical because the other evidence justified the conclusion that he was 'somewhat involved'. Once that conclusion was properly reached, dismissal fell within the range of reasonable responses, and the tribunal found the dismissal unfair but still awarded compensation totalling £36,187.36 (basic £12,596 plus compensatory £23,591.36). A reconsideration application seeking reinstatement based on the manager's departure was later refused.
deep.award_basis: basic award (£12,596) plus compensatory award (£23,591.36) for unfair dismissal

deep.facts: The claimant was employed by Softcat plc from August 2021, becoming a Sales Development Programme Coordinator in November 2022. His manager Lucy Coates was aware he had a part-time M&S job and was studying for a diploma and asked him to be honest about any clashes. The claimant resigned from M&S and took a job at John Lewis without informing the respondent, and took annual leave to work at John Lewis without disclosing the real reason. He was dismissed for gross misconduct and brought an unfair dismissal claim, which was subject to a deposit order.
issues: Was the claimant unfairly dismissed, or was he dismissed for gross misconduct?
Did the respondent hold a genuine belief in misconduct on reasonable grounds after a reasonable investigation, and was dismissal within the band of reasonable responses?
Was the disciplinary process fair despite the line manager conducting the investigation, and whether any defect was cured on appeal?
deep.legal_test: unfair dismissal under s.98 ERA applying the Burchell test (genuine belief, reasonable grounds, reasonable investigation) and the band of reasonable responses
deep.evidence_weighing: The tribunal found the claimant's denial of deception unconvincing, noting he did not disclose the real reason for his absence yet took offence at the manager's pleasantry, and accepted the respondent's witnesses; any procedural shortcoming from the line manager investigating was cured by an independent appeal officer (Cameron Turner).
deep.reasoning: The tribunal was satisfied the respondent genuinely and reasonably believed the claimant was guilty of gross misconduct after a reasonable investigation, given his contractual obligation to disclose other employment and his lack of candour. While another employer might have handled it differently, dismissal was not outside the range of reasonable responses, and the independent appeal cured any procedural defect, so the claim was dismissed. The £100 deposit was ordered paid to the respondent under rule 40(7).

deep.facts: The claimant was a founder, statutory director, shareholder and CEO of Adaptix Limited, an early-stage pre-revenue X-ray technology company, employed from October 2014 until dismissal on 16 June 2023. There was a long-running dispute over his remuneration, including whether a £2M convertible loan note counted as 'equity investment' triggering a salary increase under letters of 31 March 2021 (as revised 6 July 2022). The respondent dismissed him for 'some other substantial reason', namely a breakdown in the employment relationship driven by his escalating and antagonistic conduct over pay; he claimed unfair dismissal and breach of contract.
issues: Breach of contract: did the claimant meet the conditions of the 31 March 2021 letter (as revised), and what did 'equity investment' mean — did the £2M convertible loan note qualify so as to trigger a pay increase?
Unfair dismissal: what was the reason or principal reason for dismissal (SOSR/breakdown in relationship)?
Did the respondent act reasonably in treating the breakdown in relationship as a sufficient reason to dismiss?
Whether the ACAS Code applied to this SOSR dismissal
deep.legal_test: unfair dismissal under s.94/s.98 ERA for 'some other substantial reason' (breakdown in relationship), with reasonableness assessed under s.98(4); applicability of the ACAS Code turning on whether the procedure was disciplinary in nature; breach of contract turning on construction of 'equity investment'
deep.evidence_weighing: The tribunal accepted the respondent's witnesses, particularly Mr Baralt's emphatic evidence that every improved pay offer was met by escalating further demands, finding the claimant's conduct increasingly aggressive and antagonistic and destructive of the working relationship; the dismissal was found to have been decided before his grievance was raised.
deep.reasoning: On the contract issue the tribunal construed the remuneration letters against the claimant, finding the convertible loan note was not the 'equity investment' that triggered a pay rise, so there was no breach. On unfair dismissal it accepted the genuine reason was an irretrievable breakdown in the relationship (SOSR) caused largely by the claimant's own escalating conduct, and that dismissing without a protracted procedure was reasonable in the circumstances; both claims were dismissed. A later reconsideration application based on new evidence was refused.

cases.respondent: Commissioner of Police of the Metropolis

deep.facts: The claimant, a serving Metropolitan Police Constable since 1997 and disabled by reason of physical impairments from two on-duty road traffic incidents, had shielded during COVID and worked exclusively from home on adjusted desk-based duties since March 2020, being declared non-deployable by Occupational Health. After restrictions eased he requested permanent home working as a reasonable adjustment; the respondent sought his return to office working at least part-time once control measures were in place, carried out a risk assessment, and warned that refusal could engage the Unsatisfactory Performance Procedure. He brought claims of direct and indirect discrimination, discrimination arising from disability, and failure to make reasonable adjustments.
issues: Were the discrimination complaints in time under s.123 Equality Act, or was there conduct extending over a period?
Was the adjustment of permanent home working (and other adjustments sought) a reasonable adjustment the respondent was required to make?
Was the respondent's treatment (requiring office attendance / risk of UPP) discrimination arising from disability or otherwise unlawful?
Were the respondent's actions a proportionate means of achieving a legitimate aim?
deep.legal_test: Equality Act 2010 claims for direct (s.13) and indirect (s.19) discrimination, discrimination arising from disability (s.15), and reasonable adjustments (s.20/21), with the justification defence of proportionate means of achieving a legitimate aim; time limits under s.123
deep.evidence_weighing: The tribunal weighed the OH evidence (claimant fit for office-based work, not too clinically vulnerable to be in a police building) and Government guidance that CEV individuals were no longer at substantially greater risk, against the claimant's anxiety about returning, and accepted the respondent's evidence about its operational nature and limited suitability for permanent home working.
deep.reasoning: Assessing reasonableness in the context of the respondent's nature, aims and operational responsibilities (an organisation not suited to home working), the tribunal held that permanent home working was not a reasonable adjustment, partly because it failed to allow for change in the claimant's condition (Ahmed). It found the respondent's actions in seeking a return to the office and exploring informal resolution were a proportionate means of achieving a legitimate aim, so the discrimination claims failed and were dismissed.

deep.facts: The claimant, employed by LHR Airports (Heathrow operator) since 2015 and a Passenger Experience Manager with a March 2022 dyslexia diagnosis, applied in October 2022 for an internal Security Operations Manager (SOM) role. He claimed he was treated less favourably in the recruitment exercise: being assigned an interview date without choice, and at a 17 December 2022 feedback meeting being told he would be a 'risk to the operation' and that he lacked leadership skills. He brought claims of direct and indirect disability discrimination, discrimination arising from disability, failure to make reasonable adjustments, and harassment.
issues: Did the respondent treat the claimant less favourably because of disability in the SOM recruitment (e.g. allocating his interview slot without choice)?
Were the feedback comments ('risk to the operation', 'lacks leadership skills') a detriment, harassment or less favourable treatment?
Was there indirect discrimination, discrimination arising from disability, or a failure to make reasonable adjustments?
deep.legal_test: Equality Act 2010 disability claims: direct discrimination (s.13, comparator under s.23), indirect (s.19), with the s.136 burden of proof applied per Igen v Wong and Madarassy v Nomura
deep.evidence_weighing: The tribunal accepted Mrs Stopa's explanation that the single interview day with allocated first/last slots was a logistical measure to guarantee candidates needing extra time received it, and found Mr Snowball's feedback comments were general/explanatory rather than derogatory or directed at the claimant's disability.
deep.reasoning: The tribunal found the allocation of a specific interview slot was not less favourable treatment but a measure to accommodate extra-time needs, and that the feedback comments were not detriments and would have been made to a non-disabled comparator in the same circumstances. With benign, non-discriminatory explanations accepted and no less favourable treatment because of disability shown, the burden of proof was not satisfied and the disability discrimination complaints were dismissed.

deep.facts: Mr Saint, a Coxswain at Aldeburgh Lifeboat Station, could not return to his role after 2021 spinal surgery and was dismissed on grounds of ill-health capability following a meeting on 27 February 2023. There was a contradiction in the respondent's documents: an email from Stephen Pope dated 3 March stated his last day was "today" (3 March), while the attached dismissal letter said his notice ran to 2 June. The claimant brought claims of unfair dismissal and disability discrimination but the respondent disputed whether they were brought in time. At the substantive final hearing the merits of all the discrimination and unfair dismissal claims were then tried.
issues: What was the effective date of termination (3 March or 2 June 2023)?
Was it reasonably practicable for the claimant to present his claims in time, and if not were they presented within a further reasonable period?
Was the dismissal for ill-health capability unfair?
Was there discrimination arising from disability under s.15 Equality Act 2010?
Was there a failure to make reasonable adjustments under s.21 Equality Act 2010?
Was there harassment related to disability under s.26 Equality Act 2010?
deep.legal_test: Time-bar: whether it was reasonably practicable to present the claim in time (s.111 ERA / s.123 EqA framework) plus a further reasonable period; on the merits (inferred) band of reasonable responses for capability dismissal and the statutory tests under ss.15, 21 and 26 Equality Act 2010.
