deep.evidence_weighing: On the jurisdiction point the judge accepted the claimant genuinely and reasonably believed 2 June was the relevant date, evidenced by his consistent prior conduct (spending his own money on advice, approaching Acas on 25 June) showing a person intent on protecting his rights.
deep.reasoning: On jurisdiction the judge held the claimant had genuinely muddled the dates and reasonably believed the relevant date was 2 June, so it was not reasonably practicable to claim in time and he acted within a further reasonable period, giving the tribunal jurisdiction. At the subsequent final hearing, however, EJ Palmer determined the substantive merits against the claimant, finding the dismissal fair and no discrimination established. All four claims (unfair dismissal, s.15, s.21 and s.26) accordingly failed and were dismissed.

deep.facts: The claimant was employed by Hammersmith Medicines Research (a clinical trials company) as an Accounts Payable Manager (later also Zahara Systems Administrator) from April 2019 until 31 May 2022. He brought claims of unfair dismissal (amended from constructive to express dismissal), discrimination arising from disability, and failure to make reasonable adjustments. The litigation featured extensive procedural disputes, including the claimant's late complaints about receiving a 1,116-page bundle versus the 2,079-page trial bundle and an unless order regarding his witness statement.
issues: Was the claimant unfairly (expressly) dismissed?
Was there discrimination arising from disability under s.15 Equality Act?
Did the respondent fail in its duty to make reasonable adjustments?
Procedural/credibility questions including whether the claimant had been provided the correct trial bundle
deep.legal_test: (inferred) unfair dismissal under s.98 ERA (band of reasonable responses), and Equality Act 2010 claims for discrimination arising from disability (s.15) and reasonable adjustments (s.20/21)
deep.evidence_weighing: The tribunal treated the claimant's account with caution, accepting the respondent's submission that he was at best an unreliable historian and at worst constructing a false narrative — citing his misrepresentations that he was involved in the Zahara purchase decision and did software engineering, and his maintained but unsustainable assault allegation.
deep.reasoning: Having found the claimant an unreliable witness and rejecting his procedural complaints (including the bundle dispute and allegations of respondent obstruction) as not assisting on the substantive issues, the tribunal concluded his complaints of unfair dismissal, discrimination arising from disability and failure to make reasonable adjustments were not well founded and dismissed them. A subsequent reconsideration application was refused for disclosing no error of fact or law.

cases.respondent: South East Coast Ambulance Service NHS Foundation Trust

deep.facts: The claimant, an Advanced Technician with South East Coast Ambulance Service from 2001 until dismissal on 5 August 2022, was disabled by bilateral neuro foraminal stenosis (a neck condition) and traumatic stress disorder. Her frontline role required manual handling, CPR and lifting, which her conditions impaired. She progressed through the Trust's Managing Health and Attendance procedure from a Stage 1 meeting in January 2020 (after 67 days' absence) through to a Stage 3 hearing, and was dismissed on ill-health capability grounds. She claimed unfair dismissal and disability discrimination, including failure to make reasonable adjustments.
issues: Was the claimant unfairly dismissed on capability/ill-health grounds, including whether a fair procedure was followed under the sickness policy?
Was there a PCP requiring full contractual duties or a certain level of attendance that placed the claimant at a substantial disadvantage?
Did the respondent fail to make reasonable adjustments (e.g. temporary administrative duties, phased return, alternative employment, more recovery time)?
deep.legal_test: (inferred) unfair dismissal under s.98 ERA for capability (reasonableness / band of reasonable responses, adequate medical evidence), and Equality Act 2010 reasonable adjustments (s.20/21) requiring a PCP, substantial disadvantage and a step that would alleviate it
deep.evidence_weighing: The tribunal found the respondent obtained proper medical advice and was not required to pursue every possible treatment avenue, and that the claimant had been clearly and repeatedly notified of the Stage 3 hearings and possible dismissal; it noted she did not apply for the alternative vacancies flagged for her.
deep.reasoning: The tribunal held the dismissal was reasonable at the time it was made given a long absence history, no diagnosis and no foreseeable return date, and that the procedure was fair with adequate notice and warnings. On adjustments it found no relevant PCP requiring full duties (the Trust considered alternatives) and that the further adjustments sought — more recovery time, alternative roles the claimant declined to apply for — had no real prospect of alleviating the disadvantage, so were not reasonable. Both the unfair dismissal and disability discrimination complaints were dismissed.

deep.facts: The claimant, a 25-year-old man (who said at the hearing he had an undisclosed Asperger's diagnosis), was employed by Bubblegum Balloons (a helium balloon retailer with a 95% female workforce) as a digital marketing executive from 2 August 2022. He alleged sex discrimination/harassment over a comment at the November 2022 Christmas party (he said a director said the awards would not go to any of the men; the respondent said an employee said 'Sorry boys' because she was about to name a female winner). He further alleged he was dismissed during a phone call between his mother and director Laura Slater in February 2023; the respondent said he was suspended on full pay pending an investigation into unexplained communications found in his work. He brought claims of unfair dismissal, age and sex discrimination, harassment, victimisation, notice pay and holiday pay.
issues: Was the claimant dismissed at all, or merely suspended pending investigation (i.e. was anything said intended to communicate dismissal)?
Did the Christmas party comment amount to sex discrimination or harassment?
Were the claims of age and sex discrimination, harassment and victimisation made out?
Was the contact with the claimant's uncle and the blocking of system access a detriment/victimisation, and were notice pay and holiday pay due?
deep.legal_test: (inferred) Equality Act 2010 claims for direct sex/age discrimination (s.13) and harassment (s.26) with the s.136 burden of proof; unfair dismissal under s.98 ERA contingent on establishing a dismissal; plus contractual notice and holiday pay claims
deep.evidence_weighing: The tribunal found the claimant's recollection flawed (e.g. wrongly placing the party at New Year's Eve) and accepted Laura Slater's evidence that she did not intend to and did not communicate any dismissal during the phone call, and that the contact with the claimant's uncle arose from investigating unexplained communications, not from his complaints.
deep.reasoning: The tribunal concluded there was no dismissal because the director neither intended nor said anything communicating dismissal — the claimant was suspended on full pay pending a genuine investigation into unexplained communications he failed to explain. It rejected the discrimination/harassment account, preferring the respondent's innocent explanation of the awards comment, and found the investigatory steps were not detriments connected to any protected act. All complaints were found not well founded and dismissed.

deep.facts: Mr Jallow, a customer assistant at an M&S store, was dismissed for gross misconduct after a colleague (CW) and others complained of sexual harassment, including an incident on 22 August 2023. The respondent investigated, held a disciplinary hearing and an appeal, all of which upheld the dismissal. The claimant contended the investigation was inadequate, that alternative accounts were not investigated, that there was no adequate notice or reasonable adjustments for his poor English/disability, and that cultural misunderstanding should have been considered.
issues: Whether the respondent followed a fair procedure in dismissing the claimant
Whether the respondent could properly conclude the claimant was guilty of gross misconduct (genuine belief on reasonable grounds after reasonable investigation)
Whether dismissal fell within the range of reasonable responses of a reasonable employer
Whether to allow the claimant's late application to amend to add wages and discrimination claims
deep.legal_test: Unfair dismissal under s.98 ERA 1996 with the band/range of reasonable responses and the Burchell test (British Home Stores v Burchell; Iceland Frozen Foods v Jones; Sainsbury's Supermarket v Hitt)
deep.evidence_weighing: The respondent's three managers (investigation, dismissal, appeal) gave live evidence; the claimant's supporting statements from colleagues were unsigned, lacked statements of truth and their makers did not attend, so they carried little weight. The tribunal accepted the respondent had carried out a thorough investigation across investigation, disciplinary and appeal stages.
deep.reasoning: The tribunal found the respondent had a genuine belief in the claimant's guilt, formed on reasonable grounds after a sufficient investigation that was repeated at the appeal stage where the appeal manager made further inquiries. The procedure followed fell within the bounds of fairness and dismissal for sexual harassment was within the range of reasonable responses. The complaint was therefore not well founded.

deep.facts: Ms Shaheen, a part-time Engagement Officer at the Home Office working with detained persons, has several disabilities (depression/anxiety, chronic back pain, RSI and foot pain) and brought claims of disability discrimination (including indirect discrimination), victimisation and harassment over the application of clear-desk/hot-desk, annualised hours and detainee-engagement practices. The respondent accepted she was disabled (save for the foot pain) and that it operated the policies, but denied the claims. The hearing ran over 12 days across April-May 2025.
issues: Whether the respondent's PCPs (clear desks/screen policy, annualised hours policy, requirement to engage detainees in far-side interview rooms) put disabled persons / the claimant at a particular disadvantage (indirect discrimination)
Whether the claimant was subjected to disability-related harassment and victimisation
Whether acts before 5 March 2024 were out of time / time should be extended
deep.legal_test: Indirect discrimination, harassment and victimisation under the Equality Act 2010, with the s.136 burden-of-proof provision; time limits under s.123 EA 2010
deep.evidence_weighing: On indirect discrimination the claimant's own evidence did not address whether the PCPs put others sharing her characteristic at a group disadvantage; the tribunal accepted she was personally disadvantaged by the clear-desk policy but her evidence did not establish the comparative group disadvantage for the annualised hours policy.
deep.reasoning: Applying the EA 2010 framework to the agreed list of issues, the tribunal found the claimant had not established the necessary elements of her claims (notably the group disadvantage required for indirect discrimination and the factual basis for harassment/victimisation), so the burden did not shift to the respondent. The complaints were accordingly not well founded and were dismissed.

deep.facts: Mrs Elmes, a Contract Performance Manager at Gigaclear, was invited while on holiday to what turned out to be a disciplinary investigation meeting, then signed off sick and, on receiving a disciplinary hearing invitation, resigned on 15 September 2022. She later tried to retract her resignation saying her judgment had been clouded by her mental health, but was told on 14 October 2022 she could not rescind it. The respondent had discovered WhatsApp messages in which the claimant was said to be disparaging about the company and to have helped team members, including apparent contact with another company.
issues: Whether the claimant was constructively (and so unfairly) dismissed under s.95(1)(c) ERA
Whether the claimant was wrongfully dismissed (breach of contract as to notice)
Whether the claimant suffered direct disability discrimination contrary to s.13 EA 2010
Whether the respondent knew the claimant's anxiety amounted to a disability at the material time
deep.legal_test: Constructive dismissal under s.95(1)(c) ERA 1996 (Western Excavating (ECC) v Sharp; Waltham Forest v Omilaju) and unfair dismissal under ss.94/98; direct discrimination under s.13 EA 2010 with the s.6 disability definition
deep.evidence_weighing: The tribunal found the respondent only learned that the claimant's history of anxiety amounted to a disability via an Occupational Health report that post-dated the relevant events, so there was no contemporaneous knowledge linking her disability to its actions.
deep.reasoning: On the direct discrimination claim the tribunal found no link between the claimant's disability and the reasons for the respondent's conduct (the respondent did not know it was a disability at the time), so that complaint failed. Having considered the Western Excavating/Omilaju principles, the tribunal also rejected the constructive and wrongful dismissal claims, concluding all surviving complaints were not well founded.

deep.facts: Ms Browne was head-hunted into a role at LAVAT Consulting (t/a PSTAX) on a £55,000 base salary plus contractual commission tied to technical campaigns, with the offer letter suggesting potential earnings of £80k plus. After her employment ended she claimed breach of contract and unauthorised deduction from wages in respect of unpaid commission. The respondent argued the claims were out of time and that any post-termination commission was not within tribunal jurisdiction.
issues: Whether any commission due under the contract was owed and unpaid at the point her employment ended
Whether the unauthorised deduction claim under s.13 ERA can cover sums falling due after employment ended
Whether the claims were presented within the applicable time limits (and whether it was reasonably practicable to present in time)
deep.legal_test: Unauthorised deduction from wages under s.13 ERA 1996 and breach of contract under the Extension of Jurisdiction Order, with the 'not reasonably practicable' time-limit test
deep.evidence_weighing: The claimant did not provide the dates on which any obligation to pay commission arose, so it was not possible to show whether any wages claim was in or out of time, and she had not shown it was not reasonably practicable to present in time.
deep.reasoning: The judge held s.13 ERA only applies while a person is in continuing employment when the payment obligation arises; sums falling due to a former employee after employment ends are recoverable only as contractual claims outside the tribunal's jurisdiction. In any event the claims were presented out of time and the claimant had not shown it was not reasonably practicable to present them in time, so the tribunal lacked jurisdiction and the claims were dismissed.

deep.facts: Mr Cole (aged 61) was a Sales Enablement Specialist at Micro Focus Software (acquired by Open Text), which triggered a harmonisation process and a new, expanded job description. He was placed on a PIP in October 2023 and a further PIP in January 2024 and dismissed for capability/performance on 27 February 2024 after failing to carry out tasks (e.g. setting up stakeholder calls and live sessions) which he said were administrative and outside his skills. He accepted he was dismissed for capability but said the PIP was unfair and used to manage him out, and that he was treated less favourably because of his age compared with younger colleagues.
issues: Whether placing the claimant on the PIPs and dismissing him was less favourable treatment because of age (direct age discrimination)
If so, whether it was a proportionate means of achieving a legitimate aim
Whether the capability dismissal was fair under s.98 ERA
Whether the respondent should have considered redeployment, voluntary redundancy or early retirement
deep.legal_test: Direct discrimination under s.13 EA 2010 with the s.136 burden-shifting test (needing 'something more' than difference in treatment and status); unfair dismissal under s.98 ERA 1996 (band of reasonable responses)
deep.evidence_weighing: The claimant did not produce evidence that there was no material difference between him and his named younger comparators, and a contemporaneous note showed he had told the manager the new job description 'sounds like him apart from the administrative side', undermining his claim that the role had been unfairly expanded; the tribunal accepted training was available.
deep.reasoning: On age discrimination the claimant failed to establish facts from which discrimination could be inferred (no 'something more' connecting the treatment to age), so the burden did not shift and the claim failed. On unfair dismissal, given the claimant's failure of and response to the PIP, it was reasonable not to offer redeployment, voluntary redundancy or early retirement, and the capability dismissal fell within the range of reasonable responses; both complaints were dismissed.

cases.respondent: Oxford University Hospital NHS Foundation Trust

deep.facts: Mr Shaba, a medical secretary at Oxford University Hospitals NHS Trust, brought two claims alleging direct race discrimination, race-related harassment, victimisation and holiday pay, including an allegation that a colleague made offensive remarks about Mr Mugabe/Zimbabwe. At the 2019 hearing the judge refused the claimant's postponement application and his application to recuse the judge (made on the basis that the judge was Zimbabwean). The respondent showed accrued holiday pay had been calculated to his last day and paid in June 2017.
issues: Whether to postpone the hearing on medical grounds
Whether the Employment Judge should recuse himself for apparent bias
Whether the 2017-claim discrimination/harassment complaints were out of time and whether it was just and equitable to extend time
Whether the direct race discrimination, harassment and victimisation complaints in the 2018 claim were well founded
Whether the claimant was owed outstanding holiday pay
deep.legal_test: Direct discrimination, harassment and victimisation under the Equality Act 2010 (with s.123 time limits and the just-and-equitable extension); Working Time Regulations holiday pay; overriding objective and Presidential Guidance for the postponement application
deep.evidence_weighing: The respondent produced documentary evidence (leaving form and pay advice report) showing accrued holiday pay had been calculated and paid in June 2017, against which the claimant gave only an unspecified assertion; the tribunal found the claim mendacious and the claimant's conduct unreasonable.
deep.reasoning: The tribunal refused the postponement (the medical note did not establish unfitness against the Presidential Guidance) and the recusal application. It found the 2017-claim complaints out of time with no basis to extend, dismissed the 2018-claim discrimination/harassment/victimisation complaints as not well founded, and rejected the holiday pay claim on the documentary evidence of payment. A later 2025 hearing dismissed the surviving matters under rule 47 when the claimant did not attend.

cases.respondent: Mr H Awad T/a Moda Cuts 5 Ladies

deep.facts: Ms Puslednik, a Polish hairdresser employed at Moda Cuts since about 2018, took leave to be with her mother who was undergoing cancer surgery in Poland. Around the same time there was an altercation between her and a new employee (Teodora Grueva) on 7 September 2022, and on 8 September the claimant sent WhatsApp messages to the business partner Edyta Skowron, including words capable of being read as resignation. The respondent contended the claimant had resigned; the claimant contended she was dismissed and brought claims of unfair dismissal, wrongful dismissal and direct disability discrimination.
issues: Whether the claimant resigned or was dismissed (construing the WhatsApp words objectively under Omar v Epping Forest)
Whether any dismissal was unfair under s.98(4) ERA
What period of notice the claimant was entitled to for the wrongful dismissal claim
Whether the claimant suffered direct disability discrimination
deep.legal_test: Objective construction of words of resignation (Omar v Epping Forest District Citizens Advice [2023] EAT 132); unfair dismissal under s.98(4) ERA 1996; wrongful dismissal (notice); direct disability discrimination under EA 2010
deep.evidence_weighing: The tribunal preferred the claimant's account, finding it more likely Edyta Skowron's deleted WhatsApp messages were inappropriate/accusatory (otherwise there was no reason to delete them) and that the claimant's voicemails showed her distressed emotional state, supporting that her apparent words of resignation were not seriously meant.
deep.reasoning: Applying the Omar objective test, the tribunal accepted the claimant used words capable of being resignation but, viewed in all the surrounding circumstances, they were not 'seriously meant' or 'really intended', so she was dismissed rather than having resigned. The dismissal was unfair and she was entitled to 4 weeks' notice; the disability discrimination complaint, however, was not well founded and was dismissed. A separate remedy judgment awarded compensation.
deep.award_basis: notice pay (£684), basic award (£1,026) and compensatory award (£171) for unfair dismissal, plus a s.38 Employment Act 2002 award (£684)

deep.facts: Mr Richardson, a Sales Advisor at LKQ Group (UK), suffered a stroke and was absent from work; his manager Mr Middlecote belatedly recorded the absences on the new 'Connect' HRIS system, which resulted in a reduction in his pay. The claimant alleged this was discrimination arising from disability (an element of punishment once the employer learned his absences would continue due to the stroke). The respondent said Middlecote simply belatedly performed his record-keeping duty and did not know the claimant was disabled at the relevant time.
issues: Whether to allow amendment to add a failure to make reasonable adjustments claim
Whether the pay reduction was unfavourable treatment because of something arising in consequence of disability (s.15 EA 2010)
Whether the respondent had actual or constructive knowledge of the claimant's disability at the relevant time
deep.legal_test: (inferred) Discrimination arising from disability under s.15 Equality Act 2010, including the knowledge requirement (no discrimination where the respondent neither knew nor could reasonably be expected to know of the disability)
deep.evidence_weighing: The tribunal found Mr Middlecote's explanation (that he was belatedly completing the Connect record he should have done earlier, prompted by the claimant's 10 October report) credible and convincing, noting it did not show him in a good light, which lent it credibility against the claimant's 'punishment' theory which lacked supporting evidence.
deep.reasoning: The tribunal concluded Mr Middlecote, through whom the respondent acted, neither had actual nor constructive knowledge of the claimant's disability at the relevant time, and accepted his credible non-discriminatory explanation for the pay entry. The discrimination arising from disability complaint was therefore not well founded and was dismissed, and the amendment application was refused.

deep.facts: Mr Polley, a dyslexic shop assistant at MPK Garages' Wallingford service station, was dismissed on 18 December 2020. He claimed he had been dismissed for making a protected disclosure / raising health and safety concerns (alleging he reported that a colleague JS, with whom he had been in a relationship, was stealing) and for disability discrimination including failure to make reasonable adjustments and a complaint about working at a till without a protective screen. The respondent denied receiving any such report from him and denied knowledge of his disability.
issues: Whether the claimant made a qualifying/protected disclosure (s.43B/s.103A ERA) and whether that was the reason for dismissal
Whether the dismissal was automatically unfair for raising health and safety concerns (s.100 ERA)
Whether the respondent failed in the duty to make reasonable adjustments and whether it had actual or constructive knowledge of his disability
Whether requiring work at a till without a protective screen put him at a substantial disadvantage
deep.legal_test: Automatically unfair dismissal for protected disclosure (s.103A ERA) and for health and safety reasons (s.100 ERA); disability discrimination under the Equality Act 2010 including the reasonable adjustments duty and its knowledge requirement
deep.evidence_weighing: The judge accepted the claimant was doing his best to be truthful despite some inconsistency attributable to his dyslexia and the passage of time, but found that without the claimant having told a fellow employee of his difficulty, the respondent could not have known of his disability; on the screen complaint he gave no evidence of substantial disadvantage.
deep.reasoning: The tribunal found the respondent had neither actual nor constructive knowledge of the claimant's dyslexia/disability at the relevant time, so the reasonable adjustments claim could not succeed, and the screen complaint failed for the additional reason that no substantial disadvantage was shown. The whistleblowing/health-and-safety and remaining disability complaints were likewise not made out, so all complaints were dismissed.

deep.facts: Mr Mogg worked for Prestige Network from October 2018 in senior roles (latterly Technology and Strategy Director) until dismissal on 14 April 2022, with the respondent contending that between August and December 2021 he was a contractor (paid £300/day via 'Pulse Consultancy') rather than an employee, breaking continuity. He claimed unfair dismissal, protected disclosure dismissal/detriment, wrongful dismissal and unlawful deduction from wages; the respondent conceded the dismissal was procedurally unfair but disputed his qualifying service and brought an employer's contract counterclaim alleging malicious acts by the claimant on 11 and 14 April. Unfair dismissal was ultimately declared by consent.
issues: Whether the claimant was an employee with continuous service during the August-December 2021 period
Whether the claimant was dismissed/subjected to detriment because of a protected disclosure (s.103A ERA)
Whether the claimant was wrongfully dismissed and whether the respondent's contract counterclaim succeeded
Whether there had been an unlawful deduction from wages
Whether compensation should be reduced for contributory fault or under Polkey
deep.legal_test: Employment status (Ready Mixed Concrete v Minister of Pensions); unfair dismissal under ss.94/98 ERA 1996; protected disclosure detriment/dismissal under s.103A ERA; unlawful deduction from wages; Polkey reduction and contributory fault
deep.evidence_weighing: Applying the Ready Mixed Concrete criteria the tribunal was satisfied the claimant was an employee in the 'consultant period' (no one else could have provided the services); it found the claimant's 11/14 April conduct was malicious, but that this only emerged later and there was no evidence the respondent suffered a pecuniary loss on its counterclaim.
deep.reasoning: The tribunal found continuity of employment was preserved (he was an employee throughout), so he had the right to claim unfair dismissal, which was conceded as procedurally unfair. The whistleblowing claims failed (no protected disclosure was made at the 28 March 2022 meeting). It made no deduction for contributory fault because the malicious conduct only came to light after dismissal, but applied a 100% Polkey reduction holding that a fair procedure would have uncovered the malicious acts and led inevitably to dismissal; the employer's counterclaim failed for want of proven pecuniary loss.
deep.award_basis: unlawful deduction from wages (£3,408.64 net) plus unfair dismissal basic award (£2,569.50), compensatory award (£4,406.55) and a s.207A TULRCA uplift (£781.52); wrongful dismissal claim and employer's counterclaim dismissed

deep.facts: Mr Perez Vargas was promoted to joint Head Chef at The Wild Pot and was even in partnership discussions, but after his fellow chef 'Wolf' resigned the kitchen was left short-staffed and covers were reduced, creating extra pressure. He claimed he was constructively dismissed and brought complaints of direct race and sexual orientation discrimination and related harassment, including conduct by Mr Rockcliff who approached him on 7 August 2022 on his way home and at his home, and a later social media post about chefs with 'sautéed egos'. The respondent disputed his account.
issues: Whether the claimant was constructively (and unfairly) dismissed under s.95(1)(c) ERA
Whether he suffered direct race and sexual orientation discrimination
Whether he was subjected to harassment related to race and to sexual orientation
Entitlement to notice pay (wrongful dismissal), holiday pay and unpaid wages
deep.legal_test: Constructive unfair dismissal under s.95(1)(c) ERA 1996 (Western Excavating principles); direct discrimination and harassment under the Equality Act 2010 (harassment: unwanted conduct related to a protected characteristic violating dignity/creating a hostile environment, judged with regard to the claimant's perception and reasonableness)
deep.evidence_weighing: The tribunal preferred the claimant's account over Mr Rockcliff's, finding it more likely than not the complained-of conduct occurred as the claimant described; Mr Rockcliff conceded an act might be viewed as vindictive and the tribunal found the social media post would reasonably be understood as referring to the claimant.
deep.reasoning: Accepting the claimant's version, the tribunal found Mr Rockcliff's 7 August conduct was unwanted, violated the claimant's dignity and created a hostile/humiliating environment, and was related to race and (via references to harassing male staff) sexual orientation, so the harassment claims succeeded and amounted to a constructive (unfair) dismissal. The direct discrimination claims were not made out and were dismissed. Compensation including injury to feelings was awarded.
deep.award_basis: unfair dismissal basic award (£1,142) and compensatory award (loss of statutory rights £500 and post-notice loss of earnings £2,073.28), breach of contract notice pay (£3,109.92), accrued holiday pay (£663.32), unpaid wages (£303.04 and £518.32) and injury to feelings for harassment (£11,000) plus interest (£1,134.36)

cases.respondent: The Chancellor Masters and Scholars of University of Oxford

deep.facts: Dr Czeh-Bhardwaj (part Hungarian, part German), a CRUK Clinical Scientist Fellow hosted at Oxford's WIMM whose salary was paid from her Fellowship award, complained she had been paid since 2017 at a lower point on the clinical pay scale (E64) than her experience warranted, and that her German Certificate of Completion of Training (CCT) was treated as less than equivalent to NHS consultant training. The plan had been for her to start in a post-CCT clinical fellow capacity (grade E64.9) and move to consultant grade (E82) once the NHS provided a consultant post. She brought direct and indirect race (nationality) discrimination and unlawful deduction from wages claims; the respondent said she was paid her contractual entitlement.
issues: Whether the respondent subjected the claimant to direct race discrimination by paying her on a lower salary point (E64) than her experience could expect
Whether treating the German CCT as less than equivalent to NHS consultant training/experience was a PCP causing group disadvantage (indirect race discrimination)
Whether wages 'properly payable' were at NHS consultant level (~£80,000) such that there was an unlawful deduction
Whether to allow late amendments adding two further direct discrimination allegations
Time limits under s.123 EA 2010
deep.legal_test: Direct discrimination (s.13 EA 2010 - no material difference between comparators), indirect discrimination (PCP and group disadvantage), the s.136 burden-of-proof provision (Igen v Wong; Madarassy v Nomura), time limits under s.123, and unlawful deduction from wages (wages 'properly payable')
deep.evidence_weighing: Contemporaneous correspondence showed it had been agreed and understood that the claimant would start on grade E64.9 for an initial 12-18 month transition period and move to consultant grade E82 only once the OUH NHS provided a consultant post, supporting the respondent's case that she was paid her contractual entitlement.
deep.reasoning: The tribunal refused the late amendment (new last-minute allegations not in the claim forms) and, applying the Equality Act framework, found the claimant's contractual pay was as agreed in the documented arrangement (E64 pending a consultant post), so the wages claim failed because consultant-level pay was not 'properly payable'. The claimant did not establish facts from which direct or indirect nationality discrimination could be inferred, so those complaints were not well founded and were dismissed.

reasoning_profile.disposition_summary: Burns J is a merits-driven, claimant-receptive judge with a notably high rate of claimant wins, particularly in unfair-dismissal and TUPE cases where contemporaneous documents expose predetermined or sham decisions. He is decisive on liability but disciplined and unsentimental on remedy, regularly cutting awards for failure to mitigate, contributory fault or Polkey/affirmation. Where the evidence favours the employer (genuine misconduct, breakdown of trust, no employee status) he dismisses firmly.
reasoning_profile.procedural_vs_substantive: substance-focused - he overwhelmingly decides on the factual merits and the reasonableness/genuineness of the employer's process and decision, reserving time-bar and status thresholds for the minority of cases where they are determinative.
reasoning_profile.evidence_approach: He gives decisive weight to contemporaneous documents (emails, WhatsApp, payslips, texts) and treats them as 'particularly telling', especially where they contradict oral evidence or reveal a predetermined outcome; he discounts witnesses who do not attend for cross-examination and notes the absence of contemporaneous support against the party who should have it.
recurring_themes: contemporaneous documents are decisive, especially on predetermined/sham dismissals
rigorous Burchell band-of-reasonable-responses analysis
disciplined remedy: mitigation, contributory fault, Polkey, ACAS uplift
trust-and-confidence / constructive dismissal scrutiny
burden does not shift on discrimination without a proven foundational fact
real-substance approach to employee/worker status and TUPE (Autoclenz, multifactorial)
common_legal_tests: s.98(4) ERA reasonableness and band of reasonable responses (Burchell, Madden)
constructive dismissal - fundamental breach of trust and confidence
TUPE reg.3 service-provision-change / multifactorial transfer test
s.136 EqA burden of proof
Polkey, mitigation and s.207A ACAS uplift on remedy
employee/worker status (Ready Mixed Concrete, Autoclenz)
reasoning_profile.deliberation_guidance: Build your view from the contemporaneous record first - emails, texts, payslips - and ask whether the documents reveal the employer's true reason and whether the decision was made before any consultation or process (a sham). Apply Burchell and the band of reasonable responses without substituting your own view, but be willing to find for the claimant where the process was predetermined or absent. On discrimination, do not let the burden shift until a foundational fact is proved. Then turn to remedy with discipline: scrutinise mitigation evidence, consider Polkey and contributory fault, and do not award ongoing loss the claimant has not substantiated.

deep.facts: Mrs Woodhead, a long-serving NHS administrator (15 years, aged 58, working 18 hours/week near minimum wage), resigned and claimed constructive unfair dismissal and wrongful dismissal. Her resignation followed a team meeting on 25/4/2024 convened by manager Ms Sloper to address communication problems, during which the Claimant felt singled out, publicly accused of 'ganging up', and subjected to sarcastic and inappropriate comments. The Respondent's own grievance investigation (by Ms Stevens) found she was justifiably aggrieved, but her appeal was dismissed.
issues: Was there a fundamental/repudiatory breach of the implied term of trust and confidence?
Did the Claimant resign in response to that breach rather than for an unconnected reason?
Did the Claimant affirm the contract before resigning?
What remedy is appropriate, including whether the Claimant failed to mitigate her loss?
deep.legal_test: Constructive dismissal: fundamental breach of the implied term of trust and confidence (conduct without reasonable and proper cause calculated or likely to destroy/seriously damage the relationship), causation, and absence of affirmation
deep.evidence_weighing: Although the Claimant's accounts of the meeting were inconsistent in places and she was found to be at least partly to blame for poor team relations, the judge accepted the Respondent's own grievance findings that the conduct at the 25/4/2024 meeting (public singling-out, accusing her of ganging up, sarcastic comments) was genuinely aggrieving. On remedy, the Claimant's total failure to produce any evidence of job applications was decisive in finding she had not mitigated.
deep.reasoning: The judge found that Ms Sloper's public and unfair conduct at the meeting, accepted by the Respondent's own grievance process as wrongful, amounted to a breach of trust and confidence with no reasonable cause, which the Claimant resigned in response to without affirming. The claims therefore succeeded. However, because she failed to take reasonable steps to mitigate (no documented job applications), the judge awarded notice pay, basic award, loss of statutory rights and notice-period pension loss only, declining to award ongoing loss of earnings or holiday pay.
deep.award_basis: notice pay (wrongful dismissal) plus basic award, loss of statutory rights and notice-period pension loss for unfair (constructive) dismissal

deep.facts: Miss Kolaniak was employed by Nice Systems UK as Information Security Compliance Manager and dismissed on 4 December 2024, the Respondent contending the reason was redundancy. A US-based HR director (Ms Lanaido), described as unfamiliar with UK redundancy law, sent emails in October 2024 directing that the Claimant be 'released', and her work (e.g. a Prague audit) was removed around that time. A consultation process followed but the employer did not contact anyone on the information-security personnel list to seek alternative roles and proceeded with the final meeting in her absence.
issues: Was there a genuine redundancy situation and was redundancy the reason for dismissal?
Was placing the Claimant in a pool of one within the band of reasonable responses?
Was the consultation genuine, or had the decision to dismiss been taken before consultation began?
Was the handling of the grievance/Speak-up complaint and proceeding in her absence reasonable?
Remedy, including contributory fault and recoupment.
deep.legal_test: Redundancy under s.139(1) ERA 1996 and fairness under s.98(4) ERA (band of reasonable responses), with consideration of whether dismissal was predetermined
deep.evidence_weighing: The contemporaneous emails from Ms Lanaido (9 and 16 October 2024) using firm 'release' language, together with the removal of the Claimant's duties before consultation, were 'particularly telling' and led the judge to conclude the dismissal decision had been made before consultation started.
deep.reasoning: The judge accepted there was a genuine redundancy and that the pool of one, grievance handling and proceeding in absence were all within the range of reasonable responses. However, because the emails and removal of duties showed the dismissal had been decided before consultation, the consultation was a sham and the dismissal was unfair. He reduced the compensatory award by 35% for contributory fault.
deep.award_basis: compensatory award for unfair dismissal (loss of salary, pension, statutory rights, bonus, lower earnings) less PILON and 35% contributory fault; basic award nil due to redundancy payment received

cases.respondent: AAA Properties Group Ltd T/a Servicemaster and The Enquire Learning Trust T/a Elliston Primary Academy

deep.facts: The Claimant, a cleaner, worked almost exclusively (98% of her time) at Elliston Primary Academy as an employee of the First Respondent (R1, ServiceMaster). In May 2024 R1 lost the cleaning contract and R2 (The Enquire Learning Trust) took the cleaning back in house from 7/8/2024, taking on one of the five R1 cleaners (Paula) but not the Claimant. R2 filed no response and did not appear. The Claimant claimed TUPE applied and that R2 had unfairly dismissed her by refusing to recognise her as its employee.
issues: Was there a TUPE transfer of an economic entity (the cleaning at the academy) from R1 to R2?
Was the Claimant assigned to the transferred undertaking?
Did R2 dismiss the Claimant and was the dismissal automatically unfair as transfer-related?
What remedy, including mitigation and ACAS uplift?
Should the claim against R1 be dismissed?
deep.legal_test: TUPE Regulations 2006 reg.3(1)(a): whether an economic entity retaining its identity transferred (multifactorial approach), assignment of the employee, and automatic unfair dismissal where the transfer is the reason for dismissal
deep.evidence_weighing: Payslips showing work location plus the evidence of the Claimant and R1's regional manager Ms Dutton confirmed she spent 98% of her time at the academy, establishing she was part of an organised grouping assigned to the transferred cleaning activity. Lack of any procedure by R2 and limited mitigation evidence (no CV produced, only one job-application email) shaped the remedy.
deep.reasoning: Applying the multifactorial test, the judge found an organised grouping of R1 employees dedicated to cleaning at the academy and that the same activity continued after 7/8/2024, so a service-provision-change TUPE transfer occurred and the Claimant was assigned to it. She therefore automatically became R2's employee; R2's refusal to recognise her was a transfer-related, automatically unfair dismissal with no procedure (warranting a 25% ACAS uplift). The claim against R1 was dismissed because the Claimant had transferred away from it. Loss of earnings was limited to 26 weeks for failure to fully mitigate.
deep.award_basis: unfair dismissal basic award plus compensatory award (loss of statutory rights and 26 weeks' loss of earnings) with 25% ACAS uplift, against R2

deep.facts: Ms Sulman, a Transport Supervisor of Black/relevant ethnicity, resigned on 16/4/2024 and claimed constructive unfair dismissal, direct race discrimination, harassment related to race and religion, and victimisation. Her relationship with management deteriorated after a new assertive MD (Mr Turner) arrived in July 2023, and she was described by multiple managers and an independent trainer as curt, rude and combative. The alleged 'last straw' was Mr Hussein accessing her computer and making errors on a driver's timesheet while she was on leave on 12 April 2024, following her 27 February 2024 grievance (an accepted protected act).
issues: Was there a fundamental breach of the implied term of trust and confidence (including the alleged 'last straw')?
Did the Claimant affirm the contract before resigning?
Were the pleaded acts direct race discrimination?
Did the pleaded conduct amount to harassment related to race and/or religion?
Was the Claimant subjected to detriment because of her protected act (victimisation)?
Were any complaints out of time?
deep.legal_test: Constructive dismissal (fundamental breach of trust and confidence, objective test); direct discrimination s.13, harassment s.26 and victimisation s.27 Equality Act 2010 with burden of proof under s.136
deep.evidence_weighing: The judge found the Claimant generally truthful but with exceptions (recording conversations, password handling), and found her witness Ms Parpa largely relayed only what the Claimant told her. The Respondent's consistent evidence, corroborated by an independent third-party trainer, that the Claimant's conduct was rude and combative was accepted without hesitation.
deep.reasoning: The text shows the judge accepted the Respondent's account that the Claimant's own poor conduct and the personality clash with the new MD, rather than any breach by the employer, underlay the deterioration, and the Equality Act claims lacked the character/connection to protected characteristics needed. On that basis the constructive dismissal and discrimination, harassment and victimisation claims were all dismissed.

deep.facts: Mr Tasyurdu, a Corporate Security Officer describing himself as White Turkish Kurd and aged 59, brought claims of direct age and race discrimination, harassment, and unlawful deduction from wages (4 days' pay in December 2023) against Mitie. The core of the case was his poor relationship with a younger black Ghanaian-born shift manager, Mr Boasiakoh (KB), whom he alleged abused his authority to favour some and disadvantage others. He alleged KB had told him he was 'too old for the job' in June 2022, but a victimisation claim based on this was not permitted to be added.
issues: Did KB make the alleged ageist remarks so as to shift the burden of proof?
Was the Claimant subjected to direct discrimination because of age or race (s.13)?
Did the alleged conduct amount to harassment related to age or race (s.26)?
Was there an unauthorised deduction from wages for 4 days' pay?
deep.legal_test: Direct discrimination s.13, harassment s.26 and burden of proof s.136 Equality Act 2010; unauthorised deduction from wages under ERA 1996
deep.evidence_weighing: The judge found the key allegation of ageist comments unproven: they were denied by KB, denied by Mr Patten (whom the Claimant accepted was honest and to whom he claimed to have reported them), not referred to by his own witnesses, and absent from his original ET1. He preferred KB's account of the post-leaving incident, finding the Claimant was argumentative and refused to engage.
deep.reasoning: Because the foundational ageist-remark allegation was not proved, the burden did not shift to the Respondent and the otherwise race/age-neutral incidents (e.g. the final written warning for leaving his post) showed no connection to a protected characteristic. The judge found KB was simply doing his job; despite misgivings that he had not got to the bottom of the workplace dynamics, he made no positive finding of discrimination and dismissed all claims, including the wages claim.

deep.facts: The Claimant (anonymised as X), employed as Head of Development at Bupa Cromwell Hospital from January 2024, was dismissed at the end of her probation on 19 April 2024 (effective 26 April 2024). She claimed detriment for protected disclosures, automatic unfair dismissal, harassment related to disability, and failure to make reasonable adjustments, relying on a long-term foot impairment and musculoskeletal injuries from a cycling accident on 20/2/2024. Her contract named the hospital as her base with possible travel to other sites including HSK about a mile away.
issues: Did the Claimant make qualifying protected disclosures in the reasonable public-interest belief?
Was she subjected to detriment or dismissed because of any protected disclosure?
Was she disabled within s.6 Equality Act (foot impairment and/or cycling-accident injuries)?
Did any conduct amount to harassment related to disability or a failure to make reasonable adjustments?
deep.legal_test: Protected disclosure / detriment under ss.43B, 47B and automatic unfair dismissal under s.103A ERA 1996 (Chesterton v Nurmohamed public-interest test; causation); disability definition s.6 and harassment/reasonable adjustments under the Equality Act 2010
deep.evidence_weighing: The judge noted there was no contemporaneous documentation supporting much of the Claimant's case, despite both she and her manager being the type to record important matters and despite a personal diary being in the bundle. On disability, medical evidence (GP and orthopaedic surgeon) indicated the cycling injuries would resolve within months, and no objective evidence showed a likely 12-month duration.
deep.reasoning: The judge found the Claimant was not disabled: her foot impairment had no substantial adverse effect on day-to-day activities at the relevant time, and the cycling-accident injuries were not shown likely to last 12 months. With the disability claims failing on the threshold and the protected-disclosure case lacking contemporaneous support, the claims were dismissed.

deep.facts: Mrs Gwiazda, employed by Royal Mail, requested unpaid parental leave for two weeks in August 2024 (notice given 19 February 2024). Royal Mail failed to serve a counternotice within 7 days as required, and refused/postponed the leave; she ultimately used annual leave to take a three-week trip to Poland. She withdrew her sex discrimination claim, and by consent it was declared that the employer unreasonably postponed/prevented her parental leave under s.80 ERA 1996. A separate remedy hearing (before EJ Clark) determined compensation.
issues: Was the s.80 ERA parental leave complaint well founded (decided by consent)?
What compensation is just and equitable under s.80(4) ERA?
Does the Tribunal have power to award injury to feelings, personal injury, aggravated damages or an ACAS uplift for this type of claim?
deep.legal_test: Compensation under s.80(4) ERA 1996 (just and equitable having regard to the employer's behaviour and loss attributable), informed by Working Time Regs reg.30 approach (Miles v Linkage); no injury to feelings/aggravated damages or ACAS uplift available outside Schedule A2 jurisdictions
deep.evidence_weighing: The Tribunal accepted that the Claimant was taking the Poland trip regardless of the leave decision (so no direct financial loss such as childcare), and that the dispute contributed to a decline in her mental health, but legal analysis (Santos, Dunnachie, TULRCA Schedule A2) confined the available remedy.
deep.reasoning: Liability was established by consent before EJ Burns. At the remedy hearing EJ Clark held that injury to feelings, personal injury, aggravated damages and an ACAS uplift were not available for a s.80(4) parental-leave claim, so the £219,412.50 claimed could not be awarded. Treating the breach as a single act of preventing two weeks' leave and benchmarking against comparable regulatory defaults, the Tribunal awarded a proportionate just-and-equitable sum of £3,700.77.
deep.award_basis: just and equitable compensation under s.80(4) ERA 1996 for unreasonable postponement/prevention of two weeks' parental leave

deep.facts: Mr Osokin was employed by Moss and Coleman Solicitors from December 2020 to 31 January 2025 under a contract entitling him to a bonus of 10% of fees billed and recovered above a fee target. He claimed an unpaid contractual bonus for 2024 as an unlawful deduction from wages under s.13 ERA 1996; the respondent paid £4,500 but disputed the balance, arguing the bonus calculation was too complex to be a wages claim. The respondent had previously paid his 2022 bonus in January 2023, supporting the claimant's expectation of January 2025 payment. The respondent's conditional counterclaim was withdrawn after the claimant confirmed he had not brought a contract claim.
issues: Did the tribunal have jurisdiction over the bonus claim as an unlawful deduction from wages under s.13 ERA, or was it too complex/unquantified to be a wages claim?
Had the claimant identified a significant, identifiable sum that was properly payable?
What sum, if any, was due?
deep.legal_test: Whether there was an unlawful deduction from wages under s.13 ERA 1996 (wages defined in s.27 to include a bonus), applying Coors Brewers Ltd v Adcock [2007] IRLR 440 on whether a significant, identifiable/quantified sum exists rather than a matter requiring detailed investigation.
deep.evidence_weighing: The judge regarded the claimant's evidence and figures as the most reliable and best evidence of his entitlement, and found the respondent had failed to show they were inaccurate, treating the respondent's late-raised difficulties and excuses as unpersuasive.
deep.reasoning: The judge rejected the respondent's submission that the claim was too complicated to be a wages claim, noting the respondent had drafted the contract, offered no answers to its own claimed ambiguities, and was effectively seeking an open-ended right to keep reassessing. Applying Coors, the claimant had identified a significant, quantified sum due by end of January 2025, so the s.13 claim succeeded in the amount of £4,660.20 gross (£9,160.20 less the £4,500 already paid), payable net of tax and NI; interest and consequential losses were not awardable.
deep.award_basis: Unpaid contractual bonus as unlawful deduction from wages (gross, less tax/NI)

deep.facts: Miss Emmons, who describes herself as Black British Caribbean, was a retail store manager at Krispy Kreme's Bromley store and was dismissed on 20 February 2024. She had a history of performance and conduct concerns, a PIP she did not engage with, and was suspended on 10 November 2023 to investigate allegations of racist language and drug dealing. The investigation did not corroborate those allegations but uncovered breaches of Natasha's Law food-safety protocols, falsified audits, ignored rota instructions and poor timekeeping, leading to dismissal for gross misconduct. She claimed unfair dismissal, notice pay, direct race discrimination and harassment related to race.
issues: Was the dismissal for misconduct fair under s.98(4) ERA (genuine belief on reasonable grounds after reasonable investigation)?
Was the Claimant entitled to notice pay?
Did the matters relied on constitute direct race discrimination (s.13)?
Did the conduct amount to harassment related to race (s.26)?
deep.legal_test: Unfair dismissal: band of reasonable responses with Burchell (BHS v Burchell) and HSBC v Madden; direct discrimination s.13, harassment s.26 and burden of proof s.136 Equality Act 2010
deep.evidence_weighing: The investigation (Ms Saha) found no support for the racist-language or drug-dealing allegations but did find a photographed Natasha's Law breach (misplaced tongs, prepacked TGTG boxes), a false audit, ignored rota instructions and admitted lateness; the Claimant showed confusion about protocols and no remorse over an offensive audio message. The tribunal accepted Ms Adamova would have treated a differently-raced comparator the same way.
deep.reasoning: The tribunal found the employer held a genuine belief in misconduct on reasonable grounds after a reasonable investigation, and dismissal fell within the band of reasonable responses, so the unfair dismissal and notice claims failed. On discrimination, the Claimant failed to show a prima facie case of less favourable treatment because of race, and the matters complained of did not relate to race for harassment purposes, so the Equality Act claims were dismissed.

deep.facts: Ms Willis, formerly Head of Operational Continuity in Resolution at NatWest, had previously won a disability discrimination claim against the bank (the 'former claim'). She later applied for a new 'Operational Resilience Lead' role and was not called to interview, which she alleged was victimisation because of her former claim (a protected act). The bank's case was that the hiring manager Ms Morris wanted someone with proven recent UK experience implementing the Operational Resilience rules ahead of a March 2025 compliance deadline, and the Claimant's CV did not show sufficient such experience.
issues: Was the Claimant subjected to a detriment (not being interviewed) because of the protected act?
Did the recruiter (Ms Rafter) promise her an interview, and did the decision-maker (Ms Morris) act because of the protected act?
Had the Claimant adduced facts shifting the burden of proof under s.136?
deep.legal_test: Victimisation under s.27 Equality Act 2010 with burden of proof under s.136
deep.evidence_weighing: The judge accepted Ms Rafter did not know the Claimant or the former claim and had not promised an interview, and accepted Ms Morris's evidence that she did not recognise/remember the Claimant's name when reviewing the CV. The non-discriminatory explanation was corroborated by contemporary documents (the contracting call template, job description, CV and Ms Morris's 19/3/24 email).
deep.reasoning: The judge found the Claimant had not adduced facts to shift the burden of proof, and in any event accepted the Respondent's genuine non-discriminatory reason - that the role demanded proven recent UK Operational Resilience implementation experience which the CV did not demonstrate - so the failure to interview was not because of the protected act. The victimisation claim was dismissed.

cases.respondent: Gloucester Care Services Ltd T/a Caremark Cheltenham Gloucester and Tewkesbury

deep.facts: Ms Lamptey was a Domiciliary Care Assistant employed from 6/9/2022 on a Health and Care Worker Visa, providing care visits in clients' homes and driving her own car between them. She was not paid for travel time getting to and from work or properly for hours worked, which she complained about; the issue was unresolved when she resigned on 4/11/24 and she claimed constructive unfair dismissal, arrears of pay, holiday pay, breach of contract and other payments (including a visa-fee refund and an unpaid bonus/DBS refund). The employment contracts were silent on whether driving time was paid working time.
issues: Was driving/travel time payable working time, giving rise to arrears of pay/NMW shortfalls?
Was the Claimant constructively unfairly dismissed by the failure to pay her properly?
Was she owed holiday pay, a visa-fee refund and the £280 bonus/DBS refund?
Should an award be made under s.38 Employment Act 2002 for failure to provide accurate written particulars?
deep.legal_test: Unauthorised deduction from wages / breach of contract for arrears and holiday pay; constructive unfair dismissal (fundamental breach of trust and confidence); s.38 Employment Act 2002 award for inaccurate written statement of terms
deep.evidence_weighing: It was agreed the Claimant was unpaid for getting to/from work, and the various contract versions were all silent on driving/working time, evidenced by her unanswered 7/11/22 email seeking clarification. On the bonus/DBS refund the employer (Mr Folkes) could produce no payslip or document proving payment, so the judge was not satisfied it was paid.
deep.reasoning: The judge found the Claimant was not paid properly for her hours and that failing to pay an employee, unresolved by resignation, breached trust and confidence so the constructive unfair dismissal claim succeeded. The arrears, holiday pay, visa refund and £280 bonus/DBS claims succeeded as a series of unauthorised deductions or contractual sums on termination. Because the written particulars were defective regarding basic remuneration matters (and unilaterally amended, including a late £3,000 clause), he awarded the maximum 4 weeks' pay under s.38, given the impact on vulnerable workers.
deep.award_basis: arrears of wages, holiday pay, visa refund, bonus/DBS refund, unfair dismissal basic and compensatory awards plus loss of statutory rights, and a 4-week s.38 Employment Act 2002 award

deep.facts: Ms Lam, a qualified accountant, was employed from 1/8/2020 as managing director of the Respondent FCA-regulated investment firm (formerly GWM London Ltd, acquired by DSAM in June 2023). She was summarily dismissed for misconduct relating to her involvement in facilitating unlawful 'introducer payments' to third parties for client introductions, contrary to MiFID II/FCA inducement rules, including approving payments to personal accounts with fraudulent descriptions and allegedly withholding information during the acquisition due diligence. She claimed unfair dismissal and wrongful dismissal.
issues: Was misconduct the genuine reason for dismissal?
Did the employer have reasonable grounds for its belief after a reasonable investigation, and was dismissal within the band of reasonable responses (unfair dismissal)?
Was the Claimant in fundamental breach of contract entitling the employer to dismiss summarily (wrongful dismissal)?
Were the Claimant's alternative explanations (cost-saving motive; hypocrisy over a £45,000 payment; prior knowledge by Mr Morjaria) made out?
deep.legal_test: Unfair dismissal: misconduct under s.98(4) ERA with Burchell (BHS v Burchell) genuine belief on reasonable grounds after reasonable investigation, and band of reasonable responses (HSBC v Madden); wrongful dismissal: whether the Claimant was in fundamental/repudiatory breach justifying summary dismissal
deep.evidence_weighing: The judge accepted Mr Morjaria's and (compelled witness) Mr Ahmedi's evidence that introducer payments were knowingly disguised to evade regulation and that the Claimant, though junior to Ahmedi and in a difficult position, was knowingly involved and approved payments. He rejected the Claimant's suggestions of a cost-saving motive (no June/July 2023 restructure occurred) and that the £45,000 Regis Capital payment was improper (it was contractual).
deep.reasoning: As a qualified accountant in a senior compliance role, the Claimant had a duty to oppose the unlawful introducer payments, put concerns in writing and refuse to make them, but she failed to do so. The judge found on the balance of probabilities that she was in fundamental breach of her employment contract, so the Respondent was entitled to dismiss summarily; both the unfair dismissal and wrongful dismissal claims failed.

deep.facts: The claimant was employed at a Hatton Garden diamond trader, latterly as Operations Logistics Manager, from February 2022 until 12 July 2024. On that date, with no prior warning, she was called into a meeting one hour before the end of her shift and told her role was being made redundant with immediate effect, and was asked to leave. The employer characterised this as part of a global review of team structure, but the decision had already been made before the meeting, and no genuine consultation or appeal hearing took place.
issues: Whether the dismissal was by reason of redundancy under s.139(1) ERA 1996
Whether the employer acted reasonably under s.98(4) ERA 1996 in dismissing without warning, consultation or a fair procedure
Whether the claimant failed to mitigate her loss
Whether an award was due under s.38 Employment Act 2002 for failure to provide updated written particulars
deep.legal_test: Unfair dismissal: whether redundancy was a potentially fair reason under s.98(1)-(2) ERA 1996 and whether the employer acted reasonably under s.98(4), including the requirement to warn and consult in redundancy
deep.evidence_weighing: The judge gave less weight to the three respondent witnesses who served statements but failed to attend for cross-examination, and relied on Mr Mendieta's own statement, which confirmed the redundancy decision had been made before the 12 July meeting, demonstrating the absence of consultation.
deep.reasoning: The judge accepted redundancy as the reason but found the employer had pre-determined the decision and dismissed the claimant on the spot with no warning, no consultation and no real appeal, so it fell outside the band of reasonable responses required by s.98(4). Having found the dismissal unfair, the judge assessed remedy, finding the claimant a hard-working person who would have found work if fit, and that the employer had not shown a failure to mitigate. He awarded loss of earnings over an 8-month period plus pension loss, basic award shortfall, loss of statutory rights and a s.38 award.
deep.award_basis: unfair dismissal: basic award shortfall, compensatory award (8 months' loss of earnings), pension loss, loss of statutory rights, plus s.38 Employment Act 2002 award for failure to provide updated written particulars

cases.claimant: Mr S Haberfield and Mr K Bond

deep.facts: Two brothers-in-arms (brothers to the owner's brother), both over 55, were employed by a small railway drainage services company. After returning in 2021 they were assured they would not be required to work weekends regularly, though they helped out occasionally. When they declined weekend work in September 2024, the operations manager Mr Brier dismissed Mr Haberfield summarily and Mr K Bond on one week's notice by text message. The employer initially admitted dismissal in its ET3 but later sought to argue the claimants had resigned.
issues: Whether the claimants were dismissed or resigned
Whether there was an enforceable contractual obligation to work weekends
Whether dismissal for refusing weekend work was fair under s.98(4) ERA 1996 (misconduct)
Whether the ACAS Code was breached, justifying an uplift
Whether a s.38 Employment Act 2002 award was due for failure to provide written particulars
Quantum and mitigation of loss
deep.legal_test: Unfair dismissal for misconduct: genuine belief on reasonable grounds following reasonable investigation (Burchell), band of reasonable responses (Madden), and s.98(4) ERA 1996; ACAS Code uplift under s.207A TULRCA 1992
deep.evidence_weighing: The judge found the claimants clearer and more convincing than the respondent's witnesses, whose testimony was inconsistent with contemporaneous documents; Mr Brier abandoned his denial of dismissal under cross-examination when confronted with his own text messages, and the dismissal texts of 13/9 and 2/10 removed any doubt that the claimants had been dismissed.
deep.reasoning: The judge held both claimants were expressly dismissed by Mr Brier's texts, not resignations, and that the reason was a belief they were guilty of misconduct in refusing weekend work. That belief was not on reasonable grounds because the claimants had no legal obligation to work weekends, so there was no misconduct and no fair procedure (no investigation, hearing or appeal). The dismissals were therefore unfair and wrongful, with a 25% ACAS uplift and a s.38 award for the complete failure to provide written terms. Loss of earnings was awarded to 14/4/25, with mitigation findings limiting the period.
deep.award_basis: per claimant: unfair and wrongful dismissal - basic award, loss of statutory rights, loss of earnings, pension loss, 25% ACAS uplift, plus 4 weeks' pay under s.38 Employment Act 2002 for failure to provide written particulars

deep.facts: The claimant was employed as a Driver/Operative from August 2023 until her dismissal on capability grounds in March 2024. She sustained a head injury at work on 25 September 2023, was diagnosed with concussion and later PTSD, and remained off sick until dismissal. Occupational health reports stated her condition was unlikely to last longer than 12 months. This preliminary hearing decided only whether she was disabled at the material time (September 2023 to March 2024).
issues: Whether the claimant had a physical or mental impairment with a substantial adverse effect on day-to-day activities under s.6 Equality Act 2010
Whether, judged at the time of the events, the adverse effect was likely to last at least 12 months (long-term, Sch 1)
What weight to give the occupational health reports on the duration question
deep.legal_test: Definition of disability under s.6 and Sch 1 Equality Act 2010: substantial (more than minor or trivial) and long-term (lasted or likely to last at least 12 months, 'likely' meaning 'could well happen'), assessed at the time of the alleged discrimination per the 2011 Code
deep.evidence_weighing: The judge gave little weight to the two OH reports because they used contradictory stock phrases, misstated the legal test (referring to 'longer than 12 months'), referred only to 'concussion' while ignoring the recorded PTSD diagnosis, and contained no internal reasoning; he accepted the claimant's unchallenged impact statement, consistent with the neurologist and GP records.
deep.reasoning: Applying the correct test at March 2024, the judge found the condition had already lasted nearly six months, had worsened despite treatment, and that PTSD and severe depression are significant impairments of uncertain duration. An informed observer with knowledge of the facts would reasonably conclude it 'could well happen' that the substantial adverse effect would last at least 12 months. Therefore the claimant was disabled at the material time.

cases.claimant: Mr C Goodman and Mrs A Goodman
cases.respondent: Secretary of State For Business and Trade

deep.facts: A husband and wife, directors and majority shareholders of a freight-forwarding company that went into voluntary liquidation in July 2023, claimed payments from the National Insurance Fund (redundancy, unpaid salary, notice and holiday pay) under ss.166/182 ERA 1996. The Secretary of State rejected the claims and disputed that they were genuine employees. The husband's non-redundancy claims were also presented significantly out of time.
issues: Whether the husband's claims (other than redundancy) were presented in time and, if not, whether it was reasonably practicable to present them in time under s.188
Whether the claimants were employees within s.230 ERA 1996 such that the company (and hence the Fund) was liable for the claimed payments
Whether the claimed written contracts were genuine or a sham
deep.legal_test: Employee status under s.230 ERA 1996: control and mutuality of obligation as the irreducible minimum (Ready Mixed Concrete), focusing on the actual legal obligations and the reality over written terms (Autoclenz); plus the reasonably practicable time-limit test under s.188
deep.evidence_weighing: No employment contract for the husband was produced; the wife's claimed contract was unsigned, undated, contained internal anomalies (an employment start date and a letterhead address that postdated the claimed period), and the P60 salary figures bore no real correlation to hours worked or sums actually paid, which were ad hoc and irregular.
deep.reasoning: The judge held the husband's non-redundancy claims were out of time and he had not shown it was not reasonably practicable to present them in time. On the merits, the claimed salaries were tax-avoidance figures unrelated to real pay, there was no genuine mutuality of obligation and no real control by the company over a husband-and-wife team running it for their own benefit, so the contracts were a sham. Neither claimant discharged the burden of proving employee status, so the company and the Fund were not liable, and all claims were dismissed.

cases.respondent: The Millwall Football and Athletic Company

deep.facts: The claimant, a part-time academy football coach engaged as a worker by Millwall, repeatedly raised concerns about a young player's apparent injury (Osgood-Schlatter's disease) and another player's mental health, which had previously been held to be two protected disclosures. He frequently challenged his more senior line manager Mr Jones, breached communication and safeguarding policies, and his relationship with Jones deteriorated. His contract was not renewed for the 2023/24 season. He claimed breach of contract (notice pay) and detriment for making protected disclosures.
issues: Whether the non-renewal of the claimant's coaching contract was a detriment done on the ground of his protected disclosures under s.47B ERA 1996
Whether the breach of contract (notice pay) claim succeeded
Whether an award was due under s.38 Employment Act 2002
Whether the claimant's preparation time application should be granted
deep.legal_test: Detriment for protected disclosure under s.47B ERA 1996: the disclosure must be a material (not trivial) cause of the detriment, examining the employer's mental processes; s.48(2) places the burden on the employer to show the ground for its act
deep.evidence_weighing: The judge found the relationship between the claimant and Mr Jones was already bad by February 2023, before the first protected disclosure in March 2023, evidenced by complaints, a public argument and the reassignment of his appraisal; Mr Mlinar even praised the claimant for raising the second disclosure, undercutting any link to detriment.
deep.reasoning: The judge found Mr Mlinar decided not to renew the contract because the working relationship with Mr Jones was untenable and the coaching standard inadequate, not because of the disclosures. The bad relationship predated the disclosures and arose from the claimant repeatedly overriding more senior staff, so the disclosures were not a material cause of the non-renewal and the s.47B claim was dismissed. The breach of contract (notice pay) claim succeeded for a small sum, a s.38 award was made, and the preparation time application was dismissed as the withheld document was irrelevant and could not have saved the proceedings.
deep.award_basis: breach of contract (notice pay) of £273.04 plus £553 under s.38 Employment Act 2002; the s.47B protected disclosure detriment claim was dismissed

cases.respondent: Griffin Catering Services Ltd and Fuller Smith and Turner plc

deep.facts: The claimant worked weekends as a waiter on a zero-hours contract from July to November 2024. He had under two years' service, so could not bring an ordinary unfair dismissal claim, and instead alleged automatic unfair dismissal for taking time off for dependants under s.57A ERA 1996 (relating to his partner's accident). The employer dismissed him relying on a series of absences and latenesses, including some that predated the accident and some where he failed to follow the absence reporting procedure. He also claimed one week's notice pay.
issues: Whether the claim against the Second Respondent should be dismissed on withdrawal
Whether the notice pay claim succeeded (conceded/by consent)
Whether the claimant's absences qualified as protected time off for dependants under s.57A ERA 1996, including compliance with the notice requirements in s.57A(2)
Whether the sole or principal reason for dismissal was the s.57A time off, making it automatically unfair
deep.legal_test: Automatic unfair dismissal under s.57A ERA 1996: whether the reason or principal reason for dismissal was the taking of (qualifying) time off for dependants, including the notice requirements in s.57A(2); fairness of procedure is irrelevant
deep.evidence_weighing: The hearing established that the 3/8/24 lateness relied on by the employer was a mistake (he was on time), and that the 25-26 August absences predated the partner's accident; the claimant could not explain why he failed to follow the reporting procedure, and contemporaneous texts showed he gave no advance notice for the 8/9/24 absence.
deep.reasoning: The judge found only the 7/9/24 absence was qualifying time off under s.57A, while the 8/9/24 and later absences either failed the s.57A(2) notice requirements or fell after the 'occasion' of the injury had ended, and the August incidents were unrelated. Since the employer relied on a range of absences and latenesses, the s.57A time off was not the sole or principal reason for dismissal, so the automatic unfair dismissal claim failed. The notice pay claim was settled by consent and the claim against the Second Respondent was dismissed on withdrawal.
deep.award_basis: one week's notice pay agreed by consent against the First Respondent; the automatic unfair dismissal claim was dismissed and the claim against the Second Respondent dismissed on withdrawal

cases.respondent: Atomics Educational Trust (formerly Tees Valley Collaborative Trust)

deep.facts: The claimant had worked for the Multi-Academy Trust continuously since 1998, latterly as a Liaison Manager focused on SEND students, but was not a qualified teacher. In 2024 the Trust restructured to separate teaching from support functions. The claimant applied for the new Deputy Head SEND role but was unsuccessful because it required formal teaching qualifications, and he was dismissed by reason of redundancy in September 2024.
issues: Whether the dismissal was by reason of redundancy under s.139(1) ERA 1996
Whether the Trust acted reasonably under s.98(4), including whether requiring teaching qualifications for the new role was reasonable
Quantum of compensation, including the appropriate period of loss and mitigation
deep.legal_test: Unfair dismissal by redundancy: redundancy as a potentially fair reason under s.139(1) and ss.98(1)-(2), and reasonableness under s.98(4) ERA 1996, including warning and consultation in redundancy
deep.evidence_weighing: The judge accepted there was a genuine restructure and reduced need for unqualified staff doing a mixed pastoral/teaching role, and noted significant evidence (line manager support) that the claimant could have done the Deputy Head role, but found his poor track record in obtaining teaching qualifications meant he likely would not have gained them.
deep.reasoning: The judge found a genuine redundancy: the Trust was entitled to restructure and to stipulate formal teaching qualifications as essential for the new Deputy Head role, which was within the band of reasonable responses even though the claimant could not meet them. Although the judgment records the claim of unfair dismissal succeeds and awards compensation, the reasoning emphasises the redundancy and qualification requirements were fair; the compensation reflects loss over roughly one year to 1/9/25 with full mitigation, pension loss and loss of statutory rights, subject to recoupment.
deep.award_basis: unfair dismissal compensatory award: salary loss (£23,579), pension loss (£6,744) and loss of statutory rights (£400), subject to the Recoupment Regulations

cases.respondent: Marldon Service Station Ltd (Cox of Torbay)

deep.facts: The claimant worked for a service station from 2006, latterly as a forecourt assistant/cashier, and had been continuously on sick leave since March 2020. In May 2023 her line manager visited her home for a 'friendly chat', asked whether she could return in any capacity, and when the claimant said she could not, suggested she resign there and then, which she declined. The employer, which had no written capability or attendance policy, then dismissed her for capability without a fair procedure. She claimed unfair dismissal, notice pay and holiday pay.
issues: Whether the capability dismissal was fair under s.98(4) ERA 1996, in particular whether the employer adopted a fair procedure
Whether the employer could be expected to wait any longer before dismissing
Whether the holiday pay and notice pay claims succeeded
Whether any compensatory award for lost income should be made given the claimant's continued incapacity
