deep.legal_test: Unfair dismissal on capability (ill-health) grounds under s.98(4) ERA 1996: whether the employer could be expected to wait longer (Spencer v Paragon Wallpapers; Dundee CC v Sharp) and took reasonable steps to consult and ascertain the medical position (East Lindsey DC v Daubney)
deep.evidence_weighing: The judge found the employer had no written capability policy and gave no reasonable warning that dismissal was contemplated or fair opportunity to respond; however, the medical evidence showed the claimant had been absent over three years with no return date in sight and no evidence she would have been fit to return at any point.
deep.reasoning: The judge held the dismissal was procedurally unfair because the employer failed to warn the claimant, give her a fair opportunity to respond, or follow a proper procedure. However, applying a Polkey-type analysis, since the claimant had been absent over three years with no prospect of return, a fair procedure would have produced the same outcome (save a week or two's delay at nil pay), so no compensatory award for lost income was made. The basic award, notice pay and loss of statutory rights were awarded; the holiday pay claim was dismissed.
deep.award_basis: unfair dismissal: notice pay (£3,000), basic award (£6,125) and loss of statutory rights (£350); no compensatory award for lost income; holiday pay claim dismissed

reasoning_profile.disposition_summary: Campbell is a meticulous, causation-focused judge who dismisses or only partially upholds the large majority of claims, typically accepting that employer conduct flowed from genuine processes, redundancy or conduct rather than from disclosures, disability or a protected characteristic. He is even-handed and precise: he will accept that a claimant held a reasonable, public-interest belief or was genuinely aggrieved, yet still dismiss because the statutory causal or 'related to' link fails. Where a discrete deduction, a single discriminatory act or a procedural failing is proven, he upholds it and quantifies carefully.
reasoning_profile.procedural_vs_substantive: substance-focused - he engages deeply with the substantive statutory tests (qualifying disclosure, causation, justification, properly-payable wages), turning to time-limit and status gateways only in the minority of cases where they dispose of the claim.
reasoning_profile.evidence_approach: He examines the actual words and context of alleged disclosures and comments, accepts genuine but legally insufficient beliefs, and relies on comparator analysis and contemporaneous documents/payslips/contracts to find benign, non-discriminatory explanations; he requires the claimant to show sums were 'properly payable' and reads scheme/contract rules closely.
recurring_themes: causation: conduct followed established process, not the protected reason
qualifying disclosure tested on actual words and reasonable belief (Williams v Brown)
comparator analysis to explain different treatment on non-protected grounds
deductions/bonus turn on whether the sum was 'properly payable' and authorised
proportionate-means justification for genuine restructures/operational needs
careful, proportionate remedy and Polkey on procedurally unfair dismissals
common_legal_tests: s.43B ERA qualifying disclosure (Williams v Brown five elements) and s.47B/s.103A causation
s.13 ERA unlawful deductions - 'properly payable' and authorisation
ss.13/15/26 EqA with proportionate-means justification and s.136 burden
s.98(4) ERA band of reasonable responses; redundancy fairness (Compair Maxam); Polkey
s.18 EqA / s.99 ERA pregnancy-maternity and comparator analysis
s.123 EqA just-and-equitable extension
reasoning_profile.deliberation_guidance: Centre your reasoning on causation: even if you accept the claimant made a genuine, reasonable, public-interest disclosure or was genuinely upset, ask whether the impugned treatment was actually 'on the ground of' or 'because of' that, or whether it followed an established process, a genuine redundancy or conduct concern. Test alleged disclosures and comments by their actual words and context, and use comparators to see whether a non-protected person would have been treated the same. For money claims, decide strictly whether the sum was 'properly payable' and contractually authorised. Where you find a procedurally unfair dismissal or a single proven discriminatory act, uphold it but apply Polkey and proportionate, well-evidenced remedy.

deep.facts: The claimant, a Finance Manager dismissed short of two years' service, discovered that a regional operations manager (Mr Bonnar) had taken £1,500 from a cash bag and made disclosures to his line manager Mr Purcell in March 2025 about apparent financial wrongdoing and amended reports. He was later dismissed for being aware of fraudulent activity and failing to report it immediately, contrary to the company code. He claimed detriment and automatic unfair dismissal for making protected disclosures.
issues: Whether the claimant made qualifying protected disclosures under ss.43A-43B ERA 1996
Whether he was subjected to the four alleged detriments on the ground of those disclosures under s.47B
Whether the sole or principal reason for his dismissal was the making of protected disclosures under s.103A
deep.legal_test: Protected disclosure detriment (s.47B) and automatic unfair dismissal (s.103A) ERA 1996: detriment requires the disclosure to be on the ground of (a material influence on) the act; dismissal requires the disclosures to be the sole or principal reason, a stronger causal link
deep.evidence_weighing: The judge accepted the respondent's policies encouraged speaking up and that the disclosures pointed only at Mr Bonnar (who was himself disciplined and resigned), not at the decision-makers, so there was no motive to suppress them; the later procedural detriments were the product of independent expediency-driven decisions.
deep.reasoning: The judge found that even assuming disclosures were made, the disciplinary investigation and the procedural shortcomings were not on the ground of the disclosures: they targeted Mr Bonnar's wrongdoing and were administrative decisions, so the s.47B detriment claims failed. On the dismissal, applying the stronger s.103A test, the evidence showed the employer dismissed the claimant because it considered him culpable for delaying reporting a colleague's wrongdoing, not because he made disclosures. The judge expressly made no finding of misconduct against the claimant but dismissed both complaints on causation.

deep.facts: The claimant, Head of Technical Innovation at a Scottish advice charity, was employed from May 2023 to January 2025 (under two years). He alleged he made protected disclosures in January 2025 emails, Teams messages and meetings, claiming the charity was over-reporting service volumes to Citizens Advice and the Scottish Government by counting out-of-scope, abandoned and missed calls as completed cases. This open preliminary hearing decided only whether he made protected disclosures.
issues: What disclosures the claimant relied on
Whether information was disclosed (as opposed to questions being asked)
Whether the claimant reasonably believed the disclosures tended to show a relevant failure under s.43B(1)
Whether he reasonably believed the disclosures were made in the public interest
Whether the disclosures were made to the employer or another relevant person
deep.legal_test: Qualifying and protected disclosure under ss.43A-43L ERA 1996: whether there was a disclosure of information in the reasonable belief of the worker that it was made in the public interest and tended to show a relevant failure under s.43B(1), and whether made to the employer/relevant person
deep.evidence_weighing: The judge found the claimant's underlying belief was based on incorrect premises - he wrongly believed the charity was paid per contact and would gain financially or face repercussions from the figures, when its funding was a flat grant, and he did not know the actual reporting terms; several of his communications and meetings involved asking questions rather than conveying information.
deep.reasoning: The judge held the claimant could not reasonably hold a belief in a legal breach or fraud because he lacked correct information and his belief rested on factual misunderstandings about the funding model. Some alleged disclosures conveyed no 'information' (being questions), and others were not made to his employer or a relevant person as the recipients lacked sufficient seniority. As none of the communications amounted to protected disclosures, the entire claim, founded on that premise, was dismissed.

deep.facts: The claimant worked as a Heating Engineer from February to June 2025 and was dismissed verbally during a probation review meeting. He claimed automatic unfair dismissal for asserting a statutory right (to be paid for home-to-job travel time), unlawful deductions/unauthorised payments (unpaid timesheets/overtime and deductions for a water cylinder, vacuum and van valeting), and breach of contract for notice pay. The provided text also includes a later reconsideration judgment confirming the original dismissal of all claims.
issues: Whether the claimant asserted a statutory right and, if so, whether that was the sole or principal reason for dismissal under s.104 ERA 1996
Whether unlawful deductions were made from wages under s.13 or unauthorised payments required under s.15 ERA 1996
Whether there was a breach of contract regarding payment in lieu of notice
On reconsideration, whether it was necessary in the interests of justice to vary or revoke the original judgment
deep.legal_test: Automatic unfair dismissal for asserting a statutory right (s.104 ERA 1996); unlawful deduction (s.13) and unauthorised payment (s.15) ERA 1996; and on reconsideration, the 'interests of justice' test under rr.68-71 Employment Tribunal Procedure Rules 2024 (Ebury Partners; Trimble; Burton)
deep.evidence_weighing: The judge found the claimant had no statutory right to be paid for home-to-first/last-job travel (only a potential right to count it as working time, which the respondent conceded), and accepted the managers' consistent sworn evidence that he was dismissed for conduct (honesty/integrity over timesheets) and his agitated behaviour in the meeting, despite this not being fully captured in the meeting note.
deep.reasoning: The judge held the claimant did not in fact have the statutory right he claimed (pay for travel time), so he could not have been dismissed for asserting it, and in any event the principal reason for dismissal was his conduct and behaviour in the probation review, not any assertion of a right, so the s.104 claim failed. The deduction claims failed because the contract permitted or justified the relevant deductions and the overtime was not owed (travel time being non-payable and his records unreliable), and the notice claim failed as one week's pay in lieu was correctly paid on failed probation. On reconsideration the judge found no material procedural error and confirmed the dismissal of all claims.

cases.respondent: European Living Retail Ltd (in Administration) and Others

deep.facts: Six consolidated claims arose after a furniture design business (the first respondent), holding exclusive BoConcept franchise rights in Scotland, went into administration. It operated Edinburgh and Glasgow stores plus concessions, and ceased employing the claimants on 31 October 2024. The second and third respondents (run by a former director) each began operating one of the stores, taking on some but not all staff and buying stock, fixtures and the customer book. This hearing decided whether relevant TUPE transfers occurred and on what date.
issues: Whether there were relevant transfers under regulation 3(1)(a) TUPE 2006 of the Edinburgh and Glasgow stores
Whether the stores were stable, distinct and severable economic entities capable of transferring
On what date(s) any relevant transfer occurred
Whether the insolvency/administration affected the analysis
deep.legal_test: Relevant transfer under regulation 3(1)(a) and 3(2) TUPE 2006: whether there was a stable economic entity retaining its identity (Cheesman v R Brewer; Spijkers), whether part of a business is severable (Fairhurst Ward Abbotts), the single transfer date rule (Celtec/North Wales TEC v Astley), and administration not being terminal insolvency (Key2Law v De'Antiquis)
deep.evidence_weighing: The judge accepted the economic reality that by 14 October 2024 the franchise had transferred to the new companies, staff were already instructed to use the new bank accounts, the first respondent's account was frozen, and it was always intended that a substantially similar business would continue; the formal completion of leases and asset purchases on 8 November 2024 was not determinative.
deep.reasoning: Applying Cheesman, the judge found the first respondent was a stable economic entity, and its Edinburgh and Glasgow stores were sufficiently distinct and severable to be stable economic entities in their own right, each taken over by a separate transferee company with the stock, fixtures and customer book. The economic reality, not the later formal completion of leases/asset purchases or the administration (which is not 'terminal' insolvency), determined matters, so two relevant transfers under reg 3(1)(a) occurred on 1 November 2024. The remaining issues were left to further case management.

deep.facts: The claimant, an autistic hospital porter at Queen Elizabeth University Hospital in Glasgow employed from April 2020, was dismissed without notice on 25 April 2024 for gross misconduct following an altercation and a pattern of behavioural incidents. The respondent treated the conduct as the reason for dismissal, while the claimant said his autism affected how he interpreted situations and that he was discriminated against, harassed, victimised and denied reasonable adjustments. The respondent accepted his autism was a disability but denied the complaints.
issues: Were the discrimination/harassment/victimisation claims presented in time, part of a continuing act, or should time be extended on just-and-equitable grounds?
Did the respondent apply a PCP (requiring employees to regulate emotional behaviour) that put the claimant at a substantial disadvantage, and were reasonable adjustments required?
Was the claimant treated unfavourably because of something arising in consequence of his disability, and if so was it a proportionate means of achieving a legitimate aim (s.15 EqA)?
Was the dismissal for conduct unfair under s.98(4) ERA?
deep.legal_test: band of reasonable responses under s.98(4) ERA for conduct dismissal; plus Equality Act 2010 framework (ss.15, 20/21 reasonable adjustments) and Keeble/Marshall factors for just-and-equitable time extension
deep.evidence_weighing: Over eleven days the tribunal heard extensive evidence from both sides; it accepted the respondent's decision-makers (Ms Gemmell, Mr Steele) had reasonably concluded there was too great a risk of further unsustainable incidents and nowhere the claimant could realistically be deployed, especially as the claimant declined updated OH advice and refused alternative working environments.
deep.reasoning: Applying the band of reasonable responses and not substituting its own view, the tribunal found dismissal fell within the range of reasonable options given the gross misconduct finding and the claimant's refusal to accept alternative work; even absent the conduct dismissal, dismissal for the other substantial reason of fundamental disagreement over what work he would perform would have been reasonable. The discrimination, harassment, victimisation and reasonable-adjustment complaints all failed on the merits. Each legal complaint was therefore unsuccessful and the claim dismissed.

cases.respondent: Funeral Services Ltd T/a Co-Op Funeralcare

deep.facts: The claimant, a Funeral Arranger at Co-Op Funeralcare's Shotts branch employed since 2008 and with type-2 diabetes, resigned with immediate effect on 25 February 2025 after a disciplinary investigation into her conduct was initiated and her grievances were handled in a way she objected to. She claimed she had made protected disclosures about a GDPR/data breach and was subjected to detriment, automatic and constructive unfair dismissal, direct disability discrimination, failure to make reasonable adjustments and harassment. The respondent accepted her diabetes was a disability but denied the claims.
issues: Did the claimant make qualifying/protected disclosures under s.43B ERA (the alleged GDPR breach)?
Was she subjected to detriment because of protected disclosures?
Was she automatically unfairly dismissed and/or constructively unfairly dismissed (repudiatory breach / final straw)?
Was she directly discriminated against, denied reasonable adjustments, or harassed in relation to her disability?
deep.legal_test: qualifying disclosure under s.43B ERA (Williams v Brown elements); constructive dismissal repudiatory-breach/last-straw test; Equality Act 2010 framework (ss.13, 20/21, 26)
deep.evidence_weighing: The tribunal accepted the claimant genuinely and reasonably believed there had been a data breach (via 'jigsaw identification') and that her belief was in the public interest, but found the alleged harassing/discriminatory acts (e.g. treatment of her fit note, attempts to progress the investigation) were standard procedure not 'related to' disability, as her absence was driven by stress/anxiety and bereavement rather than diabetes.
deep.reasoning: Although the tribunal found the claimant held a reasonable belief in a legal-obligation breach, it concluded none of the complaints were established on the evidence when the statutory tests were applied: the detriment/disclosure, automatic and constructive dismissal, direct discrimination, reasonable adjustment and harassment claims each failed because the impugned conduct followed established processes and was not because of disclosures or disability. All six complaints were therefore dismissed and remedy was not reached.

deep.facts: The claimant, a care worker (later Senior Care Assistant) employed by Newlands Care Angus from February 2022, was dismissed with one week's notice on 24 January 2023, the respondent citing her treatment of a colleague, poor documentation, a dog in a work vehicle and failure to return the company car. She brought wide-ranging claims of age and race discrimination, harassment, victimisation, protected-disclosure detriment, automatic unfair dismissal, unlawful deduction from wages and related claims. She is of English national origin.
issues: Were the discrimination claims in time or eligible for a just-and-equitable extension?
Was the claimant subjected to direct age and race discrimination, harassment related to race, and victimisation?
Was her dismissal automatically unfair on protected-disclosure grounds?
Were unlawful deductions made from her wages, and was she due notice/holiday pay?
deep.legal_test: s.13/s.26/s.27 Equality Act 2010 with shifting burden of proof; s.47B/s.103A ERA protected-disclosure detriment/automatic unfair dismissal; s.13 ERA unlawful deductions; Vento bands for injury to feelings; Keeble/Marshall for time extension
deep.evidence_weighing: The tribunal found the deductions from pay had no statutory or contractual basis and no written consent, so the wages claim succeeded (net £16.97 after offsetting a uniform overpayment). On the 14 December 2022 meeting it found that those present speaking in Polish amounted to race discrimination and harassment, the claimant credibly describing feeling intimidated and humiliated, though it found her dismissal was for genuine conduct/performance reasons, not disclosures or race.
deep.reasoning: Applying the Equality Act tests, the tribunal upheld only the race discrimination and harassment arising from the December 2022 meeting (placing injury to feelings at the lower end of the bottom Vento band given the one-off, non-serious nature) and the unlawful deductions claim; it extended time on a just-and-equitable basis for the discrimination claims. All other claims failed because the dismissal was driven by irreconcilable conduct/performance issues and the company had genuinely engaged with the matters the claimant raised, so race/age/disclosures were not the reason.
deep.award_basis: £16.97 net for unlawful deduction from wages plus £2,500 injury to feelings for race discrimination and harassment (lowest Vento band), with 8% interest to be calculated

deep.facts: The claimant, a Financial/Accounts Assistant employed by Vallourec Oil & Gas UK from October 2019 and working from home permanently (granted as a flexible-working request, partly linked to her fibromyalgia), was dismissed on 11 April 2025 in a 2024 redundancy exercise that consolidated the finance team into fewer, Aberdeen-based roles. She claimed unfair dismissal and disability discrimination; the respondent accepted fibromyalgia was a disability but said the reason was genuine redundancy.
issues: Was the reason for dismissal redundancy and did the respondent act reasonably (warning/consultation, selection, alternative employment, range of reasonable responses) under s.98(4) ERA?
Was the claimant's selection direct disability discrimination under s.13 EqA?
Was selecting her for redundancy unfavourable treatment because of something arising in consequence of disability (restricted mobility / home-working need), and if so was it proportionate (s.15 EqA)?
deep.legal_test: redundancy fairness under s.98(4) ERA (Williams/Compair Maxam-type factors: consultation, selection, alternative employment, range of reasonable responses); s.13 and s.15 Equality Act 2010 with proportionality/justification
deep.evidence_weighing: The tribunal accepted the restructure was a genuine commercial decision driven by North Sea market conditions which it could not second-guess, and accepted Mr Graham's evidence that a smaller two-person finance team needed to be office-based; it found the claimant lacked the skills/experience/qualification for the surviving Finance Accountant role and would have refused to relocate to Aberdeen.
deep.reasoning: There was a fair reason (redundancy) but the respondent fell short of s.98(4) reasonableness in the process, so the dismissal was procedurally unfair and that complaint succeeded. However, on a Polkey analysis the claimant would have been dismissed in any event no later than she was, since she could not perform the surviving role and would not relocate, which affects claimable loss. The s.13 and s.15 discrimination complaints failed because her selection was not because of, or because of something arising from, disability but because of the genuine restructure.

cases.respondent: Simply Solutions (Europe) Ltd and M McPhillips c/o Simply Solutions (Europe) Ltd

deep.facts: The claimant, a Client Relations Manager at facilities firm Simply Solutions employed from June 2024 on a six-month probation, was dismissed on 7 January 2025 at a probation review meeting by her line manager Mr McPhillips. She was pregnant (having told him in October 2024) and contended she was dismissed because of her pregnancy and her intention to take maternity leave; the respondent said the dismissal was for genuine performance/conduct reasons. She withdrew a notice-pay breach-of-contract claim.
issues: Did the respondent subject the claimant to detriments (e.g. ambush meeting, failure to give clear reasons, mishandling her appeal) under s.47C ERA / MAPLE reg.19?
Was the reason for the treatment her pregnancy or intention to take maternity leave?
Was she treated unfavourably because of pregnancy or pregnancy-related illness under s.18 EqA?
Was her dismissal automatically unfair under s.99 ERA?
deep.legal_test: s.47C ERA / MAPLE reg.19 detriment and s.99 ERA automatic unfair dismissal (reason for treatment); s.18 Equality Act 2010 unfavourable treatment because of pregnancy/maternity
deep.evidence_weighing: Witnesses on both sides were found generally credible. The tribunal relied on a comparator analysis: a non-pregnant colleague (Ms Hutchinson) facing similar criticisms had her probation extended rather than being dismissed, but the differences (longer service, promotion rather than new role, better attitude, no colleague-upset allegations, good timekeeping) explained the different treatment on non-pregnancy grounds.
deep.reasoning: The tribunal found Mr McPhillips genuinely believed the probation review had been scheduled and gave brief reasons only because that was always his intention and the claimant became upset; the failures the claimant complained of flowed from administrative/process reasons (e.g. reassigning the appeal officer) rather than her pregnancy. Applying the statutory tests, none of the detriment, s.18 discrimination or s.99 automatic unfair dismissal complaints was supported by the evidence, so all were dismissed and remedy was not reached.

deep.facts: The claimant, a Night Shift Supervisor at adult gaming premises (The Razz) in Inverness employed from 12 August 2024, was summarily dismissed on 30 September 2024. The respondent's manager Ms De Vita had lost confidence in her, partly because she believed the claimant left a two-hour gap in site cover without adequately covering it or alerting a manager; the claimant said she was ill that night. She claimed direct race discrimination and wrongful dismissal (no notice).
issues: Was the claimant directly discriminated against because of race under s.13 EqA (including whether her chosen comparators were valid and whether the burden of proof shifted)?
Was the claimant wrongfully dismissed, i.e. dismissed in breach of contract without notice, and had she committed a repudiatory breach justifying summary dismissal?
If wrongfully dismissed, what damages (if any) are due?
deep.legal_test: s.13 Equality Act 2010 with s.23 comparator requirement and the shifting burden of proof; common-law wrongful dismissal (whether conduct amounted to a repudiatory breach justifying summary termination)
deep.evidence_weighing: Ms De Vita was generally credible but had poor recollection; Mr Dolman's evidence was unproblematic. The claimant's proffered comparators were more junior with less responsibility (and one, Mr Russell, was himself dismissed for performance), so were not valid comparators, and there were no primary facts pointing to race; on the contract claim her undisputed illness meant her failure to cover was at most a minor breach.
deep.reasoning: On the discrimination claim there were no facts from which discrimination could be inferred, so the burden never shifted; the real reason was Ms De Vita's loss of confidence over the cover gap, and the comparators were invalid, so the s.13 claim was dismissed. On the contract claim the claimant did not commit a repudiatory breach (her conduct was 'too little too late' at worst given her genuine illness), so she was wrongfully dismissed for lack of notice; however she was later paid one week's notice value, so she was fully compensated and no damages were awarded.
deep.award_basis: Wrongful dismissal complaint succeeded but no damages awarded because the claimant had already been paid one week's notice value

deep.facts: The claimant, a Techno-Economic Analyst employed by Offshore Renewable Energy Catapult from November 2022 (identifying as Arab), resigned in June 2024 for a better-paid role and on his leaver's questionnaire expressly said his departure was not due to discrimination. His claims concerned a 2023 grievance/performance episode and the non-payment of a bonus in July 2024, brought as race discrimination, harassment, victimisation, unlawful deduction from wages and breach of contract.
issues: Was the claimant directly discriminated against, harassed or victimised because of race (s.13/s.26/s.27 EqA)?
Did the non-payment of the July 2024 bonus amount to an unlawful deduction from wages under s.13 ERA?
Did the non-payment of the bonus breach his contract at common law (was there a legitimate expectation/contractual entitlement to a bonus)?
deep.legal_test: s.13/s.26/s.27 Equality Act 2010 with shifting burden of proof; s.13 ERA 'properly payable' wages test; common-law contractual entitlement (whether a discretionary bonus gave a legitimate/contractual expectation)
deep.evidence_weighing: The claimant was found generally credible but could not directly challenge the respondent's evidence on the key issues, and the evidence pointed away from discrimination; the bonus scheme rules provided that no employee under notice would receive a bonus, applied consistently to all staff, so the claimant had no legitimate or contractual expectation of one.
deep.reasoning: Applying the Equality Act tests, there were no facts shifting the burden of proof and the discrimination, harassment and victimisation claims failed. Because the bonus was discretionary and the scheme excluded employees under notice (and was applied consistently), no amount was 'properly payable', so there was no unlawful deduction and no breach of contract. The whole claim was dismissed, and on reconsideration the tribunal confirmed its judgment, finding no material errors.

deep.facts: The claimant, a Residential Officer at HMP Grampian employed by the Scottish Ministers (Scottish Prison Service) from 2015, was dismissed without notice on 12 January 2024 for conduct, namely improperly accessing confidential prisoner intelligence records. The tribunal found she knew she should not access those records but did so to satisfy herself about a transferred prisoner and to obtain information about other prisoners for personal gain or to pass on. She claimed unfair dismissal and wrongful dismissal.
issues: Was the claimant dismissed for a fair statutory reason (conduct) under s.98(1)/(2) ERA?
Did the respondent act reasonably in dismissing her for that reason under s.98(4) ERA?
Did the respondent breach her contract by not paying notice (wrongful dismissal), or was it released by a material breach?
deep.legal_test: conduct dismissal under s.98(1)/(2) and (4) ERA (Burchell genuine belief/reasonable investigation and band of reasonable responses); common-law wrongful dismissal (whether a material/repudiatory breach released the employer from giving notice)
deep.evidence_weighing: The tribunal found, on the evidence including the claimant's own admissions, that she knew she should not access the records but did so to obtain and pass on information for personal gain, which breached the fundamental obligation of mutual trust and confidence underpinning her contract.
deep.reasoning: The respondent satisfied the tribunal that the reason for dismissal was conduct and that it acted reasonably throughout investigation, dismissal and appeal, so the unfair dismissal claim failed under s.98(4) and there was no need to consider Polkey, contributory fault or remedy. Separately, the claimant's deliberate unauthorised access materially breached the implied term of trust and confidence, entitling the respondent to terminate summarily, so she was not wrongfully dismissed and was due no notice or payment in lieu. Both claims were dismissed.

deep.facts: The claimant was engaged as Head Housekeeper by Stardust Estates, a short-term apartment letting company in Glasgow, starting 31 October 2024 after an interview at which an annual salary of £24,960 (paid monthly) for 40 hours per week was agreed. He stopped working after about two weeks and was paid only £420. The respondent argued it had correctly paid him on a different basis (£15 per apartment) because he had not countersigned a statement of terms. He claimed unlawful deduction from wages.
issues: What were the agreed contractual pay terms, and was the salary conditional on the claimant signing a written statement of terms?
When did the employment begin and end?
Was the claimant paid less than was 'properly payable', amounting to an unlawful deduction under s.13 ERA?
deep.legal_test: was there a relevant deduction under s.13 ERA (whether the sum was 'properly payable' under s.13(3) and whether any deduction was statutorily/contractually authorised or consented to under s.13(1)); Scots-law contract formation principles
deep.evidence_weighing: Both witnesses were credible. The tribunal found that at the 30 October interview Ms Bis offered, and the claimant accepted, a £24,960 salary with no mention that it was conditional on signing a statement or that a £15-per-apartment alternative applied, and there was no evidence of any such industry-standard practice; both parties then acted consistently with the salary contract.
deep.reasoning: Applying Scots contract-formation principles, a binding employment contract on a £24,960 annual salary formed on 30 October 2024. Employment ran 31 October to 13 November 2024 (two weeks) by mutual agreement, entitling the claimant to 2/52 of £24,960 = £960 gross. He was paid only £420, so the £540 shortfall was 'properly payable' and, since no statutory/contractual authorisation or written consent existed under s.13(1), it was an unlawful deduction. The claim succeeded for £540 less tax and NI.
deep.award_basis: Unlawful deduction from wages: £540 shortfall in agreed salary, less income tax and employee National Insurance

deep.facts: The claimant, employed by translation company Global Voices from 2008 (latterly 'Head of EMEA and Governance', and the separated wife of the CEO/owner), had a cancer diagnosis accepted as a disability from June 2024. Following a cost-cutting restructure her role was made redundant and she was dismissed on 22 April 2025, being offered an alternative telesales-type role she saw as a demotion. She claimed unfair dismissal, discrimination arising from disability (s.15) and harassment (s.26), including an instruction to colleagues not to contact her.
issues: Was the dismissal by reason of redundancy and was the redundancy process (pool, consultation, search for alternatives, range of reasonable responses) fair under s.98 ERA?
Was the claimant treated unfavourably because of something arising in consequence of disability under s.15 EqA, and was any such treatment justified?
Was she subjected to harassment related to disability under s.26 EqA?
What remedy (basic award, Polkey/contributory reductions, injury to feelings) is appropriate?
deep.legal_test: redundancy fairness under s.98 ERA (pool, consultation, alternative employment, range of reasonable responses, Polkey); s.15 Equality Act 2010 unfavourable-treatment/justification; s.26 harassment; Vento bands for injury to feelings
deep.evidence_weighing: Witnesses were all generally credible with little factual dispute; the tribunal accepted Mr Lovatt's evidence, supported by contemporaneous documents, that the restructure was a genuine response to a predicted year-end loss threatening the business. On the s.15 claim it found one proven act of unfavourable treatment (an email effectively contacting/excluding her) had only a low, short-lived impact, given her measured response and continued project involvement.
deep.reasoning: There was a genuine redundancy reason but procedural failings rendered the dismissal unfair, so the unfair dismissal complaint succeeded with a basic award of £408.50. One act amounted to discrimination arising from disability under s.15, for which £3,000 injury to feelings (between the bottom and midpoint of the lower Vento band, with 8% interest) was awarded, the tribunal weighing the one-off, low-impact nature against her vulnerability while recovering from cancer. The s.26 harassment complaint was not well founded and was dismissed.
deep.award_basis: £408.50 basic award for unfair dismissal plus £3,000 injury to feelings for s.15 disability discrimination (lower Vento band), with 8% interest

cases.respondent: Paisley Secretarial Services Ltd T/a Allstaff and MBM Print SCS Ltd

deep.facts: This was an open preliminary hearing concerning a claimant placed via agency Paisley Secretarial Services (t/a Allstaff, first respondent) to work for MBM Print (second respondent). The claimant alleged he had made three protected disclosures and carried out protected acts by refusing to opt out of the 48-hour weekly working time limit, after being pressed to work 12-hour shifts; he alleged the disclosures/acts led to termination of his assignment. The hearing decided only whether protected disclosures/acts had occurred.
issues: Did the claimant make any qualifying/protected disclosures under s.43B ERA (his three alleged disclosures)?
Did the claimant do anything qualifying as a protected act under s.45A(1) of the Act (refusing/proposing to refuse to opt out of, or forgo, the weekly working time limit, or alleging infringement)?
Which respondent was his 'employer' for s.45A purposes, and can the s.45A detriment claim be determined now?
deep.legal_test: qualifying disclosure under s.43B(1) ERA applying the five Williams v Brown elements (reasonable belief, public interest, that a listed scenario exists); s.45A(1) Working Time protected-act provisions and the s.230(4) definition of 'employer'
deep.evidence_weighing: The tribunal heard the claimant under oath and found his alleged disclosures rested on a belief that the respondents were already breaching reg.4 of the Working Time Regulations by pressuring workers into 12-hour shifts, but that belief was not reasonably held; none of his statements conveyed a reasonably held belief in a breach of a legal obligation. On the s.45A point the second respondent led no evidence on its asserted safety-rule reason for termination.
deep.reasoning: Applying the Williams elements to each of the three alleged disclosures, the tribunal found none met all the s.43B(1) criteria because the underlying belief in a current breach was not reasonably held, so the claimant made no protected disclosures and the s.47B detriment complaint was dismissed. However, the s.45A protected-act/detriment claim could not be resolved at the preliminary stage: the true reason for terminating the assignment required further evidence, so that complaint was directed to a full hearing. (A later judgment by Judge O'Donnell dismissed the claim against the second respondent, leaving it to proceed against the first respondent.)

deep.facts: The claimant, an ASDA delivery driver based at the Irvine store employed from November 2020, was summarily dismissed on 6 May 2024 after a disciplinary hearing for gross misconduct: he had admitted using offensive language (a curse) at a customer, which the respondent treated as against its core values and bringing it into disrepute. He disputed that this was the true reason and said dismissal was too harsh, and separately claimed unpaid wages for March/April 2024 and pay for accrued annual leave.
issues: Was the claimant dismissed for a fair reason (conduct) under s.98(1)/(2) ERA and did the respondent act reasonably under s.98(4)?
Was the claimant subjected to an unlawful deduction from wages for March/April 2024 under s.13 ERA?
Was the claimant denied pay for accrued but untaken annual leave under the Working Time Regulations 1998?
deep.legal_test: conduct dismissal under s.98(1)/(2) and (4) ERA (band of reasonable responses); s.13 ERA unlawful deductions; Working Time Regulations 1998 regs.13/13A/14 (accrual, carry-over, payment in lieu only on termination)
deep.evidence_weighing: The tribunal heard from the dismissing manager Mr Hamilton and the claimant; on holidays it found from the evidence (including the claimant's own) that he had taken roughly a week in November, a week in December, a day, a week in February and two fully paid weeks in March 2024, more than covering his entitlement, and the claimant could not specify what he was owed, accepting he might be due nothing.
deep.reasoning: The respondent satisfied the tribunal that the reason for dismissal was the claimant's admitted conduct and that, overall, dismissal was within the band of reasonable responses, so the dismissal was not unfair. On wages/holidays, the respondent was legally entitled to require leave to be taken in the holiday year or lost (carry-over only for sickness etc.), the claimant had in fact taken his full entitlement and been paid all due, and he could not discharge the onus of showing any unlawful deduction. All complaints were dismissed.

deep.facts: Ms Savage was conditionally offered a Psychological Wellbeing Officer role with NHS24, but after a period exploring adjustments (specialist software and an adjustable wheelchair-compatible desk) the offer was withdrawn on 18 December 2023. She alleged the withdrawal was disability discrimination. She did not begin ACAS Early Conciliation until 12 December 2024 and presented her tribunal claim on 10 January 2025, almost a year late.
issues: Was the disability discrimination claim presented out of time?
Should the tribunal exercise its discretion under section 123(1)(b) EqA to extend time on the basis that it was just and equitable to do so?
deep.legal_test: just and equitable extension of time under section 123(1)(b) Equality Act 2010
deep.evidence_weighing: The claimant's own evidence that she had researched her options in December 2023, consciously chose not to pursue a claim to protect future NHS prospects, and was only medically incapacitated from mid/late January 2024, undermined her case for extension.
deep.reasoning: The judge took the claim at its highest but found the claimant had the capacity and resources to explore a claim immediately after the act complained of yet chose not to, and could have returned to it in summer 2024 when her symptoms abated but did not. Given that deliberate choice and the significant passage of time, it was not just and equitable to extend time. The claim was therefore out of time and dismissed for want of jurisdiction.

deep.facts: Ms Onyan, a care assistant, was dismissed by Eildon Care Ltd after just over two months for failing to satisfactorily complete probation. She claimed she was not paid for her final day (3 July 2024 when she was sent home), was not paid in lieu of her one week's notice, and was not paid for holiday accrued during the unserved notice week. The respondent maintained she was paid only for shifts worked, that PILON was included in her final pay, and that holiday accrued only to the termination date.
issues: Was there an unlawful deduction or breach of contract for not paying the claimant for 3 July 2024?
Was there an unlawful deduction or breach of contract for failing to pay one week's notice (PILON)?
Was there an unlawful deduction, breach of contract or WTR breach for not paying holiday accrued during the unserved notice week?
deep.legal_test: unauthorised deduction from wages under section 13 Employment Rights Act 1996, statutory notice under ss.86-91 ERA, and holiday pay on termination under Regulations 13 and 13A Working Time Regulations 1998
deep.evidence_weighing: The claimant's own contract and her payslip dated 25 July 2024 (which separately itemised PILON at the correct weekly value) were decisive; she accepted prior pay had been correct.
deep.reasoning: On unpaid wages, the contract entitled her only to pay for shifts actually worked and she worked no shift on 3 July, so there was no entitlement. On notice, the contract permitted immediate termination with PILON, which her final payslip showed had been correctly paid. On holiday, accrual ran only to the termination date, not through an unserved notice period. All three complaints therefore failed.

reasoning_profile.disposition_summary: Adkin is an analytically thorough judge who decides discrimination and whistleblowing cases on tightly applied causation and threshold tests, dismissing many claims at the s.43B 'qualifying disclosure' or burden-of-proof stage while upholding discrete heads (victimisation, specific protected disclosures, worker status, reasonable adjustments) where the causal link is genuinely made out. He leans neither way, expressing sympathy for claimants whose claims nonetheless fail on the law, and is precise about which specific allegations succeed. He is decisive but issue-by-issue rather than sweeping.
reasoning_profile.procedural_vs_substantive: balanced - he frequently resolves cases on substantive causation and reasonable-belief thresholds, but also disposes of claims on employee/worker status and just-and-equitable time-extension gateways.
reasoning_profile.evidence_approach: He works from agreed chronologies and contemporaneous documents, drawing adverse inferences where a respondent fails to disclose key communications (e.g. WhatsApp between decision-makers) or its witnesses do not attend, while requiring claimants to identify real comparators and a reasonable, public-interest belief; absence of contemporaneous support for a respondent's performance narrative tells against it.
recurring_themes: qualifying/protected disclosure threshold under s.43B (reasonable belief, public interest)
causation 'because of the protected act' for victimisation
adverse inference from undisclosed documents or non-attending witnesses
employee/worker status as a gateway (Ready Mixed Concrete, Autoclenz, Deliveroo)
just-and-equitable time extension and continuing-act analysis
sympathy noted but claims decided strictly on the statutory test
common_legal_tests: s.43B ERA qualifying disclosure (Chesterton public interest) and s.47B/s.103A
s.27 EqA victimisation and s.136 burden of proof (Igen, Madarassy)
ss.20/21 reasonable adjustments and s.15 EqA
s.230 ERA employee/worker status (Ready Mixed Concrete, Autoclenz)
s.98 ERA band of reasonable responses / SOSR; Polkey
s.123 EqA just-and-equitable extension and continuing act
reasoning_profile.deliberation_guidance: Approach the claim allegation-by-allegation rather than holistically. For whistleblowing, test each alleged disclosure against every element of s.43B before going further - did the claimant hold a reasonable, public-interest belief that it tended to show a relevant failure? For discrimination, require a valid comparator and a proven foundational fact before the burden shifts, and analyse causation tightly ('because of' the protected act). Check employee/worker status and time limits as gateways. Be candid in expressing sympathy where warranted, but uphold only those specific heads where the statutory test is met, and draw adverse inferences where a respondent withholds obvious contemporaneous evidence.

cases.respondent: Midasplayer.com Ltd and Mr C Wurzinger

deep.facts: Mr Plata Martinez, Senior Finance Director at King (Midasplayer.com), was dismissed purportedly for redundancy on 6 June 2024 as part of a Microsoft Games division cut of 1,900 employees. He alleged that 7-8 protected disclosures and protected acts, principally relating to his line manager the CFO (Mr Wurzinger), were the real reason for his treatment. The respondents said he had been identified as a poor performer in an experimental role before the redundancy and before the CFO knew of his complaints.
issues: Did the alleged disclosures satisfy the statutory definition of a qualifying/protected disclosure under s.43B ERA?
Was the claimant automatically unfairly dismissed under s.103A ERA because of a protected disclosure?
Was the claimant subjected to detriments under s.47B ERA because of a protected disclosure?
Was the claimant victimised under s.27 EqA because of protected acts?
deep.legal_test: qualifying disclosure under s.43B ERA (reasonable belief, public interest), automatic unfair dismissal under s.103A ERA, detriment under s.47B ERA, and victimisation under s.27 EqA with burden of proof under s.136 EqA (Igen v Wong / Madarassy)
deep.evidence_weighing: The tribunal found five protected acts established but accepted the respondents' evidence (and noted the absence of contradicting evidence) that the decision to make the role redundant originated in November 2023, before the manager was aware of the complaints; none of the alleged disclosures met every element of s.43B.
deep.reasoning: Because none of the alleged disclosures satisfied all elements of the s.43B definition, the whistleblowing detriment and automatic unfair dismissal complaints failed at the threshold. On victimisation, although five protected acts were established, the tribunal found the detriments (including the dismissal and lack of redundancy appeal) were not done because of the protected acts, the genesis of the termination predating awareness of the complaints. All three complaints were dismissed.

deep.facts: Ms Thornton, an English lecturer of nearly 10 years at Capital City College Group, resigned on 1 August 2024 and claimed constructive unfair dismissal. The dispute centred on management changes, repeated lesson observations without proper written feedback, a joint grievance with a colleague, and the Principal's failure to follow up with a promised explanation of 'interim arrangements' for the next academic year. There was also unreasonable delay in providing the grievance outcome (the report not reaching the claimant until July 2025).
issues: Did the respondent commit a fundamental breach of the implied term of trust and confidence entitling the claimant to resign?
Was the constructive dismissal unfair?
What deductions (chance of resignation in any event / contributory conduct) and ACAS uplift should apply to the award?
deep.legal_test: constructive unfair dismissal under ss.95 and 98 ERA 1996, with ACAS Code uplift under s.207A TULR(C)A 1992 applying the Rentplus UK Ltd v Coulson framework
deep.evidence_weighing: The resignation letter showed the claimant was particularly upset by the Principal not getting back to her about a plan for the next year; the unexplained and deliberate delay in the grievance process (requiring a subject access request to obtain the report) justified the maximum ACAS uplift.
deep.reasoning: The judge found the claim of constructive unfair dismissal well founded, the operative breach being the failure to follow up on the promised interim arrangements rather than grievance delay per se. Applying Rentplus, the unreasonable and unexcused grievance delay warranted the maximum 25% ACAS uplift on the compensatory award. The judge also found a chance the claimant would have resigned anyway, applying 25% reductions to both basic and compensatory awards, producing a net award of £11,364.56.
deep.award_basis: basic award (£5,751.51 after 25% reduction) plus compensatory award (£5,613.05 after 25% ACAS uplift then 25% reduction) for constructive unfair dismissal

deep.facts: Mr Platt, a Sales Director at Bidvest Noonan on a £145,000 salary, disclosed at a 24 January 2024 board meeting that pipeline/sales opportunities were being incorrectly valued (e.g. a contract worth £17 million given a £1 value) on the Agresso system, figures he believed were being sent to the South African parent for forecasting. He was dismissed during his probationary period. He alleged the disclosure was the real reason for his dismissal and for detriments, while the respondent relied on performance.
issues: Did the claimant make one or more qualifying protected disclosures under s.43B ERA, including a reasonable belief it was in the public interest?
Was the claimant automatically unfairly dismissed under s.103A ERA because of the protected disclosure?
Was the claimant subjected to detriment under s.47B ERA because of the protected disclosure?
Should compensation be reduced for contributory fault under s.123(6)?
deep.legal_test: qualifying/protected disclosure under s.43B ERA with the Chesterton public interest threshold, automatic unfair dismissal under s.103A ERA, and detriment under s.47B ERA
deep.evidence_weighing: The absence of any contemporaneous documentary evidence supporting the respondent's claims of poor performance (e.g. at the sales conference), and the fact key managers (Flanagan and Sneath) did not give evidence, told against the respondent; the 24 January disclosure was found to be a clear turning point.
deep.reasoning: The tribunal accepted the claimant disclosed information he reasonably and in the public interest believed showed a legal-obligation breach (inaccurate valuations sent to the parent). It found the disclosure marked a turning point leading to his dismissal, so both the s.103A automatic unfair dismissal and s.47B detriment complaints were well founded. As his conduct was not blameworthy and no expenses/conduct issue caused the dismissal, there was no s.123(6) reduction. Remedy (including Polkey, Devis v Atkins and mitigation) was left to a separate hearing.

cases.respondent: City Site Solutions Ltd and Rocket PAYE Ltd

deep.facts: Mr Patykivskyi, a Ukrainian building labourer, worked January-October 2023 under a 'Contract for Services' and brought claims of holiday pay and direct race discrimination based on his Ukrainian nationality against City Site Solutions Ltd (first respondent) and Rocket PAYE Ltd (second respondent). He alleged the respondent decided he was ineligible for the construction industry CIS payment scheme because of his nationality, having heard a UK labourer was paid through CIS. The respondents said his payment treatment turned on whether he was subject to supervision, direction or control, not nationality.
issues: Was the claimant a 'worker' within s.230(3)(b) ERA so as to be entitled to holiday pay?
Was the claimant subjected to direct race discrimination under s.13 EqA based on his Ukrainian nationality regarding the CIS payment scheme?
Which respondent was liable?
deep.legal_test: worker status under s.230(3)(b) ERA (Ready Mixed Concrete / Autoclenz / Stuart Delivery v Augustine, substitution per Deliveroo) for holiday pay; direct discrimination under s.13 EqA with the shifting burden of proof
deep.evidence_weighing: The claimant could give no name or description of the alleged comparator UK labourer paid through CIS; the respondents' witnesses adamantly denied any such comparator and the documentary evidence supported their distinction between those subject to supervision/control and those not.
deep.reasoning: On worker status, the tribunal found the claimant was a worker under s.230(3)(b) and his holiday pay claim succeeded against the second respondent for £1,754.32. On race discrimination, the claimant failed to establish primary facts shifting the burden; the tribunal accepted the genuine reason he was not paid under CIS was that, unlike a site manager, he was subject to supervision, direction or control, not his nationality. The race claim was dismissed and all complaints against the first respondent were dismissed.
deep.award_basis: accrued but unpaid holiday pay (gross) payable by the second respondent

deep.facts: Ms Harrington, lead of Vodafone's Analyst Relations team, made allegations of sex discrimination against her line manager Mr Kapadia in 2022 and later raised a formal grievance. She was placed on garden leave from 15 September 2022 and dismissed with effect from 31 October 2022, purportedly for redundancy arising from an 'Opex challenge' to cut operating costs. She claimed unfair dismissal and victimisation for having done protected acts; the respondent conceded unfair dismissal subject to Polkey and mitigation.
issues: Which of the claimant's complaints amounted to protected acts under s.27 EqA?
Was the claimant victimised (subjected to detriment because of protected acts), in particular by being placed on garden leave and by being dismissed?
Which of the various alleged victimisation detriments were because of the protected acts versus other reasons?
deep.legal_test: unfair dismissal under ss.94 and 98 ERA (conceded); victimisation under s.27 EqA with the burden of proof under s.136 EqA (Durrani, Fullah, Chalmers on what amounts to a protected act)
deep.evidence_weighing: The respondent's unexplained failure to disclose WhatsApp communications between key decision-makers (Kelly and Jobbins) counted against it on the garden leave and dismissal allegations; on the pay-rise allegation the tribunal accepted the documented 'comp ratio' explanation that the claimant already earned above the band maximum.
deep.reasoning: Unfair dismissal was well founded by concession. On victimisation, the tribunal found the admitted grievance and certain later complaints were protected acts but that earlier statements did not clearly imply discrimination. It upheld victimisation only for the garden leave (allegation 22) and the dismissal (allegation 26), inferring the protected acts were an operative reason given the evidential gaps, while dismissing other allegations where innocent explanations (e.g. timing pre-dating protected acts, comp ratio) were accepted.

deep.facts: Mr Rothwell worked for FremantleMedia on various production engagements (e.g. Britain's Got Talent, X Factor) for over twelve years from 2012 to June 2024, alternating between PAYE and self-employment. He alleged the company engineered movement between statuses to circumvent employment law and brought claims including whistleblowing detriment, the sole detriment being the failure to re-engage him after his last contract ended 7 June 2024. A preliminary hearing first determined his employment status.
issues: Was the claimant an employee within s.230(3)(a) ERA?
Did the alleged disclosures (PD1-PD8) amount to qualifying protected disclosures under s.43B ERA, in particular whether the claimant held a reasonable belief they were in the public interest?
Was the claimant subjected to whistleblowing detriment (failure to re-engage) under s.47B ERA?
deep.legal_test: employee status under s.230(3)(a) ERA (Autoclenz, substitution per Deliveroo); qualifying/protected disclosure under s.43B ERA (information, reasonable belief, public interest); detriment under s.47B ERA
deep.evidence_weighing: On the disclosures, the tribunal accepted the respondent's written analysis in full, finding the claimant lacked a reasonable belief that any disclosure was in the public interest; covert recordings and WhatsApp messages showing the claimant actively pursuing Schedule D (self-employed) terms cut against his employee-status case.
deep.reasoning: At the preliminary hearing the judge found the claimant was not an employee within s.230(3)(a), which caused all complaints except whistleblowing detriment to fall away. At the final hearing the tribunal accepted the respondent's analysis that none of the eight alleged disclosures was a protected disclosure, principally because the claimant lacked a reasonable belief they were in the public interest, so the whistleblowing detriment complaint failed at the first stage. The tribunal nonetheless made findings on the alleged detriments, but the claim did not succeed.

deep.facts: Dr Kumar, a wheelchair-using Teaching Fellow at University College London with Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome and severe sight impairment, claimed disability discrimination. Her department's Grade II listed Georgian buildings at Tavistock Square and Gordon Square were not wheelchair accessible, social events and away days were held in inaccessible venues, no Personal Emergency Evacuation Plan was in place, she was not given longer or fewer papers to mark, and she was unsuccessful in an FTE uplift application. She brought failure to make reasonable adjustments, harassment and other Equality Act complaints.
issues: Did the respondent fail to make reasonable adjustments under ss.20-21 EqA in respect of accessible venues, a platform lift, a PEEP, and marking workload?
Did conduct amount to harassment related to disability under s.26 EqA?
Was the FTE uplift refusal discrimination arising from disability under s.15 EqA?
Were complaints in time, including whether there was a continuing discriminatory state of affairs and whether to extend time?
deep.legal_test: reasonable adjustments under ss.20-21 EqA; harassment under s.26 EqA ('related to' per Tees Esk and Wear Valleys NHS v Aslam); discrimination arising from disability under s.15 EqA; time limits and just and equitable extension under s.123 EqA (continuing act)
deep.evidence_weighing: The tribunal accepted Professor Lauderdale's evidence that the successful FTE candidates could deliver more core teaching and that the claimant's proposed external work was incompatible with the uplift, defeating the s.15 complaint; it distinguished infrequent social events/away days (which should have been accessible) from c.100 seminars (where full accessibility was not a reasonable adjustment).
deep.reasoning: The tribunal found a continuing discriminatory state of affairs (exclusion from the buildings 2017-2025), so the complaints were in time. It upheld reasonable-adjustment failures for accessible social/away-day venues, the platform lift, the PEEP and marking workload, and upheld a harassment complaint, but held that providing accessible venues for all ~100 seminars was not reasonable. The FTE uplift refusal was justified on Professor Lauderdale's accepted reasoning. Liability was established with remedy directions (later superseded by a reconsideration judgment).

deep.facts: Mr Scaburri, an assistant store manager at Hackett Limited's One New Change store, was dismissed for misconduct relating to an inappropriate/flirtatious message and conduct towards his (anonymised) store manager SS, together with a breach of his suspension instructions (he was in store for 20-22 minutes talking to employees while suspended). He claimed unfair dismissal, suggesting prior friction with the HRBP over a recruitment exercise and a colleague's visa application coloured the process.
issues: Did the respondent have a genuine belief in the claimant's misconduct on reasonable grounds after a reasonable investigation?
Did the sanction of dismissal fall within the band of reasonable responses?
deep.legal_test: band of reasonable responses for conduct dismissal (Burchell v BHS three-stage test; British Leyland v Swift; Iceland Frozen Foods v Jones) under s.98(4) ERA 1996
deep.evidence_weighing: The judge found the alleged prior friction with the HRBP insignificant (the HRBP did not recall it and the polite email exchange did not support it); there was clear undisputed evidence the claimant breached the suspension policy by remaining in store and talking to staff.
deep.reasoning: Applying Burchell and the band of reasonable responses, the judge found the inappropriate message, the office flirtation and the undisputed breach of the suspension policy together merited disciplinary sanction. While some employers might have given a final written warning instead, a reasonable employer could have dismissed, so the sanction fell within the range of reasonable responses. The dismissal was therefore fair and the claim did not succeed.

cases.respondent: Evcia Assets Ltd and T S Doyle

deep.facts: Mrs Yadid was engaged in connection with Mr Doyle's venture to install EV charging units in residential blocks. The First Respondent (Evcia Assets Limited) admitted she was its employee from 9 November 2023 and conceded two months' unpaid wages. The contested part was whether she had been promised a £50,000 annual salary payable personally by Mr Doyle (the Second Respondent) for a minimum six months, versus the respondent's case that the early arrangement with her brother was commission-only ('keep what you catch') at £250 per building.
issues: Was there an unauthorised deduction from wages by the First Respondent for the conceded period?
Had the claimant agreed a £50,000 salary for which Mr Doyle was personally liable?
Was there an ACAS uplift and what holiday pay was due?
deep.legal_test: unauthorised deduction from wages under s.13 ERA 1996; contractual analysis of the terms agreed (burden on the claimant to prove the alleged £50,000 salary and personal liability)
deep.evidence_weighing: The contemporaneous November 2023 message exchange supported Mr Doyle's commission account and there was no September 2023 evidence supporting a £50,000 salary; the tribunal reasoned the claimant would have pushed back if she had already agreed £50k but was being offered only £15k, which she did not.
deep.reasoning: The First Respondent's concession plus an unless order (which dismissed its response) meant the unauthorised deductions claim against it was well founded, and judgment was entered for the conceded £8,333.34 (two months at £4,166.67). On the contested claim against Mr Doyle personally, the burden was on the claimant to prove the £50,000 salary and personal liability; on conflicting accounts the tribunal found the contemporaneous evidence supported a commission-only arrangement never triggered, so that claim was dismissed despite sympathy for the claimant.
deep.award_basis: two months' unpaid wages (unauthorised deduction) payable by the First Respondent, less tax and NI

cases.claimant: Mr E Somboonsarn and Ms H Dudar
cases.respondent: Anglo Thai Ltd and Finfish Catering Ltd

deep.facts: The two claimants, Mr Somboonsarn (Eggy) and his wife Ms Dudar (Helen), claimed unfair dismissal and breach of contract against two family-run Thai restaurant companies, against a background of bitter family litigation including a prior High Court judgment on business ownership. The First Claimant had been a statutory director of both respondents and the case turned on whether each claimant was an employee under s.230 ERA and, if so, whether they were constructively dismissed. The First Claimant's claims were not well founded; the Second Claimant's were.
issues: Were the claimants employees of the respondents within the meaning of s.230(1) ERA 1996?
If so, were they constructively dismissed?
Was each claimant entitled to notice pay as a breach of contract claim?
What basic award and breach of contract sums were due to any successful claimant?
deep.legal_test: Employment status under s.230(1) ERA 1996 applying the Ready Mixed Concrete v Minister of Pensions [1968] 2 QB 497 three-fold test (work/skill for remuneration, control, and consistency with a contract of service), as endorsed in Autoclenz v Belcher [2011] ICR 1157; constructive unfair dismissal and breach of contract (notice pay) under the ET Extension of Jurisdiction Order 1994.
deep.evidence_weighing: The judge had a very large documentary bundle and witness statements from both claimants and the respondents' owner Mrs Walker (the First Claimant's mother) and her daughter, and deferred to the High Court's findings of fact on the disputed family/ownership background.
deep.reasoning: Applying the Ready Mixed Concrete/Autoclenz framework to employment status and then assessing the circumstances of termination, the judge found the First Claimant's unfair dismissal and breach of contract claims not well founded and dismissed them, while finding the Second Claimant's claims well founded. The Second Claimant was awarded basic awards calculated on her years of service and weekly pay (£323.08) for each respondent, plus breach of contract notice pay of £1,400 against each, capped to avoid double recovery with the compensatory element.
deep.award_basis: Second Claimant: basic awards £5,169.28 (R1) + £5,815.44 (R2) plus breach of contract notice pay £1,400 against each respondent (less tax)

cases.respondent: Ground Truth Intelligence Ltd and Others

deep.facts: Mrs de Mentaberry joined Ground Truth Intelligence as Head of Sales & Marketing, first as a consultant then as an employee, and was later replaced in the sales leadership by a more highly-paid US hire (Bill Yong) recruited as Chief Revenue Officer. The respondents pursued a 'protected conversation' and proposed an agreed termination/reduced severance, and threatened to make her redundant if she did not accept. She claimed she was misled about pay discrepancies, harassed, victimised after raising a discrimination complaint, and ultimately dismissed.
issues: Was the claimant unfairly dismissed under ss.94 & 98 ERA 1996?
Did the respondents victimise the claimant under s.27 EqA 2010 by threatening redundancy if she refused the reduced severance and by dismissing her?
Was there direct sex discrimination under ss.13/39 EqA?
Was there harassment related to sex under ss.26/40 EqA?
Was there an equal pay breach under ss.64-71 EqA?
Was there a breach of contract?
deep.legal_test: Unfair dismissal under ss.94 & 98 ERA (fair reason + band of reasonable responses, with Polkey/Software 2000 on remedy); victimisation under s.27 EqA (detriment because of a protected act); direct discrimination/harassment under ss.13/26 EqA and equal pay under ss.64-71 EqA
deep.evidence_weighing: The Tribunal relied on contemporaneous correspondence (including WhatsApp/email about the 'protected conversation' and severance) and made findings on the balance of probabilities and inherent plausibility; it found the dismissal and the redundancy threat were tied to her protected complaint of discrimination, but the underlying pay and harassment allegations were not supported (she had received commission male comparators did not, and prioritised base salary).
deep.reasoning: The judge found the dismissal unfair and that two specific acts - threatening redundancy if she refused the reduced severance, and dismissing her - were acts of victimisation following her protected act (the September 2023 discrimination complaint). However, the broader claims of direct sex discrimination, harassment, equal pay and breach of contract were not made out because the pay differential was explained by commission arrangements and her own salary choices, and no discriminatory motive was established. The claims against the second respondent were stayed and the remaining claims against the third respondent dismissed.

deep.facts: Dr Jiang was a Marie Curie post-doctoral research fellow hosted by SOAS, funded by an EU Commission fellowship, researching the Chinese criminal justice system. After her relationships with successive supervisors broke down and the funder chased outstanding deliverables, SOAS dismissed her for 'some other substantial reason' (breakdown in trust and confidence) without a hearing or appeal, saying she had failed to evidence required work. She claimed she made five protected disclosures (including alleged falsification of an ethics report) and was automatically unfairly dismissed and subjected to detriment for whistleblowing, plus owed wages.
issues: Were the claimant's five alleged disclosures qualifying protected disclosures under s.43B/43G ERA?
Was she automatically unfairly dismissed under s.103A ERA because of a protected disclosure?
Was she subjected to detriment under s.47B ERA?
Was there an unlawful deduction from wages under s.13 ERA (and any arrears/holiday pay)?
deep.legal_test: Whether disclosures were qualifying protected disclosures within s.43B ERA (reasonable belief, public interest, tending to show a relevant failure); automatic unfair dismissal under s.103A and detriment under s.47B ERA; unlawful deduction under s.13 ERA
deep.evidence_weighing: The Tribunal worked from a largely agreed chronology and found the dismissal genuinely flowed from the breakdown in trust/confidence and failure to produce deliverables as the funder demanded, not from any disclosure; on wages, the claimant conceded the respondent never agreed to extend her contract and she had received three months' notice pay.
deep.reasoning: The Tribunal concluded none of the alleged disclosures qualified for protection under s.43B, so the s.103A and s.47B whistleblowing complaints necessarily failed. The dismissal was not on the ground of any protected disclosure but because of the genuine breakdown in trust and the absence of deliverable work. The wages claim failed because there was no agreement to extend the contract and the framing of a 'balancing' sum could not succeed; holiday pay was not pursued.

deep.facts: Ms Pennington MBE, a long-serving Home Office employee, applied during October 2022 to September 2023 for various roles after meeting the standard for an SCO grade but was not put forward through the Home Office Resourcing Centre (HORC) reserve-list process. She has dyslexia and complained that the HORC system operated to discriminate against her. The Home Office's witnesses explained the system matches roles to anonymised reserve lists, not individuals, and recruiters were unaware of her disability.
issues: Was the claimant subjected to direct disability discrimination under ss.13 & 39 EqA 2010 in not being put forward for roles through the HORC reserve-list process?
deep.legal_test: Direct disability discrimination under ss.13 & 39 EqA 2010 - less favourable treatment because of disability (with the burden of proof / s.136 principle noted, but the Tribunal able to make positive findings on motivation)
deep.evidence_weighing: Key was David Barnes's oral evidence (confirmed) that recruiting consultants and vacancy holders were unaware of the claimant's disability because the reserve-list system matches lists not individuals; the claimant could not name anyone who had 'blacklisted' her and conceded the 13 listed roles were irrelevant.
deep.reasoning: Because the HORC process matched roles to anonymised reserve lists and the data that the claimant was disabled was not visible to those making selections, the Tribunal could not see how her disability could have influenced any outcome. It made a positive finding that the system operated non-discriminatorily and that dyslexia was not the reason she did not obtain a role, so the s.13 claim failed, though the Tribunal noted unsatisfactory aspects of the system and a possible lack of positive support for disabled applicants.

deep.facts: Mr Walcott, an Afro-Caribbean Automatic Technician at London Underground, complained that he received no backdated pay (a difference agreed to be worth GBP 18,900) calculated from licensing date to course-passing date, whereas two white colleagues did. The respondent explained the discrepancy as arising from a 'change of circumstances' over five years, with the decision-maker Mr Darke defaulting to a 'custom and practice' expectation about timely licensing. The Tribunal accepted he was treated less favourably than the white comparators.
issues: Was the claimant subjected to direct race discrimination under ss.13 & 39 EqA 2010 in the denial of backdated pay relative to white comparators?
deep.legal_test: Direct race discrimination under ss.13 & 39 EqA 2010 - whether the established less favourable treatment was because of race (significant influence test)
deep.evidence_weighing: Decisive was the Tribunal's finding, on the balance of probabilities, that the decision-maker Mr Darke did not know the claimant's race (his clear testimony, responsible for some 800 staff, was unchallenged), and that no other mechanism for race to have influenced the decision was suggested.
deep.reasoning: The Tribunal accepted the claimant was treated less favourably than two white colleagues and that the disparity was stark and his sense of injustice understandable. However, because Mr Darke (the decision-maker) did not know the claimant's race and no alternative route for race to influence the outcome was identified, the Tribunal could not find that race was a significant influence. The less favourable treatment was therefore not because of race and the claim was dismissed.

cases.respondent: Stanley-Idum v Ministry of Defence and Others

deep.facts: Mr Stanley-Idum, a civil servant at the Ministry of Defence, brought race discrimination, harassment, victimisation, associative disability discrimination and ERA detriment claims relating to performance management and treatment by various line/tasking managers between October 2021 and April 2023. The MoD's case centred on genuine performance concerns; incidents included his rude/disrespectful emails to managers (e.g. dissecting a manager's LinkedIn profile) and his refusal to answer questions (~28 times) in an internal investigation. He withdrew all claims against the four individual respondents during the hearing.
issues: Should time be extended for the out-of-time complaints (detriment under ss.44 & 47C ERA, harassment, direct race discrimination, victimisation and associative disability discrimination)?
Was victimisation allegation 5.2.11 (the only in-time allegation) well founded under s.27 EqA?
Were the substantive race discrimination, harassment, victimisation and disability discrimination allegations made out?
deep.legal_test: Just-and-equitable extension of time for EqA/ERA complaints; victimisation under s.27 EqA; direct race discrimination under s.13 EqA; harassment under s.26 EqA; ERA detriment under ss.44/47C; (with the burden of proof under s.136 EqA applied to discrimination allegations)
deep.evidence_weighing: The Tribunal accepted managers' evidence (e.g. Mr Smart's) that the claimant had not raised race/discrimination at the relevant times and that complaints were better characterised as 'micromanagement'; it found the performance concerns and managers' conduct were genuine and unrelated to race, and that several factual allegations were not made out.
deep.reasoning: Almost all complaints were brought out of time and the Tribunal declined to extend time on a just-and-equitable basis, dismissing them; it added that even if in time it would have dismissed each on the substantive merits because the treatment flowed from genuine performance concerns and the claimant's own conduct, not from race or protected acts. The only in-time allegation, victimisation 5.2.11, was dismissed on the substantive merits. The claims against the four individual respondents were dismissed on withdrawal.

deep.facts: Miss Medcraft, a long-serving Chanel employee, had her job title left in limbo during 2022-2024 (the disputed removal of 'manager' from her title) and was unsuccessful in several internal applications. She alleged she suffered detrimental treatment because she made six protected disclosures (relating to alleged breaches of the Computer Misuse Act, Data Protection Act/GDPR, including alleged deletion/amendment of emails). The respondent's grievance/appeal partly upheld some title and backdated-pay points but rejected the data-tampering allegation as technically impossible.
issues: Were the six alleged disclosures qualifying protected disclosures under s.43B ERA (reasonable belief they tended to show a relevant failure; and public interest)?
Should time be extended for the first eight alleged detriments?
Did the claimant suffer detriment, and if so was it on the ground of a protected disclosure under s.47B ERA?
deep.legal_test: Whether disclosures qualified under s.43B ERA (reasonable belief tending to show a relevant failure, made in the public interest, applying the objective-plus-personal-circumstances standard) and protected-disclosure detriment under s.47B ERA
deep.evidence_weighing: The Tribunal found the first five disclosures unprotected because it was not reasonable for the claimant to believe they tended to show the relevant failure, and the sixth lacked any genuine or reasonable public-interest belief; on the disciplinary-vs-grievance detriment, it relied on documentary evidence and Ms Roberts'/Ms Wade's confirmations that no disciplinary was in train.
deep.reasoning: The claim failed at the threshold because none of the six alleged disclosures came within s.43B - the first five failed the reasonable-belief test and the sixth failed the public-interest requirement. The first eight detriments were also out of time with no extension granted, and in any event the claimant did not establish detrimental treatment (e.g. she was not subject to a disciplinary process; an invitation letter omission was not a detriment). Despite considerable sympathy for the claimant over her title limbo, the s.47B claim was dismissed.
