deep.facts: Miss Duggal, a Banking Consultant with the respondent bank (Lloyds Banking Group), had several disabilities including photophobia, dry eye and frozen shoulder. The bank declined, on cost/principle grounds, to make all the adjustments she sought at her branch (e.g. removing ductwork costing over GBP 10,000, or removing an IT security box under her desk), and moved her to a home-based Fraud team role, which did not work out; she was then dismissed. She claimed failure to make reasonable adjustments, disability harassment, direct disability discrimination, s.15 discrimination and unfair dismissal.
issues: Did the respondent fail to make reasonable adjustments under the EqA?
Was there harassment related to disability under the EqA?
Was there direct disability discrimination under s.13 EqA?
Was there discrimination arising from disability under s.15 EqA?
Was the dismissal unfair under ss.94 & 98 ERA?
deep.legal_test: Reasonable adjustments duty, harassment, direct discrimination (s.13) and discrimination arising from disability (s.15) under the EqA 2010; unfair dismissal under ss.94 & 98 ERA - whether dismissal for 'some other substantial reason' (s.98(1)(b)) fell within the band of reasonable responses
deep.evidence_weighing: The Tribunal weighed the bank's evidence (Mrs Webster's letters/emails) showing it explored multiple adjustments and that the disputed measures were not reasonable (excessive cost, IT security), and the Fraud-team managers' evidence (Ms Perkins, Mrs Howard) that the claimant struggled with the role's basic IT/troubleshooting; it noted the claimant raised many innocuous concerns and elected not to attend the final dismissal hearing.
deep.reasoning: The judge (sitting alone) found the contended adjustments were not reasonable given excessive cost and IT-security constraints, so the reasonable-adjustments and related discrimination claims failed. On dismissal, the reason was SOSR within s.98(1)(b) and the decision to dismiss - both substantively and procedurally - fell within the band of reasonable responses, given the insurmountable obstacles to the Banking Consultant role and the failure of the Fraud role, the multiple opportunities to engage, and the exercised appeal. All claims were dismissed and remedy did not arise.

reasoning_profile.disposition_summary: Dick is a credibility-led, employer-leaning-on-the-facts judge who dismisses a large share of discrimination and unfair-dismissal claims after preferring the respondent's witnesses and finding the real reason to be conduct, capability or genuine performance rather than a protected characteristic. He nonetheless reaches measured split results, upholding procedural unfairness or discrete discrimination/deduction points and awarding undisputed sums (notably on undefended Rule 21/absent-respondent claims). He is careful and fact-specific, often making positive causation findings rather than resting on the burden of proof alone.
reasoning_profile.procedural_vs_substantive: balanced - he decides many cases on substantive credibility and causation, but also resolves a notable cluster on employment/employee status, TUPE and reasonably-practicable/just-and-equitable time limits.
reasoning_profile.evidence_approach: Credibility is frequently decisive: he scrutinises the claimant's account against contemporaneous records (logs, surveys, medical reports) and disbelieves accounts of conversations that documents do not support, while accepting unchallenged respondent evidence; on undefended claims he relies on the unchallenged claim form and sworn evidence.
recurring_themes: credibility findings drive outcomes (whose account is accepted)
separates genuine conduct/capability reason from alleged discrimination
procedural unfairness can co-exist with a supportable substantive belief
employee/employment status and TUPE/continuity as thresholds
reasonably-practicable and just-and-equitable time limits applied strictly
comparator and 'related to' analysis on direct discrimination/harassment
common_legal_tests: s.98 ERA two-stage and band of reasonable responses (Burchell); Polkey, s.123(6)
s.15 discrimination arising from disability and ss.20/21 reasonable adjustments
s.13/s.26 EqA with s.23 comparator and s.136 burden of proof
s.230 ERA / TUPE employee status and continuity (Ready Mixed Concrete)
reasonably-practicable (Palmer, Asda v Kausar, Lowri Beck) and s.123 extension
Rule 21 default judgment where no response is presented
reasoning_profile.deliberation_guidance: Resolve the factual disputes first by deciding whose account is more credible, testing each side against the contemporaneous documents and medical evidence and disbelieving conversation accounts that the records do not support. Separate the genuine operative reason (conduct, capability, performance) from the protected characteristic, and be willing to make a positive finding that the reason was not discriminatory. Recognise that a procedurally unfair dismissal can still rest on a substantively supportable belief. Check status, continuity and time-limit thresholds where raised, applying them strictly, and on undefended claims rely on the unchallenged pleaded case and sworn evidence.

cases.respondent: West Hertfordshire Teaching Hospitals NHS Trust

deep.facts: Mr Irish was a Band 2 Distribution/Delivery Officer at an NHS Trust hospital whose role was physical and required use of a 'pump truck'. After an accident at work he was on sick leave from October 2021 until his dismissal in November 2022; the Trust dismissed him for capability (long-term absence), there being no suggestion he was bad at his job. He claimed unfair dismissal (procedural and substantive, including that the Trust should have made further medical enquiries and waited longer), direct disability discrimination, s.15 discrimination arising from disability, and failure to make reasonable adjustments.
issues: Was the unfair dismissal complaint in time?
Was the dismissal for capability (long-term absence) fair under s.98 ERA?
Was the claimant directly discriminated against because of disability under s.13 EqA?
Was there discrimination arising from disability under s.15 EqA?
Did the Trust fail to make reasonable adjustments (e.g. postponing sickness meetings, redeployment, the pump-truck requirement)?
deep.legal_test: Unfair dismissal under s.98 ERA (two-stage: potentially fair reason then reasonableness within the band of reasonable responses); direct discrimination (s.13), discrimination arising from disability (s.15) and reasonable adjustments under the EqA 2010
deep.evidence_weighing: The Tribunal accepted the claimant's genuine sense of grievance but found, on the medical evidence including a December 2023 report, that he would have remained physically unfit regardless of the Trust's actions and that there was no basis to attribute his depression or non-recovery to the employer; it found he never lodged an appeal despite saying he would.
deep.reasoning: The Tribunal found the dismissal was in time, was for the potentially fair reason of capability (long-term absence), and was fair - the Trust acted reasonably and the claimant would have remained unfit regardless of any earlier or further steps. The disability discrimination and reasonable-adjustments claims failed on the facts (the absences/incapacity were addressed appropriately and the contended steps would not have made a difference), so all complaints were dismissed; the holiday-pay claim was dismissed upon withdrawal.

deep.facts: Mr Mezgebe was engaged as a Senior IT Technician by a North London secondary school, first as an agency worker (December 2019) then as an employee (September 2020), and was dismissed on 25 February 2021 at the end of his six-month probation. He had obstructive sleep apnoea (an agreed disability) and asserted he had told various staff he was clinically vulnerable and needed to shield; the school disputed its knowledge of disability and denied the shielding conversations. He pursued discrimination arising from disability (s.15), failure to make reasonable adjustments and victimisation (other claims being withdrawn).
issues: Did the respondent have knowledge (actual or constructive) of the claimant's disability?
Was the claimant treated unfavourably because of something arising in consequence of disability under s.15 EqA (e.g. inability to attend work)?
Did the respondent fail to make reasonable adjustments?
Was the claimant victimised under s.27 EqA?
Should time be extended for out-of-time parts of the reasonable-adjustments complaint?
deep.legal_test: Discrimination arising from disability under s.15 EqA (unfavourable treatment because of something arising in consequence of disability, ordinary-meaning approach per T-Systems/EHRC Code); reasonable adjustments duty; victimisation under s.27 EqA; burden of proof under s.136 EqA (Igen/Madarassy/Zafar/Hewage)
deep.evidence_weighing: Credibility was decisive: the panel unanimously disbelieved the claimant's account of the January shielding conversation with Mr Ali and Mr Davies (accepting Mr Davies's evidence that it did not happen) and found he had not told the truth; the majority found the 18 May survey was the only health information he provided, while Mr Sagar dissented, accepting he also provided the November shielding letter.
deep.reasoning: The majority found the claimant's November absence did not arise in consequence of his disability (he had not proved his disability increased Covid susceptibility), defeating the s.15 claim. The reasonable-adjustments and victimisation claims failed because the school lacked the requisite knowledge and the claimant's evidence about notifying staff and shielding requests was not accepted. The Tribunal extended time for the out-of-time reasonable-adjustments parts but still dismissed all live complaints; the withdrawn complaints were dismissed on withdrawal.

deep.facts: 3D Force Ltd, a small CIS company doing kitchen and bathroom refurbishment with two PAYE employees but significant use of subcontractors, was issued a construction industry levy of GBP 5,147 by the Construction Industry Training Board on 22 April 2024. The appellant appealed on three grounds: that it was not in a category subject to the levy, that the levy was miscalculated, and that similar businesses had not been levied. The levy figure was based principally on around GBP 407,165 it had declared.
issues: Was the appellant within the category of businesses subject to the construction industry levy under the 1964 Order?
Was the levy correctly calculated under the 2022 Levy Order?
Did the fact that other similar businesses were not levied invalidate the levy?
deep.legal_test: Statutory appeal under ss.12(4)-(5) Industrial Training Act 1982 against a levy assessment - whether the levy was correctly applied and calculated under the 1964 Order and the Industrial Training Levy (CITB) Order 2022, with the tribunal confirming the assessment unless satisfied it should be reduced/quashed
deep.evidence_weighing: The Tribunal relied on the uncontested written evidence of Mr Domnisor and the agreed bundle, including the company's own declared figure of about GBP 407,165 on which the levy was based; it was not persuaded by the appellant's grounds.
deep.reasoning: Taking the three grounds together, the Tribunal concluded the levy was correctly applied and correctly calculated and that the appellant had not satisfied it to the contrary. It accordingly confirmed the levy of GBP 5,147 and dismissed the appeal, while encouraging the parties to discuss the respondent's offer of payment by instalments (over which the tribunal had no power).

cases.respondent: Mr R Khodabux and NSSL Group Ltd

deep.facts: Miss O'Halloran worked in a housekeeper role at the first respondent's (Mr Khodabux's) home between 28 June and 14 August 2024, during a period when the respondent was going through a separation and required discretion. At a preliminary hearing the sole issue was her employment status - whether she was an employee within the meaning of s.83 EqA 2010 (for the purposes of her Equality Act discrimination/discriminatory-constructive-dismissal claims), there being no ERA/unfair dismissal claim. The respondent contended she was a contractor; she contended she was an employee.
issues: Was the claimant employed by either or both respondents in a housekeeper role during 28 June to 14 August 2024?
Was there a requirement for personal service?
Was the relationship one of subordination rather than the claimant being in business on her own account?
deep.legal_test: Whether the claimant was an 'employee' within the extended meaning of s.83 Equality Act 2010 - assessed by reference to personal service and subordination (whether the relationship was that of a business undertaking and its customer)
deep.evidence_weighing: The judge weighed the high degree of trust and discretion personally placed in the claimant (e.g. the respondent's wish that specific people not learn of his separation), the limited scope for substitution, and the fact the work extended beyond cleaning into organising personal areas of the respondent's life - concluding personal service was required despite a small sample size.
deep.reasoning: The judge found a requirement for personal service, given the trust and discretion required, the personal nature of the work and the substitution findings, and then found the claimant was subordinate rather than running her own business (she was not in business as a housekeeper and the relationship was not that of business-and-customer). It followed that she was an employee of the first respondent within s.83 EqA - a preliminary point decided in the claimant's favour, with the substantive discrimination claims to follow.

deep.facts: Mrs Ross founded and ran a beauty salon through Nikki Marks Ltd (NML), of which she and her husband were shareholders/directors. On 22 September 2023 all shares in NML were sold to Your Skin Coach Ltd (Miss Jeffrey's company) and the same day Mrs Ross signed an employment contract with NML as a Senior Beauty Therapist; she was dismissed for redundancy on 3 January 2024 with one week's notice. Her unfair dismissal, redundancy-payment and notice claims all depended on showing she was an employee of NML since 2008 (to have the requisite two years' continuous service).
issues: Was the claimant an employee of the respondent within the meaning of the ERA (or TUPE) before the share sale of 22 September 2023?
Was there a relevant TUPE transfer on or around 22 September 2023?
Did the claimant have at least two years' continuous employment to bring unfair dismissal and redundancy-payment claims?
Was she paid the notice pay to which she was entitled?
deep.legal_test: Employment status as an 'employee' under the ERA 1996 and TUPE 2006 (controlling shareholder/director status per IDS Handbook authorities); whether a share sale amounted to a relevant transfer under TUPE; continuity-of-employment / two-year qualifying period for unfair dismissal and redundancy; statutory notice entitlement
deep.evidence_weighing: The judge resolved the status question on the balance of probabilities from the claimant's own evidence about her roles (beauty therapist, head therapist, then manager) and her shareholder/director position; he expressly declined to comment on the wider fairness of Miss Jeffrey's actions, as no evidence on the merits was heard.
deep.reasoning: The judge found the claimant was not an ERA (or TUPE) employee before the share sale and that there was no relevant TUPE transfer on the share sale. Consequently she lacked the two years' continuous employment required, so the unfair dismissal and redundancy-payment complaints were dismissed. The wrongful dismissal claim was also dismissed because she had been paid the one week's statutory notice to which she was entitled.

cases.respondent: Royal Mail Group Ltd and Angard Staffing Solutions Ltd

deep.facts: Mr Adeloye, a black man over 70 with disabilities, was supplied by agency Angard to work for Royal Mail. In January 2023 two Royal Mail employees (Dobe and Buffin) alleged he had used racially discriminatory language about Indian coworkers (e.g. 'They smell of curry', 'All you Indians stick together'), leading to suspension and dismissal for gross misconduct in October 2023. He denied saying these things and claimed the allegations were false and that the dismissal and surrounding events were discrimination, harassment, victimisation and unfair dismissal; he also raised older complaints from 2018-2021 about heavy lifting and toilet-break needs.
issues: Whether complaints about events before 17 January 2023 were in time / part of conduct extending over a period, and whether it was just and equitable to extend time
Whether the dismissal was unfair (substantively and procedurally)
Whether the dismissal and disciplinary events were direct discrimination or harassment related to age, race and/or disability
Whether there was victimisation for the March 2023 grievance and ACAS contact
Whether there was indirect disability discrimination and a failure to make reasonable adjustments
deep.legal_test: Unfair dismissal: s.98 ERA reason and band of reasonable responses (Burchell); remedy adjustments under Polkey and contributory fault s.123(6) ERA. Equality Act claims: time limits / conduct extending over a period and just-and-equitable extension; direct discrimination, harassment, victimisation, indirect discrimination and reasonable adjustments under EqA 2010.
deep.evidence_weighing: The panel found Dobe and Buffin were not lying and that the claimant did make the curry/Indian comments, supported in part by Ms Bodakuntla's evidence; but it found the respondents failed to interview the other people in the room on 26-27 January, which made the process procedurally unfair.
deep.reasoning: The tribunal held the dismissal unfair because Royal Mail/Angard failed to follow a proper procedure (notably not asking the others present what they saw and heard), but separately found on the evidence that the claimant did make the alleged comments, leaving Polkey and contributory-fault reductions to be argued at remedy. Applying the band of reasonable responses, it concluded the disciplinary handling fell short procedurally while the substantive belief was supportable. It dismissed the discrimination, harassment and victimisation complaints for the in-time period as the treatment was not because of age, race or disability, and held the pre-2023 matters were not part of continuing conduct and not just and equitable to extend.

deep.facts: Mr How had driven professionally for Royal Mail since 1996 and had PTSD (an accepted disability) from a 2014 workplace event. On 22 January data showed 'missing miles' where the lorry had been driven for about eight minutes with no tachograph card inserted after stopping in a layby. Following investigation he was dismissed on 10 August 2023; he said he removed the card because the machine told him to take a break, and claimed unfair dismissal and direct disability discrimination.
issues: Whether the dismissal was unfair under s.98 ERA
If unfair, whether a Polkey reduction or contributory-fault reduction should apply
Whether the dismissal was direct disability discrimination under s.13 EqA (less favourable treatment because of disability, against a hypothetical comparator)
deep.legal_test: Unfair dismissal: s.98 ERA, ACAS-style procedural steps and band of reasonable responses (Burchell); Polkey and s.123(6) contributory fault. Direct disability discrimination: s.13 EqA read with s.6, comparator under s.23 (Hewage v Grampian).
deep.evidence_weighing: The tribunal accepted the respondent witnesses' unchallenged evidence about the tachograph operation and the logs at [285] showing the card was out from 6:23pm while the lorry was driven to the depot, and accepted Mr Farrell's evidence about the claimant's account.
deep.reasoning: The tribunal accepted the respondent's account of the tachograph breach and that a fair investigation and process had been carried out, so the conduct dismissal fell within the band of reasonable responses and was not unfair. On the discrimination claim, with disability and knowledge conceded, it found the dismissal was because of the tachograph conduct rather than because of disability, so there was no less favourable treatment relative to a non-disabled comparator with the same conduct. The unauthorised deductions, automatically unfair dismissal and victimisation claims were withdrawn.

deep.facts: Mr Annunziata worked for Milton Keynes City Council as Built Asset Lead from December 2019 until January 2021. In early 2020 he and a colleague identified an air vent installed on the listed Milton Keynes Library facade in apparent breach of the Secretary of State's listed-building consent, and a query email was sent to the Conservation manager. The council said his employment ended through a redundancy restructuring; he said it ended because of whistleblowing about the listed-building breach.
issues: Whether the claimant made a qualifying/protected disclosure under ss.43A-43C ERA about a likely breach of a legal obligation under the listed-building legislation
Whether the claimant was dismissed because of that disclosure or for redundancy
Whether the dismissal was unfair
deep.legal_test: Protected disclosure framework under ss.43A, 43B and 43C ERA (disclosure of information, reasonable belief it tends to show wrongdoing and is in the public interest); unfair dismissal under s.98 ERA, with the contested issue being the reason for dismissal (whistleblowing vs redundancy).
deep.evidence_weighing: The judge heard the claimant plus the council's Miss Lewis (Head of Property) and Mr Proffitt (Director of Environment and Property) and made findings on the balance of probabilities only on points necessary to decide the reason for dismissal.
deep.reasoning: Hearing the evidence, the judge found the dismissal was not because of any protected disclosure but for the reason the respondent advanced, and concluded the unfair dismissal complaint was not well-founded. The reasoning links the redundancy/restructuring account to the finding that the reason was not the vent disclosure, so the dismissal was fair.

deep.facts: Mr Walder claimed unfair dismissal against Mr J Edwards. The respondent purported to run a redundancy process which the claimant said was a sham, because after his employment ended his duties were carried out by two other people. The respondent presented no response and did not attend; the Rule 21 judgment found unfair dismissal, but at a later remedy stage (before EJ Murdoch) the claimant failed to engage and the remedy claim was struck out.
issues: Whether, on an undefended Rule 21 basis, the unfair dismissal complaint was well-founded
Whether the respondent had shown a fair reason (genuine redundancy under s.139 ERA)
Whether to issue judgment under Rule 21 or dismiss under Rule 47 in the claimant's absence
deep.legal_test: Rule 21 default judgment where no response is presented; redundancy as a potentially fair reason under s.139 ERA and the requirement to show a fair reason under s.98 ERA.
deep.evidence_weighing: With no response from the respondent, the judge relied on the unchallenged account in the claimant's claim form, in particular that his duties were taken over by two other people, indicating no genuine redundancy.
deep.reasoning: Under Rule 21 the judge found that, on the unanswered claim form, the respondent had not shown the dismissal was wholly or mainly attributable to a diminished requirement for the claimant's work under s.139 ERA, so no fair reason was shown under s.98 and the dismissal was unfair. Liability was established but remedy was left to a later hearing; that remedy claim was subsequently struck out for the claimant's non-engagement, so although liability was decided in his favour, no award resulted.

deep.facts: Mr Langton was a long-serving firefighter and crew commander at Buckinghamshire Fire and Rescue Service. At a meeting on 22 December 2022 he was alleged to have made misogynistic/sexualised remarks about a female member of the public he had helped rescue. He was summarily dismissed for gross misconduct. He accepted misconduct was the reason for dismissal but argued summary dismissal was disproportionate and the disciplinary process was flawed (ignoring mitigation, treating it as not isolated, no clear findings on what was actually said, relying on an admission he had not made).
issues: Whether the conduct dismissal was fair under s.98 ERA / band of reasonable responses
Whether the disciplinary procedure was flawed so as to render the dismissal unfair
Whether any Polkey reduction should be made (chance of fair dismissal anyway)
Whether and by how much to reduce the basic and compensatory awards for contributory fault
deep.legal_test: Band of reasonable responses applying the Burchell criteria (genuine belief, reasonable grounds, reasonable investigation) under s.98 ERA; Polkey v AE Dayton; contributory fault under ss.122(2) and 123(6) ERA, applying Hollier v Plysu bands and Rao v CAA.
deep.evidence_weighing: The respondent conceded genuine belief and that misconduct was the reason; the judge found the investigation reasonable and that decision-maker Mr Bell had ample evidence, but found Bell took into account too much information and failed to make clear findings on exactly what was said.
deep.reasoning: Applying Burchell and the band of reasonable responses, the judge found genuine belief, reasonable grounds and adequate investigation, but held the dismissal unfair because of procedural flaws including reliance on excessive/irrelevant material and a failure to make clear findings on the gravity of what was said. The judge declined a Polkey reduction but found the claimant's blameworthy conduct contributed to the dismissal, reducing both the basic and compensatory awards by 65% (claimant somewhat-but-not-largely to blame). Remedy quantum was left to a separate hearing.

deep.facts: Ten employees of Complete Restaurant Group Limited brought claims after the restaurant business effectively closed; the respondent did not appear. The claimants were not paid wages for January 2024, several were underpaid for December 2023, and several were owed shares of monthly 'tronc' (tip) payments between November 2023 and January 2024, plus notice pay, redundancy payments and some expenses. The restaurant manager Mr Baiano gave evidence on oath about how the tronc was collected and distributed.
issues: Whether each claimant was entitled to a statutory redundancy payment under s.163 ERA
Whether the failure to pay notice amounted to breach of contract (notice pay damages)
Whether unpaid December and January wages and unpaid tronc shares were unauthorised deductions from wages under ss.13 and 27 ERA
Whether to allow amendments to add tronc/expenses (and refusal of a late holiday-pay amendment)
deep.legal_test: Statutory redundancy entitlement under s.163 ERA; breach of contract for notice pay; unauthorised deductions from wages under ss.13 and 27 ERA, with tronc 'properly payable' per Saavedra v Aceground Ltd; interests-of-justice test for amendments (balance of prejudice).
deep.evidence_weighing: The judge accepted Mr Baiano's sworn evidence about how the tronc pot was collected and distributed monthly with PAYE deducted, which established the tronc was 'properly payable' wages; the claims were otherwise effectively undisputed as the respondent did not appear.
deep.reasoning: With the respondent absent, the judge found each claimant's claims well-founded on the evidence: statutory notice pay for all and redundancy payments for those with over two years' service, unpaid January (and shortfall December) wages as unauthorised deductions, and tronc shares as deductions because, following Saavedra, they were properly payable under ss.13/27 ERA. The judge allowed amendments for tronc/expenses (no prejudice as the respondent had notice of such claims generally) but refused Mr Rae's late holiday-pay amendment and declined to award pension or post-January loss claims as outside jurisdiction. Mr Marek's unfair dismissal complaint was dismissed on withdrawal. Specific sums were ordered in Table 1.
deep.award_basis: Statutory redundancy payments, breach-of-contract notice pay, unauthorised deductions for December and January wages and tronc, and some expenses (individual amounts per claimant in Table 1; totals not stated)

deep.facts: Mr Mughal, a Pakistani Muslim railway Revenue Protection Inspector, complained about remarks made to him by a colleague (Ms Chwohary / 'Ms TB') on 21 December 2022, including 'I respect you because of your colour, but you are all male chauvinist pigs' and 'I hate you', which he said insulted him as a Muslim. He also complained about how the respondent handled his subsequent grievance, including a phone call from Ms Harrison that he later characterised as a threat.
issues: Whether the colleague's remarks and grievance handling amounted to direct race discrimination under s.13 EqA
Whether they amounted to direct religious discrimination under s.13 EqA
Whether the conduct amounted to harassment related to race under s.26 EqA
Whether the conduct amounted to harassment related to religion under s.26 EqA
Time limits (whether complaints were in time)
deep.legal_test: Direct discrimination under s.13 EqA with a hypothetical comparator (no material difference in circumstances, s.23); harassment under s.26 EqA (unwanted conduct related to race/religion having the proscribed purpose or effect, judged on the claimant's perception and reasonableness); EqA time limits.
deep.evidence_weighing: The tribunal accepted that the colleague was generally rude to many colleagues, not just the claimant, and noted the claimant did not clearly or contemporaneously assert he had been threatened by Ms Harrison, undermining the claim that the treatment was because of, or related to, his race or religion.
deep.reasoning: The judge found the colleague's hostility was directed at colleagues generally rather than because of or related to the claimant's race or religion, so it was neither direct discrimination (a hypothetical comparator would have been treated the same) nor harassment related to those characteristics. The grievance-handling complaints, including the alleged threat, were not made out on the evidence as discriminatory or as harassment. All four complaints were dismissed.

deep.facts: Mr Lee was told on 29 January 2024 he was to be made redundant, with his effective date of termination on 29 February 2024. He brought claims for unfair dismissal, notice pay, holiday pay, bonus pay, pension contributions and a redundancy payment. He began ACAS conciliation on 13 May 2024 and presented his claim on 6 August 2024 — out of time for everything except the redundancy payment (which has a six-month limit). He said he had hoped to resolve matters via the Redundancy Payment Service and believed the three-month limit applied only to ACAS conciliation.
issues: Whether the non-redundancy complaints (unfair dismissal, notice, holiday, bonus, pension) were presented within the time limit and, if not, whether it was reasonably practicable to present them in time
Whether the redundancy payment was due (and within its six-month limit)
deep.legal_test: 'Reasonably practicable' / 'not reasonably feasible' test for ERA time limits (Palmer v Southend; Asda v Kausar — burden on claimant; Lowri Beck v Brophy — reasonableness of ignorance/mistake); statutory redundancy payment under s.163 ERA with its six-month limit.
deep.evidence_weighing: The judge accepted the claimant genuinely believed the three-month limit applied only to ACAS and was acting in good faith pursuing the Redundancy Payment Service, but found that by 3 June 2024 he knew only a Tribunal claim would resolve matters and that he had time (e.g. applying for 13 jobs) to present a claim sooner.
deep.reasoning: The judge held the claimant could reasonably have found out the Tribunal time limit, and that his good-faith attempts to resolve matters only assisted him up to 3 June 2024, after which it was reasonably practicable to present in time; the further roughly one-month delay was not reasonable. The non-redundancy claims were therefore dismissed as out of time, while the redundancy payment (undisputed and within its six-month limit) was awarded at GBP 5,144 (eight weeks' pay capped). A later reconsideration application was refused.
deep.award_basis: Statutory redundancy payment (eight weeks' pay subject to the statutory cap)

deep.facts: Ms Ansah was dismissed by Scope (for gross misconduct following a dispute with a colleague) on 8 or 9 November 2023. She brought claims for unfair dismissal, direct race discrimination (the detriment being the dismissal) and unauthorised deductions for unpaid overtime. Early conciliation ran 6-11 March 2024 and she presented her claim on 7 May 2024 — out of time. The case was a preliminary hearing on whether time should be extended; she had personal difficulties at the time but did not file the ordered statement explaining the delay.
issues: Whether the unfair dismissal and unauthorised deductions complaints were presented in time, and if not whether it was reasonably practicable to do so
Whether the race discrimination complaint was presented in time, and if not whether it was just and equitable to extend time
deep.legal_test: 'Reasonably practicable' test for the ERA claims (Asda v Kausar — burden on claimant; Lowri Beck v Brophy); just-and-equitable extension under s.123 EqA, treated as the exception not the rule (Robertson v Bexley), with regard to the Keeble/s.33 Limitation Act checklist.
deep.evidence_weighing: The judge accepted the claimant faced significant personal difficulties beyond the ordinary, but found her circumstances were no different between when she should have acted and when she did act, and noted the discrimination claim was not obviously strong (the claim form gave no basis for a race-based explanation).
deep.reasoning: For the ERA claims the judge applied practicability (not impossibility) and found that, since the claimant managed to start ACAS on 6 March and was able to look for work, it had been reasonably practicable to present in time, so those claims were dismissed. For the race claim, weighing the significant delay, likely prejudice to the respondent, and the weakness of the discrimination case, the judge found it was not just and equitable to extend time and dismissed it. All complaints were dismissed on time-limit grounds.

deep.facts: Ms Beverley, who is black, worked as a mental health support worker for Care Assist Ltd at Whitehall Road, Harrow from 2015. On 5 January 2022 she administered medication unwitnessed in breach of procedure; after a disagreement, manager Mrs Faulkner allegedly told her to leave, her shifts were cancelled, and she was investigated (resulting in no formal sanction) but never offered further shifts, receiving a P45 in August 2022. She claimed race harassment and direct race discrimination (compared with a white Team Leader not suspended after a similar August 2021 incident), detriment for protected disclosures, and unfair/automatically unfair dismissal.
issues: Whether the claimant was an 'employee' within s.230 ERA (a threshold for the unfair dismissal claims)
Whether she made qualifying protected disclosures and was subjected to detriments (not allowed to work at Whitehall Road; being told to leave) for making them
Whether she was directly discriminated against because of race (suspension/preventing work; dismissal)
Whether she was harassed related to race by Mrs Faulkner
Whether she was ordinarily or automatically unfairly dismissed
deep.legal_test: Employment status under s.230 ERA applying Ready Mixed Concrete (mutuality of obligation, personal service, control); protected disclosure framework ss.43A-43B ERA (Kilraine) with detriment under s.47B and burden-shifting under s.48(2); direct race discrimination s.13 EqA with comparator; harassment s.26 EqA; unfair dismissal s.98 / automatically unfair s.103A ERA.
deep.evidence_weighing: The tribunal found the respondent's mutuality-of-obligation argument (no obligation to offer or accept work outside each rota cycle) determined employment status against the claimant; the alleged first protected-disclosure email was never produced in evidence, and the comparator Team Leader was found not to be in a genuinely comparable situation.
deep.reasoning: The tribunal held the claimant was not an employee within s.230 ERA because there was insufficient mutuality of obligation between rota cycles, so the ordinary and automatically unfair dismissal claims failed at the threshold. On the discrimination and detriment claims it found the decision to prevent her working at Whitehall Road was not because of race and had nothing to do with any disclosure, the comparator was not truly comparable, and the harassment was not made out. The holiday pay and arrears claims were withdrawn, so all complaints were dismissed.

deep.facts: Mr Lindo, an ambulance driver for Hats Group Ltd based at Hillingdon Hospital, was the subject of an August 2023 complaint that a driver had threatened a woman at a petrol station. He was summarily dismissed for gross misconduct after a disciplinary process, but won his internal appeal; however he was not allowed back at Hillingdon (the NHS Trust refused to have him on site) and was offered work elsewhere, which he declined. He claimed unfair (including constructive) dismissal and that the dismissal and parts of the disciplinary process were direct race discrimination.
issues: Whether the claimant was dismissed (actually or constructively) given his successful appeal and refusal of the alternative offer
Whether any dismissal was unfair under s.98 ERA
Whether the dismissal and specific aspects of the disciplinary process were direct race discrimination under s.13 EqA
deep.legal_test: Unfair dismissal s.98 ERA / band of reasonable responses; whether a successful appeal vitiates the dismissal (J Sainsbury v Savage; Folkestone Nursing Home v Patel) and constructive/Hogg v Dover College analysis; direct race discrimination under s.13 EqA (with the constructive-dismissal point informed by Mervyn v BW Controls).
deep.evidence_weighing: The panel accepted that the successful internal appeal revived the contract so there was no actual dismissal, and that the refusal of alternative work did not amount to a repudiatory breach by the employer; on the discrimination complaints it found certain disciplinary process elements (issues 5.1.3-5.1.7) were tainted by race while others were not.
deep.reasoning: The tribunal found the unfair dismissal complaint not well-founded, as the successful appeal meant there was no dismissal and the claimant's refusal of the offered alternative did not make out a constructive dismissal. However, applying s.13 EqA, it upheld the direct race discrimination complaints at paragraphs 5.1.3, 5.1.4, 5.1.5 and 5.1.7 of the list of issues (specific aspects of how he was treated) while dismissing the remaining discrimination complaints. Liability for the upheld discrimination was decided, with compensation (financial loss, injury to feelings, etc. under EqA principles) left to a later remedy hearing.

reasoning_profile.disposition_summary: Jones A is a claimant-receptive, evidence-driven judge with a high proportion of claimant wins and partial wins in unfair-dismissal and whistleblowing-detriment cases, repeatedly finding employer investigations inadequate, predetermined or non-neutral. He is exacting on remedy, however, frequently limiting or eliminating loss awards (GAB Robins causation, incapacity, Polkey) and applying contributory reductions where the claimant's own conduct contributed. He dismisses whistleblowing and discrimination claims firmly where the disclosure or disability threshold is not met.
reasoning_profile.procedural_vs_substantive: substance-focused - he predominantly decides on the merits and the quality/neutrality of the employer's investigation and reason, using disclosure and constructive-dismissal/affirmation thresholds only where genuinely decisive.
reasoning_profile.evidence_approach: He prefers credible, straightforward claimants who make concessions and is sharply critical of dismissing officers who cannot explain their conclusions, gather evidence after the fact, or shift the burden onto the employee to prove innocence; he gives particular weight to contemporaneous documents over entrenched or exaggerated oral narratives and notes when respondents lead no evidence.
recurring_themes: scrutinises adequacy, neutrality and timing of the employer's investigation
alert to predetermined outcomes and reverse-burden ('prove your innocence')
strict on qualifying disclosure - construes the actual words/context (Kilraine)
disciplined, sometimes nil, remedy via causation/Polkey/incapacity (GAB Robins)
contributory-fault reductions for blameworthy claimant conduct
constructive dismissal and affirmation/last-straw analysis
common_legal_tests: s.98(4) ERA band of reasonable responses (Burchell, Madden, Salford Royal v Roldan)
s.43B ERA qualifying disclosure (Kilraine, Williams v Brown) and s.47B/s.103A
constructive dismissal s.95(1)(c) (Western Excavating, Malik v BCCI)
s.6 EqA disability and ss.20/21 reasonable adjustments
remedy: Polkey, mitigation, contributory fault, GAB Robins v Triggs causation
Selkent amendment balancing
reasoning_profile.deliberation_guidance: Probe the quality of the employer's investigation and decision-making first: was the investigator neutral, did they explore exculpatory matters, was evidence gathered after the fact, and was the outcome predetermined or the burden wrongly placed on the employee to prove innocence? Favour the straightforward claimant who makes concessions over an officer who cannot explain their reasoning. For whistleblowing, construe the actual words and context strictly against s.43B before proceeding. Having found liability, do not assume full loss follows - rigorously test causation, incapacity, Polkey and contributory fault, and be prepared to award little or nothing where the claimant could not have continued in the role.

deep.facts: Mr Toshack, a Christian holding a 'sex-realist'/gender-critical belief, was employed as a Prison Custody Officer by GEO Amey Limited from 25 November 2024, working under a contract requiring compliance with Scottish Prison Service transgender policies. During an introductory training session on 7 January 2025 he stated he believed in 'science, biology and reality' and would not comply with policies he saw as conflicting with his beliefs (e.g. recording a transgender prisoner's gender/pronouns on the PER form). He was asked to leave the session and, while still in his six-week probation, was dismissed; he claimed harassment, direct and indirect discrimination on grounds of his protected belief.
issues: Whether the claimant's sex-realist/gender-critical belief qualified for protection under the Grainger criteria and whether he genuinely held it
How he manifested the belief and whether the manifestation was dissociable from it
Whether the conduct (being asked to leave training, comments by Mr Hutton, dismissal) was harassment related to the belief under s.26 EqA
Whether there was direct discrimination under s.13 EqA or indirect discrimination under s.19 EqA, and whether any treatment was justified/proportionate
deep.legal_test: Protected belief assessed under Grainger v Nicholson; harassment under s.26 EqA ('related to' given a wide meaning, Carozzi v University of Hertfordshire); direct discrimination s.13 with comparator s.23; indirect discrimination s.19 with proportionality/justification.
deep.evidence_weighing: The tribunal accepted the broad conduct (being asked to leave, the challenges to his position) occurred, but found that being asked to leave was connected to his refusal to comply with policy rather than to the belief itself, and that dismissal during probation was driven by his stated refusal to follow policy and the impracticality of the proposed workaround.
deep.reasoning: The tribunal found the conduct of asking the claimant to leave was related to his refusal to comply with the respondent's transgender policy rather than to the protected belief, so the harassment claim was not made out. On the discrimination claims, it held the respondent was entitled to conclude (albeit peremptorily, with little process) that his proposed 'workaround' would not meet its policy obligations and that there was no practical, proportionate alternative; although the impact (dismissal in probation) was significant, the treatment was a proportionate means to a legitimate aim and any discriminatory conduct was therefore justified. The claim was dismissed.

deep.facts: The claimant was a store manager for VPZ vaping retailer (a franchise operated by DLSH Ltd) and was dismissed for alleged gross misconduct relating to hiding stock and manipulating a colleague over stock records. The respondent's position was that the claimant had admitted the misconduct, but the claimant maintained he had hidden stock for a few weeks to expose a stock error rather than dishonestly. The respondent's agents failed to comply with tribunal orders and made a last-minute strike-out application.
issues: Whether the dismissal for conduct was reasonable under s.98(4) Employment Rights Act 1996 (within the band of reasonable responses)
Whether a fair procedure was followed
Whether the claimant contributed to his dismissal and to what extent
What compensation should be awarded
deep.legal_test: reasonableness of conduct dismissal under s.98(4) Employment Rights Act 1996, applying the band of reasonable responses
deep.evidence_weighing: The judge found Mr Henderson (the dismissing officer) an unsatisfactory witness who had no clear idea what the claimant was said to have done and who appeared to have obtained WhatsApp evidence retrospectively after being challenged; the claimant by contrast was a straightforward witness who made concessions.
deep.reasoning: The judge found the dismissal unfair because the employer lacked a clear and consistent basis for the misconduct allegation and had not genuinely investigated, with evidence apparently gathered after the fact. However, the claimant admitted hiding stock and manipulating a colleague, which was blameworthy conduct that contributed to his own dismissal, so the awards were reduced by 50%.
deep.award_basis: basic award (£2700) plus compensatory award (£8222.82) plus loss of statutory rights (£500), each reduced by 50% for contributory conduct

deep.facts: The claimant was a 'Home consultant' for Tapi Carpets and Floors Ltd who resigned and claimed constructive unfair dismissal after disciplinary proceedings (a written warning over customer service), a proposed change in role, removal of a company van, and a grievance process. The claimant was off on company/statutory sick pay for an extended period and resigned over six months after being told of the proposed role change. He also raised unlawful deduction and breach of contract claims but led no evidence on them.
issues: Whether the employer fundamentally (repudiatorily) breached the claimant's contract of employment
Whether any breach caused the claimant to resign
Whether the claimant delayed too long and thereby affirmed the contract
Whether there were unlawful deductions from wages or breaches of contract
deep.legal_test: constructive dismissal under s.95(1)(c) ERA applying Western Excavating (ECC) Ltd v Sharp (fundamental breach, causation, no affirmation by delay)
deep.evidence_weighing: The tribunal found no contractual change had actually been implemented (salary and van arrangements were unchanged on the systems) and no evidence the claimant was incapacitated from making employment decisions during sick leave; he led no evidence on the deduction/contract claims.
deep.reasoning: The tribunal held that at most the proposed role change and van removal could have been a fundamental breach, but it was never implemented (so anticipatory at most), and in any event the claimant affirmed the contract by waiting over six months before resigning while in receipt of sick pay. There was no 'last straw' arising from the DSAR. Accordingly he was not constructively dismissed and the claim failed.

deep.facts: The claimant was an administrator at a residential nursing home (owned within the Pepperwood Care group) and was summarily dismissed for gross misconduct relating to allegedly unauthorised overtime hours. The respondent had deducted £2,497.95 from her wages as alleged overpayment for unauthorised hours. She claimed unfair dismissal, wrongful dismissal and unlawful deduction from wages.
issues: Whether the respondent was entitled to dismiss the claimant without notice (wrongful dismissal)
Whether the dismissal was for a potentially fair reason and whether the respondent acted reasonably under s.98(4) ERA
Whether the respondent made an unauthorised deduction from the claimant's wages under s.13 ERA
What compensation should be awarded, including Polkey, contributory conduct and ACAS uplift
deep.legal_test: unfair dismissal under s.98 and s.98(4) ERA (band of reasonable responses); unlawful deduction under s.13/s.14 ERA
deep.evidence_weighing: The dismissing officer (Ms Duffy) admitted she did not consider a lesser sanction or the claimant's length of service/clean record, ignored notes the claimant submitted, and no investigation was carried out; there was no evidence breaking down how the deducted 'overpayment' sums were calculated or that the hours were unauthorised.
deep.reasoning: On the wages claim, the tribunal found the respondent had not established that the deducted sums were a genuine overpayment of wages (no evidence of calculation or that the hours were unauthorised), so the deduction was unlawful. On dismissal, the procedure was grossly deficient (no investigation, claimant's points ignored, predetermined outcome), making it unfair; a 15% contributory reduction was applied for the claimant's culpable failure to raise her hours, and a 20% ACAS uplift applied given the significant breaches and the group's resources.
deep.award_basis: basic award £2574, compensatory award £20,462.91 (after 20% ACAS uplift and 15% contributory reduction), wrongful dismissal/notice pay £1580.48, and repayment of unlawful deduction £2497.95

deep.facts: The claimant, a co-founder whose company was acquired by Dalrada Financial Corporation (DFC, chaired by his uncle), brought combined claims against three related companies after his employment ended amid a family/corporate dispute involving climate technology companies. He resigned, the first respondent served counter-notice, and DFC later raised court proceedings against him in California and made protected-disclosure complaints to the SEC. He claimed wrongful and (constructive/automatic) unfair dismissal and whistleblowing detriment.
issues: Who was the claimant's employer
Whether the claimant was dismissed or resigned, and whether any dismissal was wrongful and/or unfair
Whether the claimant made protected disclosures
Whether he was subjected to detriment for making protected disclosures
Whether he was automatically unfairly dismissed for making a protected disclosure
What compensation should be awarded
deep.legal_test: identity of employer (Autoclenz v Belcher / dual employment authorities); wrongful dismissal via employer counter-notice converting resignation into dismissal (Harris and Russell Ltd v Slingsby, s.95(1) ERA); protected disclosure detriment under Part IVA ERA (s.43B, 43C, 43G, s.47B); injury to feelings (Vento bands, Prison Service v Johnson, Eddie Stobart v Graham)
deep.evidence_weighing: The tribunal generally preferred the claimant's evidence and that of his witnesses, finding him credible (and his wife's evidence about his deteriorated mental health compelling), while finding the respondent's witness AZ contradictory, exaggerated and inconsistent; contemporaneous documents were given particular weight given the entrenched family narratives.
deep.reasoning: The tribunal found the first respondent was the employer; the service of counter-notice converted the resignation into a wrongful dismissal entitling the claimant to the balance of his statutory notice. It found he made protected disclosures and that raising the Californian court action against him was a detriment on the ground of those disclosures, warranting a mid-Vento injury-to-feelings award; but it rejected constructive/ordinary unfair dismissal and automatic unfair dismissal, and dismissed the claims against the second and third respondents.
deep.award_basis: wrongful dismissal damages of £18,671.10 net (balance of statutory notice) plus £15,000 injury to feelings for whistleblowing detriment

deep.facts: The claimant, a transgender man who had been a hospital Chaplain for 17 years with Lothian Health Board, resigned and claimed constructive unfair dismissal following the employer's handling of media enquiries and articles arising from Pride flags/bunting displayed in the hospital sanctuary, which he experienced as transphobic hate incidents. He was off work, on injury allowance, and resigned in April 2024 after counselling led him to conclude he could not return; he had obtained part-time alternative work before resigning.
issues: Whether the respondent fundamentally breached the claimant's contract of employment
Whether the claimant resigned in response to that breach
Whether the claimant affirmed any breach by delay in resigning
Whether any constructive dismissal was unfair
What compensation should be awarded
deep.legal_test: constructive dismissal under s.95(1)(c) ERA applying Western Excavating (ECC) Ltd v Sharp and the implied term of trust and confidence (Courtaulds v Andrew, Malik v BCCI)
deep.evidence_weighing: The tribunal found the claimant an impressive, credible and reliable witness whose evidence about his trauma, fears for his safety and inability to contemplate returning to work was accepted; the respondent's witness evidence was of limited relevance to the disputed handling of the media enquiry.
deep.reasoning: The tribunal found the employer's conduct in handling the media response breached the implied term of trust and confidence (repudiatory breach), and that the claimant, focused on his mental health over a 17-year career and with no serious discussion of his return, had not affirmed the breach by his delay. The dismissal was therefore constructive and unfair. However, applying GAB Robins v Triggs, losses from his reduced (part-time) earning capacity were not recoverable as caused by the dismissal, and as his pro-rata salary was now higher no loss-of-earnings award was just and equitable, leaving only the basic award and loss of statutory rights.
deep.award_basis: basic award £17,500 plus compensatory award of £500 for loss of statutory rights

deep.facts: The claimant brought combined claims against Monarch Legal Ltd (first respondent) and two individuals for notice pay, holiday pay, arrears of pay and commission after the termination of his employment. None of the respondents responded to the claim, and the first respondent's last-minute postponement application was refused; this was a remedy hearing. The claimant argued the individual respondents should be personally liable, relying on Timis v Osipov.
issues: Whether the individual second and third respondents could be personally liable for the compensation sought
Whether an ACAS Code uplift should be applied
The quantum of notice pay, holiday pay, arrears and commission owed by the first respondent
deep.legal_test: wrongful dismissal/breach of contract (entitlement to contractual notice) and unlawful deduction from wages; individual liability point assessed against Timis and anor v Osipov (held inapplicable outside protected-disclosure claims)
deep.evidence_weighing: The respondents led no evidence and did not respond to the claim; the tribunal was satisfied the claimant had taken reasonable steps to mitigate and had provided sufficient documentary evidence to calculate the award.
deep.reasoning: The judge held that liability for notice pay and wages can only lie with an employer, and Timis v Osipov (a protected-disclosure case) was not authority for individual liability for such sums, so the individual respondents were dismissed. No ACAS uplift was just and equitable as the grievance did not relate to the unpaid sums. The first respondent was found to have wrongfully dismissed the claimant and was ordered to pay contractual notice pay with associated pension and benefits, plus outstanding December pay and unpaid commission.
deep.award_basis: gross notice pay and benefits/pension £17,654.55 (3 months' notice, pension during notice, accrued holiday during notice, December pension) plus December pay and unpaid commission of £2909.07 gross (subject to tax/NI)

deep.facts: Three claimants employed as residential prison officers / physical training instructors at HMP Edinburgh were summarily dismissed by the Scottish Ministers following a prisoner's allegation that they had assaulted him. Criminal proceedings were raised but did not go to trial. The claimants alleged the investigation was unfair and that dismissal fell outside the band of reasonable responses.
issues: Whether there was a potentially fair reason for dismissal (conduct)
Whether the investigation and dismissal were fair / within the band of reasonable responses under s.98(4) ERA
Whether the claimants contributed to their dismissals
What remedy (including reinstatement) should be awarded to each claimant
deep.legal_test: unfair conduct dismissal under s.94 and s.98(4) ERA applying British Home Stores Ltd v Burchell (genuine belief, reasonable grounds, reasonable investigation) and the band of reasonable responses
deep.evidence_weighing: The dismissing Governor (DA) was found to have approached the evidence seeking to confirm a predetermined conclusion that someone must take the blame, interpreting CCTV through that prism and effectively requiring the claimants to prove their innocence; the appeal panel member (IW) made concessions and relied on matters DA had himself discounted; the claimants were credible and straightforward.
deep.reasoning: The tribunal found the reason was conduct but the investigation and decision were not within the band of reasonable responses because the decision-maker was not neutral, treated the claimants as having to prove innocence, and the appeal did not cure this; the dismissals were therefore unfair. Each claimant was found to have contributed 20% to his dismissal. The tribunal ordered reinstatement for Mr McTague and Mr O'Hara with back-pay/benefits plus loss-of-earnings compensation, and a compensatory and basic award (reduced 20%) for Mr Milne; no ACAS uplift was warranted.
deep.award_basis: reinstatement plus loss-of-earnings of £24,061 net (McTague) and £20,159.54 net (O'Hara), and for Milne a compensatory award of £27,464.36 net plus basic award £2284 (all loss figures reduced 20% for contributory conduct)

cases.claimant: Ms C Goble and Dr N Clark

deep.facts: Two claimants, Dr Clark (NIDMAR programme manager, accepted disabled through phonological dyslexia) and Ms Goble (administrative/disability assistant), were employed by Fife Employment Access Trust, a mental-health employment charity, on a Scottish Government-funded project. Both were dismissed on 31 March 2024 amid grievance and disciplinary proceedings (including a fraud allegation against Ms Goble over recorded working hours). They brought wide-ranging claims including unfair and wrongful dismissal, whistleblowing, disability discrimination, harassment, reasonable adjustments, holiday pay and unlawful deductions.
issues: Whether each claimant was unfairly and/or wrongfully dismissed
Whether Ms Goble made a protected disclosure and was subjected to detriment for it, and whether she was automatically unfairly dismissed
Whether Ms Goble was entitled to a redundancy payment and unpaid holiday pay, and whether she was a disabled person
Whether the respondent failed in its duty to make reasonable adjustments for each claimant
Whether Dr Clark was harassed related to disability, indirectly discriminated against, treated unfavourably under s.15, or victimised for a protected act
Whether claims were in time and what remedy should be awarded
deep.legal_test: unfair dismissal under s.94/s.98(4) ERA (band of reasonable responses); wrongful dismissal under s.86 ERA; protected disclosure under s.43B/43C/43G ERA and detriment under s.47B; disability under s.6 EqA (Goodwin, J v DLA Piper); reasonable adjustments under ss.20-21 EqA; harassment, s.15 and victimisation under EqA
deep.evidence_weighing: The tribunal relied heavily on the respondent's procedural failures and unexplained conduct (statements and reports never disclosed to claimants, payroll forms altered, the respondent conceding sums were due but unpaid, and emails left unanswered); it accepted Ms Goble's protected disclosure but found her not automatically unfairly dismissed.
deep.reasoning: For Ms Goble, the tribunal upheld unfair and wrongful dismissal, found she made a protected disclosure and was subjected to detriment (suspension and a fraud-based disciplinary) for it, was disabled and owed reasonable adjustments which the respondent failed to make, and was owed holiday pay; but it rejected automatic unfair dismissal and redundancy entitlement. For Dr Clark, the tribunal upheld unfair dismissal, unlawful deduction, failure to make reasonable adjustments and disability-related harassment, but found she did no protected act and was not victimised. Both were awarded substantial compensation.
deep.award_basis: compensation to Ms Goble of £37,727.68 and to Dr Clark of £58,401.73 (covering unfair/wrongful dismissal, discrimination/reasonable adjustments, unlawful deductions and holiday pay)

deep.facts: The claimant, one of the respondent's most experienced crane operators (20 years' service), was summarily dismissed for misconduct after a crane jib was damaged / a crane collapse on a site in Edinburgh in November 2023, the respondent alleging operator error in deploying the park radius (out-of-service) device. The respondent obtained and edited time-lapse footage and did not show it to the claimant until pressed, and dismissed him without regard to his length of service or fault-reporting record. The HSE later found operator error the most likely cause but noted possible sensor/limit malfunction.
issues: Whether the conduct dismissal was fair or unfair under s.98(4) ERA
Whether any procedural and substantive failings rendered the dismissal unfair
Whether the appeal cured procedural unfairness
Whether any contributory conduct reduction should be made and what compensation should be awarded
deep.legal_test: unfair conduct dismissal under s.98(4) ERA applying British Home Stores Ltd v Burchell and the band of reasonable responses (Foley v Post Office / HSBC v Madden), with Salford Royal v Roldan and A v B on investigation where a career is at stake
deep.evidence_weighing: The tribunal found the employer carried out no proper investigation (never saw the works plan, withheld and edited footage, transcribed meeting notes only by AI later with gaps), and the dismissing officer reached conclusions he could not explain and ignored the claimant's service and reporting record; the appeal was very brief and shifted the burden onto the claimant to produce new evidence.
deep.reasoning: The tribunal held the dismissal was both procedurally and substantively unfair because the investigation was inadequate, exculpatory matters were not explored, and the appeal did not reconsider matters afresh. It found no contributory conduct. On remedy, however, because the claimant conceded he could not work due to PTSD/fear of heights and was only on statutory sick pay, he would likely have been fairly dismissed with notice for incapacity, so only a basic award, notice pay and loss of statutory rights were just and equitable.
deep.award_basis: basic award £18,550 plus compensatory award £10,665.68 net (twelve weeks' notice pay £10,165.68 and £500 loss of statutory rights)

deep.facts: The claimant, a ventilation engineer for SW Enviro Ltd, claimed he had made protected disclosures and raised health and safety concerns in a letter of 20 April 2024 (referring to lack of training, including for working at height), and that he was subjected to detriment and automatically unfairly dismissed; he also claimed unlawful deductions from wages (salary arrears from March 2023, final pay, and holiday pay). A preliminary hearing (Judge Jones) decided the disclosure/health-and-safety question; a later final hearing (Judge Beyzade) decided the wages claims.
issues: Whether the claimant's 20 April 2024 letter contained a protected disclosure under s.43B ERA
Whether the letter brought to the employer's attention health and safety circumstances under s.100(1)(c) ERA
Whether the detriment (s.47B) and automatic unfair dismissal (ss.100(1)(c), 103A) claims could succeed
Whether the respondent made unauthorised deductions from wages (salary arrears from March 2023, final pay, and holiday pay) under s.13 ERA
deep.legal_test: protected disclosure under s.43B ERA (reasonable belief, public interest, tending to show a relevant failure) per Kilraine v Wandsworth and Darnton v University of Surrey; s.100(1)(c) ERA health and safety; unlawful deduction under s.13 ERA
deep.evidence_weighing: The tribunal focused on the actual words of the letter and its context, finding the claimant was setting out training he wanted in order to demonstrate he met promotion criteria, with nothing showing he or colleagues' health and safety was or was likely to be put at risk.
deep.reasoning: Judge Jones held the letter, properly construed, recommended training to improve business operations and to show the claimant met promotion criteria, rather than disclosing information he reasonably believed showed a health and safety danger; it was therefore neither a protected disclosure nor a s.100(1)(c) health and safety communication, so the detriment and automatic unfair dismissal claims failed and were dismissed. The remaining unlawful-deduction claims were listed separately and, at the later hearing, Judge Beyzade dismissed all three deduction complaints as not succeeding.

deep.facts: Mr Gassama worked as a bank support worker for Kingdom Support and Care CIC on three occasions in July 2024 and was dismissed following a disciplinary hearing. He claimed disability discrimination (relying variously on epilepsy, liver cirrhosis and severe headaches) and race discrimination. The respondent denied he was disabled at the material time and said it had no knowledge of any disability, noting he had declared no need for adjustments and disclosed no medical conditions during recruitment.
issues: Was the claimant a disabled person under s.6 Equality Act 2010 at the material time?
Did the respondent know, or could it reasonably have been expected to know, of any disability?
Was the claimant unfavourably treated because of something arising in consequence of disability under s.15 EqA?
Was the dismissal an act of race discrimination?
Was the claimant subjected to harassment related to race under s.26 EqA?
deep.legal_test: Disability status under s.6 Equality Act 2010, knowledge defence under s.15, direct discrimination under s.13, and harassment under s.26, with the burden on the claimant to prove disability and to raise facts from which discrimination could be inferred.
deep.evidence_weighing: The Tribunal found the claimant's evidence on disability wholly inadequate (his position on which conditions he relied on shifted, and he gave almost no medical evidence beyond taking liver medication that made him sleepy), and found him lacking in credibility generally; he led no evidence that his dismissal related to race or that a hypothetical comparator would have been treated differently.
deep.reasoning: The Tribunal held the claimant had not established he was a disabled person at the material time and, in any event, the respondent neither knew nor could reasonably have known of any disability since he disclosed nothing during recruitment. On race, there was no evidence the dismissal had anything to do with race and no basis to infer differential treatment of a comparator, and the harassment allegation failed both on credibility and because nothing said had the proscribed effect. All claims were therefore dismissed in their entirety.

deep.facts: The claimant worked for McCurrach UK Ltd and claimed race discrimination, victimisation, failure to provide a contract (not pursued), and unlawful deduction from wages relating to £295 deducted for fines incurred while using a company car. He alleged his line manager (RFW) made a race-related comment about his attackers possibly being part of a gang. The claimant repeatedly tried to expand his claim beyond his claim form without amending it.
issues: Whether the respondent made an unlawful deduction from the claimant's wages under s.13 ERA
Whether the claimant was discriminated against because of race
Whether the claimant did a protected act and was victimised
deep.legal_test: unlawful deduction under s.13 ERA (deduction must be authorised and the worker notified in writing in advance); race discrimination and victimisation under the Equality Act 2010
deep.evidence_weighing: The tribunal found the contract/handbook permitted deductions only after advance notice, and the claimant was told sums were owed but not that they would be deducted nor when (no payslip or advance email before the August pay run); on discrimination, RFW's gang comment was found to be an expression of concern unrelated to race, and the claimant's evidence about an oral protected act lacked credibility and was absent from his claim form.
deep.reasoning: On wages, although a contractual deduction provision existed, the respondent breached its own undertaking to inform the claimant in advance of the actual deduction, so the £295 deduction was unlawful and repayable. On race discrimination, the manager's comment was not related to race and there was no evidence a comparator would have been treated differently, so that claim failed. On victimisation, the tribunal did not accept the claimant had done any protected act, so that claim also failed.
deep.award_basis: repayment of unlawful deduction from wages

deep.facts: Ms McKay, an Office Manager at Lothian Health Board, resigned on 22 August 2024 and lodged an unfair dismissal claim on 21 October 2024. After her son took over her representation, she applied on 17 January 2025 to amend her claim to add (a) automatic unfair dismissal under s.103A ERA based on a protected disclosure she made on 19 June 2022, and (b) detriment claims under s.47B ERA for the same disclosure. The respondent objected to the amendment.
issues: Whether the application to amend to add a claim of automatic unfair dismissal under s.103A ERA should be allowed
Whether the application to amend to add detriment claims under s.47B ERA should be allowed
How the balance of injustice and hardship falls between the parties in granting or refusing the amendments
deep.legal_test: Discretion to allow amendment under the Selkent Bus Co Ltd v Moore 1996 ICR 836 framework: balancing the nature of the amendment, applicability of time limits and the time and manner of the application, with the overriding objective and relative hardship to the parties.
deep.evidence_weighing: The Tribunal noted the factual basis of the protected disclosure and to whom it was made was already set out in the original ET1, so the s.103A claim required little additional evidence; the reasons for the resignation were a matter for the claimant's own evidence at the final hearing.
deep.reasoning: Because the protected disclosure and its recipient were already pleaded, the s.103A automatic unfair dismissal amendment would not require the respondent to undertake extensive further enquiry nor discharge the listed final hearing, so the prejudice to the claimant in being barred from arguing automatic unfair dismissal outweighed the limited prejudice to the respondent and that amendment was allowed. The detriment amendment under s.47B was treated differently and refused (the text indicates the balance there did not favour the claimant).

reasoning_profile.disposition_summary: Hendry J is a strongly threshold-oriented judge who disposes of a high proportion of cases on jurisdiction and time limits, with several outright dismissals for want of jurisdiction. Where matters do reach the merits or remedy he is even-handed and decisive, prepared to find for claimants (protected disclosure, holiday pay, victimisation) when the evidence supports it, but he holds claimants firmly to their burden and is sceptical of late or under-evidenced claims. His leaning is neutral on substance but demanding on procedure.
reasoning_profile.procedural_vs_substantive: procedure-focused - a large share of his decisions turn on s.111 'reasonably practicable', s.123 'just and equitable' extension, jurisdiction (e.g. international/territorial scope) and Selkent amendment/strike-out points rather than full merits.
reasoning_profile.evidence_approach: He closely assesses claimant capability and credibility against the surrounding facts, treating an intelligent, resourced, internet-literate or advice-supported claimant as having no good reason for delay, and requires contemporaneous corroboration (company records, ACAS contact dates, fit notes). He will accept a claimant's honest evidence but reject the inferences or motives they attach to facts where objectively unsupported.
recurring_themes: strict on s.111 reasonably-practicable and s.123 just-and-equitable time limits
extension of time is the exception, not the rule (Robertson/Bexley, Dedman)
Selkent balance-of-hardship analysis on amendments
burden firmly on the claimant to justify delay and to make out claims
scrutinises claimant's resources, knowledge of rights and capacity
decisive on merits/remedy once jurisdiction is cleared
common_legal_tests: s.111 ERA 'not reasonably practicable' (Palmer, Dedman, Porter v Bandridge)
s.123 Equality Act 'just and equitable' extension (Bexley v Robertson, Adedeji, Keeble)
Selkent Bus Co v Moore amendment balancing (Vaughan, Abercrombie)
s.43B ERA protected disclosure (Chesterton v Nurmohamed, Williams v Brown)
band of reasonable responses under s.98 ERA
s.136 burden of proof / Madarassy 'something more'
reasoning_profile.deliberation_guidance: Before touching the merits, interrogate jurisdiction first: was the claim presented in time, and if not, has the claimant discharged the burden of showing it was not reasonably practicable (ERA) or just and equitable to extend (EqA)? Probe the claimant's intelligence, access to advice and the internet, knowledge of their rights, and whether any ill-health genuinely prevented action. Treat extension of time as the exception, not the rule. Only after that gateway is passed should you weigh the substantive evidence, and there hold each side to its burden while being willing to find for a claimant who produces concrete contemporaneous proof.

deep.facts: David Low worked at Ultra Catering Ltd's King Street Pizza Hut franchise in Aberdeen, rising to Assistant Store Manager. He made a series of disclosures via WhatsApp about food-safety and health-and-safety failings (poor Hut Bot food-practice scores, an untreated burn injury, a store left without a store manager, unsafe cleaning practices). The respondent argued he refused a transfer to another branch and that his whistleblowing was a baseless campaign to oust the King Street manager.
issues: Whether the claimant's communications amounted to qualifying protected disclosures under s.43B ERA
Whether the claimant had a reasonable belief that the disclosures were made in the public interest
Whether the disclosures were the reason (or principal reason) for his dismissal, rendering it automatically unfair
The amount of compensation, including loss of earnings and whether other employment earnings should be offset
deep.legal_test: Protected disclosure definition under s.43B ERA (qualifying disclosure of information, reasonable belief, public interest) per Williams v Michelle Brown, Chesterton Global v Nurmohamed and Twist DX v Armes; automatic unfair dismissal for making protected disclosures.
deep.evidence_weighing: The judge accepted the claimant's dominant motivation was genuine public-safety concern rather than a vendetta against the manager, despite an element of self-righteousness, and found the disclosures conveyed information with sufficient factual content; on remedy he adopted the claimant's own offset of North Offshore earnings as the credible figure.
deep.reasoning: The judge found the WhatsApp messages disclosed information tending to show health and safety of the public and staff was being endangered (s.43B(1)(d)) and that the claimant reasonably and in the public interest believed this, satisfying the protected disclosure test. Concluding the disclosures were the reason for dismissal, he held the dismissal automatically unfair and calculated loss of earnings of £359/week over 49 weeks (£17,591) less £6,943.36 earned at North Offshore plus six months' future loss, totalling £11,270.14.
deep.award_basis: compensatory monetary award for unfair (whistleblowing) dismissal: past loss of earnings net of mitigation earnings plus future loss

cases.respondent: James Johnston & Co. of Elgin Ltd

deep.facts: Roy Sinclair was a long-serving Carding Operative at James Johnston & Co. of Elgin, whose role contractually required a three-shift rotation including nights. Occupational Health reports culminating in a January 2024 report found he was not fit for night work and that permanent exclusion from nights would benefit his wellbeing. The respondent consulted him and offered redeployment/adjustments to avoid nights, but no acceptable accommodation was reached and he was dismissed on capability grounds on 4 September 2024.
issues: Whether capability (health) was the genuine reason for dismissal
Whether the dismissal for incapacity to perform night-shift working was within the band of reasonable responses
Whether the respondent acted reasonably in consulting and considering alternatives to dismissal
deep.legal_test: Unfair dismissal under s.98 ERA 1996: capability relating to health under s.98(2)(a) as a potentially fair reason, and whether the employer acted reasonably under s.98(4) (band of reasonable responses).
deep.evidence_weighing: The judge found the respondent's witnesses (Hilal and Garrow) credible, with no animosity and a genuine wish to retain the claimant's experience; the claimant was honest but his anxiety/depression made him insufficiently objective, so where accounts conflicted the judge preferred the respondent's witnesses.
deep.reasoning: The judge accepted capability (inability to work the contractually required night shift) was the genuine reason and that the respondent had consulted, offered adjustments and redeployment, and the claimant should have appreciated his job was at risk. Although with hindsight a less drastic approach might have been tried, the employer acted reasonably overall, so the dismissal was a fair dismissal on capability grounds and the claim was dismissed.
