deep.facts: Peter Finlay claimed unfair dismissal and automatically unfair dismissal for whistleblowing against Merlin Travel Group Ltd, which contended he was a self-employed contractor, not a worker or employee. A preliminary hearing on worker/employee status was held; the claimant gave evidence but did not return on the second day after a grand mal seizure, and subsequently withdrew the claim on 9 June 2025 due to ongoing health issues, with a withdrawal judgment on 11 June. The respondent then applied for an expenses (costs) order.
issues: Whether the claimant (or his representatives) acted vexatiously, abusively, disruptively or otherwise unreasonably in bringing or conducting the proceedings
Whether the claim had no reasonable prospect of success
Whether the Tribunal should exercise its discretion to award expenses to the respondent
deep.legal_test: Costs/expenses order under Rule 76 (whether a party acted vexatiously, abusively, disruptively or unreasonably, or the claim had no reasonable prospect of success), applied as an exceptional remedy per McPherson v BNP Paribas.
deep.evidence_weighing: The judge found the worker-status law genuinely complex (citing Pimlico Plumbers and Maritime & Coastguard Agency v Groom) and that the litigant-in-person claimant did not properly understand it; while there were some credibility concerns and ill-tempered correspondence, the judge accepted the claimant became seriously unwell and that this genuine illness was the catalyst for withdrawal.
deep.reasoning: Applying the principle that expenses are the exception, the judge held that given the complex legal and factual issues and the claimant's status as a largely unrepresented litigant, his conduct did not meet the unreasonableness/no-reasonable-prospects threshold under Rule 76. The withdrawal was driven by genuine serious illness rather than abuse of process, so the respondent's application for expenses was refused.

cases.respondent: The Nail and Beauty Zone Ltd

deep.facts: L A Donaldson, a student, worked part-time as a Spa/Massage Therapist for The Nail & Beauty Zone Ltd from October 2023 until 14 June 2024, and was signed off sick from a January seizure until termination. He claimed accrued but unpaid holiday pay; the respondent disputed his calculations, questioned whether he was genuinely ill, and relied on a holiday policy requiring leave to be taken in the accrual year with only a discretionary 5-day carry-over (no request having been made). The claimant did not attend; his mother gave evidence on his behalf.
issues: Whether the claimant accrued statutory holiday entitlement during his period of sickness absence
Whether the employer's policy requiring leave to be taken in the accrual year extinguished that entitlement where the claimant was off sick
The amount of accrued holiday pay due on termination
deep.legal_test: Unlawful deduction from wages / accrual of statutory holiday pay during sick leave under reg.13 Working Time Regulations 1998 and the Working Time Directive, applying Stringer/Ainsworth, Schultz-Hoff, NHS Leeds v Larner and Plumb v Duncan Print Group.
deep.evidence_weighing: The judge found Mrs Donaldson a patently honest, credible and reliable witness with detailed knowledge of her son's illness, and Mr Lumsden credible but with limited first-hand knowledge of the medical condition; the period of incapacity was amply corroborated by Fit Notes and a university thesis extension.
deep.reasoning: Applying the WTR case law, the judge held that a worker absent on sick leave continues to accrue statutory holiday and the right is not extinguished at year end where sickness prevented its exercise, and the employee need not show inability to take leave. The respondent could not force or persuade the claimant to take leave during illness, so the 8.5 accrued days were not lost; he awarded £708.56 (8.5 x 8 x £10.42), with no jurisdiction to award unpaid SSP.
deep.award_basis: accrued but unpaid statutory holiday pay due at termination (8.5 days), as an unlawful deduction from wages

deep.facts: R Bialonski, a Senior Design Engineer of Polish nationality, claimed constructive unfair dismissal against National Oilwell Varco UK Ltd, alleging intimidation, exclusion from team activities, mishandling of holiday requests and biased grievance handling. He applied to amend his claim to add 'perceived race discrimination' on the basis of being treated as a foreigner/outsider versus Scottish/British 'insiders'. The respondent objected on Selkent grounds, citing time, expense and prejudice.
issues: Whether the claimant's application to amend to add a claim of perceived race discrimination should be allowed
Whether the proposed discrimination claim had reasonable prospects of success
Where the balance of injustice and hardship lay between the parties
deep.legal_test: Discretion to allow amendment under Selkent Bus Co Ltd v Moore 1996 ICR 836 (balancing nature of amendment, time limits, manner/timing, and the paramount balance of injustice/hardship per Vaughan v Modality Partnership and Abercrombie v Aga Rangemaster), informed by the prima facie threshold for discrimination in Madarassy v Nomura.
deep.evidence_weighing: The claimant conceded there were no slurs or other matters from which a discriminatory motive could be inferred, maintaining only that he was treated differently from Scottish/British colleagues; the judge found this amounted at most to a grievance about differential treatment without the 'something more' needed to infer discrimination.
deep.reasoning: The judge held that a claim framed as 'perceived' race discrimination was very difficult if not impossible to maintain, and that mere less favourable treatment without anything from which a discriminatory motive could be inferred fails the Madarassy 'something more' threshold, so the claim lacked reasonable prospects. Weighing the unclear and wide-ranging amendment against the prejudice and expense to the respondent, the balance of hardship favoured the respondent and the amendment was refused, leaving the existing unfair (constructive) dismissal claim to proceed.

deep.facts: P Cruickshank, an Advocacy worker for Circles Network, claimed unfair dismissal and that he had been sexually harassed by his line manager. He was sent a dismissal letter dated 30 August 2024, but the claims were lodged considerably out of time. The respondent contended both the unfair dismissal and sex discrimination/harassment claims were time barred.
issues: Whether it was not reasonably practicable for the claimant to present the unfair dismissal claim within the three-month limit, and if so whether it was presented within a reasonable further period
Whether it was just and equitable to extend time to admit the late sex discrimination and harassment claims
Whether the Tribunal had jurisdiction to hear the claims
deep.legal_test: Time limits: reasonable practicability test for unfair dismissal under s.111(2) ERA 1996 (per Lowri Beck Services v Brophy, Marks & Spencer v Williams-Ryan, Dedman), and the just-and-equitable discretion for discrimination claims (Keeble factors and balance of prejudice).
deep.evidence_weighing: The judge found it difficult to accept that the able and intelligent claimant, who knew sexual harassment was unlawful and had raised concerns internally before dismissal, would not have acted earlier if he genuinely intended to claim; the harassment allegations were vague and the delays predated his dismissal and later health/family difficulties.
deep.reasoning: On the unfair dismissal claim, the judge held the claim was not lodged timeously and it had not been shown that it was not reasonably practicable to present it in time, so there was no jurisdiction and it was dismissed. On the harassment/sex discrimination claims, given the lengthy unexplained delay (much of it before dismissal), the vagueness of the allegations, and the balance of prejudice, it was not just and equitable to extend time and those claims were dismissed.

deep.facts: T Smith was dismissed in October 2021 and claimed unfair dismissal and disability discrimination against Stena Drilling PTE Ltd, a Singapore-incorporated company within the Stena Group. He had not worked in the UK since 2011 and latterly worked offshore in the Bahamas under a Singapore-law contract, though Stena Drilling HR Ltd (UK) carried out his payroll/HR administration and recruitment was argued to have been conducted by SDHR staff in Aberdeen. An earlier ET finding of jurisdiction was overturned by the EAT and remitted for rehearing on international and (if necessary) territorial jurisdiction.
issues: Whether the Tribunal had international jurisdiction over the claims under s.15C of the Civil Jurisdiction and Judgments Act 1982
Whether SDHR (UK) operated as a branch, agency or establishment such that the claimant was engaged through it in the UK
If necessary, whether the EqA claim fell within the Tribunal's territorial scope given the claimant worked wholly outside Great Britain
deep.legal_test: International jurisdiction under s.15C Civil Jurisdiction and Judgments Act 1982 (branch/agency/establishment; place of engagement), informed by Voogsdgeerd v Navimer and Somafer v Saar-Ferngas; territorial scope under s.199(7) ERA and reg.3 of the 2011 Regulations per Lawson and Ravat.
deep.evidence_weighing: Evidence from HR manager Amy Boston and the claimant focused on the real relationship between SDHR and PTE; the judge found that for promoted posts such as the claimant's there was usually direct input into recruitment from PTE staff in Singapore, bolstering the respondent's case that SDHR was not a cipher and the arrangement was not a sham.
deep.reasoning: The judge concluded the claimant had not demonstrated that the Stena structure was a sham or that SDHR's role displaced PTE's; with PTE and AMS acting as Singapore-based crewing companies, the legal decision to recruit the claimant on his final contract was taken in Singapore, making Singapore the place of recruitment. Accordingly the Tribunal had no international jurisdiction over either the unfair dismissal or disability discrimination claim, and both were dismissed.

cases.respondent: Commissioners for HM Revenue and Customs

deep.facts: M Shields, a home worker and disabled person employed by HMRC, complained that she was excluded from applying for a promoted post because she was a contractual homeworker. Her ET1 raised disability discrimination claims (initially s.15 and ss.20/21 EqA) but was lodged late, and she later applied to amend to add claims under ss.13, 15, 19, 20 and 27 EqA, plus alleged breaches of the ACAS Code. She also sought a restricted reporting order over her medical history and an extension of time, citing health conditions and her mother's illness alongside protracted internal grievance delays.
issues: Whether to grant a restricted reporting/anonymity order over the claimant's medical history
Whether it was just and equitable to extend time to allow the out-of-time disability discrimination claims in the ET1 to proceed
Whether to allow the amendment to add claims under ss.13, 15, 19, 20 and 27 EqA and alleged ACAS Code breaches
deep.legal_test: Just-and-equitable extension of time under s.123 Equality Act 2010 (assessing all relevant factors per Adedeji v University Hospitals Birmingham, with Keeble factors); discretion to allow amendment under Selkent Bus Co Ltd v Moore and Cocking v Sandhurst (balance of injustice/hardship); restricted reporting order under Rule 50 / s.49(1).
deep.evidence_weighing: The judge accepted the claimant's evidence (supported by documents on her ACAS and union contacts and her mother's illness/hospital dates) that her health conditions and the diversion of energy into the lengthy internal grievance process contributed to the delay; this, while individually insufficient, was a material factor in the crystallisation of the dispute.
deep.reasoning: Weighing all the circumstances, the judge held the claimant had persuaded the Tribunal to exercise its just-and-equitable discretion to admit the late ET1 disability discrimination claims. On amendment, the new statutory claims (ss.13, 15, 19, 20) arose from the same recruitment-related facts already pleaded and were allowed, but the s.27 victimisation claim was refused as wholly new matters causing real prejudice (relevant only as background), and the ACAS Code breaches were allowed only as background since no stand-alone claim exists. A restricted reporting order over the medical history was granted.

deep.facts: Mr Mallon was dismissed from his role as a Linen Porter at the respondent's hotel on 17 May 2024 for an alleged breakdown in trust and confidence, including telling colleagues he would take the company to court. He had insufficient qualifying service for ordinary unfair dismissal and instead claimed automatically unfair dismissal (s.103A whistleblowing), plus sex and disability discrimination, but did not contact ACAS until 3 January 2025 and lodged proceedings in January 2025. He relied on faulty advice from a Quantum Claims adviser (the "two year rule") and on his depression/anxiety to explain the delay.
issues: Was it reasonably practicable for the claimant to lodge the s.103A automatically unfair dismissal claim in time, and if not whether it was lodged within a further reasonable period?
Was it just and equitable to allow the sex and disability discrimination claims to proceed out of time?
deep.legal_test: For unfair dismissal, the reasonably practicable test under s.111 ERA applying Dedman v British Building & Engineering Appliances [1974] ICR 53 (opportunities to find out rights and whether ignorance was reasonable); for the discrimination claims, the just and equitable extension under s.123 Equality Act 2010 applying Bexley Community Centre v Robertson [2003] EWCA Civ 576 (extension the exception not the rule).
deep.evidence_weighing: The judge found it implausible that the claimant, who repeatedly threatened to take the matter to court and contacted numerous advice organisations and Quantum Claims (a firm specialising in tribunal cases), did not enquire into his rights; his ill health did not prevent him working soon after dismissal or coping with life, so was not what stopped him claiming.
deep.reasoning: Applying Dedman, the judge held the claimant's ignorance of the time limit was not reasonable given his evident sense of grievance and access to advice and the internet, so it was reasonably practicable to claim in time and the s.103A claim was dismissed for want of jurisdiction. On the discrimination claims, applying Bexley, there was no impediment to claiming on time, the claims appeared weak, the respondent had not contributed to the delay, and time limits must be observed, so it was not just and equitable to extend time and those claims were also dismissed.

deep.facts: Mr McGhie, a Fitter, claimed sexual orientation discrimination arising from workplace incidents in October and November 2023, including a homophobic slur by his supervisor BD on 10 October 2023 and a series of subsequent incidents. He was dismissed on 9 January 2024 and raised proceedings on 23 April 2024 after early conciliation. He also sought to amend to add a November 2023 harassment incident involving employee Mr A Russell (AR), discovered only when preparing for the hearing. The Tribunal found a number of victimisation acts proven and awarded compensation, while treating the 10 October incident as out of time.
issues: Should the claimant be allowed to amend to add the alleged harassment incident involving Mr A Russell in November 2023?
Were the pleaded incidents (including the 10 October 2023 slur) in time, or out of time and not part of a continuing course of conduct?
Was it just and equitable to hear out-of-time harassment claims late?
Did the proven incidents amount to harassment related to sexual orientation under s.26 EqA, or victimisation?
What compensation for injury to feelings was appropriate?
deep.legal_test: Harassment under s.26 Equality Act 2010 (broad "related to" test, not strict causation, per Hartley v FCO Services and EHRC Code para 7.9); just and equitable extension of time; amendment under Selkent Bus Co v Moore [1996] ICR 836 balancing of hardship; and Vento bands for injury to feelings.
deep.evidence_weighing: The Tribunal found the incidents factually proven but, weighing BD's reaction to being disciplined and his use of the word "grass", concluded the proven conduct was related to BD's resentment at discipline rather than to the claimant's sexual orientation; it accepted the claimant was alive to his rights at an early stage (having contacted ACAS), undermining a just and equitable extension.
deep.reasoning: The Tribunal held the proven later incidents were not shown to relate to the protected characteristic, so they were victimisation rather than harassment, and the 10 October incident was out of time with no just and equitable basis to extend because the claimant was aware of his rights early. It allowed the amendment regarding the AR incident, which it treated as a one-off act of public shaming in the lower Vento band warranting £3,000, and found the listed acts of victimisation proven, awarding £2,500 for injury to feelings.
deep.award_basis: Injury to feelings: £2,500 for proven victimisation plus £3,000 (lower Vento band) for the AR harassment incident

deep.facts: Miss Vaughan, a party litigant assisted by the CAB, lodged an ET1 on 3 October 2023 claiming age and disability discrimination; the age claim fell away and she pursued disability discrimination. She applied to amend her pleadings on 30 October 2024 after a November 2024 final hearing was postponed, and a fresh merits hearing was fixed for May 2025. She withdrew an unlawful deduction from wages claim during the hearing. The respondent (EE Limited) opposed the amendment.
issues: Should the claimant be permitted to amend her pleadings to the iteration set out in her application?
How should issues of time-bar in respect of the amended claims be handled?
Should the alleged incident at paragraph 42 (comments by colleagues) and the 13 July incident be admitted as claims or only as background?
deep.legal_test: Amendment of pleadings applying Selkent Bus Co Ltd v Moore [1996] ICR 836 (Mummery J's relevant factors: nature of the amendment, applicability of time limits, timing and manner of application) and the paramount balance of injustice/hardship per Vaughan v Modality Partnership [2021] ICR 535 and Abercrombie v Aga Rangemaster [2014] ICR 209.
deep.evidence_weighing: The judge weighed the late, last-minute manner of the application and the respondent's resulting difficulties against the fact that the claimant had been trying to amend since 2023 to cure deficiencies in her self-drafted ET1, had raised her difficulties internally and in a grievance, and that the postponed hearing gave the respondent months to prepare, mitigating prejudice.
deep.reasoning: Applying Selkent and the balance-of-hardship approach, the judge identified the amendment sought and weighed prejudice on both sides, finding the broad themes of the claim unchanged and the postponement reducing prejudice to the large respondent. The balance favoured allowing the claimant to ventilate her serious disability discrimination issues, so the amendment was granted, with time-bar reserved to the full hearing and the 13 July paragraph 42 incident admitted only as background to avoid undue prejudice. This was a case-management ruling rather than a determination of the substantive claims.

deep.facts: Mrs Thomas brought claims of unfair dismissal and disability discrimination against Fedcap Employment Scotland, but both were lodged out of time. At a preliminary hearing on time-bar she explained the delay arose because her husband was disabled and became very unwell during the relevant period. She had trade union (Unison) and ACAS assistance and had returned to work on 17 June, but did not lodge her tribunal claim until after the deadlines had passed.
issues: Was it not reasonably practicable for the unfair dismissal claim to be presented within the three-month limit under s.111 ERA 1996?
Was it just and equitable to extend time to hear the disability discrimination claims under s.123 Equality Act 2010?
deep.legal_test: s.111 ERA 1996 'not reasonably practicable' (Palmer v Southend, Dedman, Asda v Kauser) for unfair dismissal; s.123 Equality Act 2010 'just and equitable' discretion (Bexley Community Centre v Robertson, Caston) for discrimination
deep.evidence_weighing: The Tribunal found the claimant a capable, intelligent and organised person who had internet access, took only about an hour to lodge the application when she finally did, and had been appraised of tribunal procedures by her union lawyer and ACAS; her mental health was no impediment given she returned to work on 17 June.
deep.reasoning: The onus was on the claimant to show it was not reasonably practicable to present in time (Porter v Bandridge), and the judge found no good reason she had not researched or noted the time limits despite available means. On the discrimination claims, extension is the exception not the rule, and while she would suffer prejudice, her husband's health and her own circumstances did not justify exercising the wide discretion in her favour against the prejudice to the respondent. Both claims were therefore dismissed for want of jurisdiction.

deep.facts: Ms William, a Trainee Dispenser/Health Partner, claimed race and religion (Israelite tradition) discrimination, harassment, victimisation and holiday pay against L Rowland & Co (Retail) Ltd; her unfair dismissal claim was withdrawn for insufficient service. The respondent said she left work on 18 December 2023 without authorisation after a confrontational holiday dispute with her manager and did not return, and that she had been paid in full. The dispute centred on a confrontation about holiday at holiday time after which she was sent home.
issues: Was the claimant subjected to direct race discrimination under s.13 Equality Act 2010?
Was she subjected to harassment related to race or religion under s.26?
Was she victimised under s.27?
Was there an unlawful deduction from wages in respect of accrued holiday pay?
deep.legal_test: Direct discrimination s.13, harassment s.26 and victimisation s.27 Equality Act 2010, with causation/'reason why' analysis (Nagarajan v London Regional Transport - 'significant influence'); Vento bands for injury to feelings; holiday pay as unlawful deduction
deep.evidence_weighing: The Tribunal found the claimant honest and generally credible but found her perception of racism and the motives she attributed to others impossible to accept (e.g. her weight loss predated her employment); on holiday pay, the company's own records showed 74.25 accrued hours, only 69 were paid, and the respondent led no evidence to explain the 5.25-hour shortfall.
deep.reasoning: The Tribunal upheld the victimisation claim as well founded and awarded injury to feelings in the lower-middle Vento band plus interest, together with loss of wages for the month she was unemployed before starting comparable work. On holiday pay, the onus was on the claimant but having produced the company's own calculation showing 74.25 hours, the burden shifted to the respondent to justify paying only 69, which it failed to do, so the 5.25-hour claim succeeded.
deep.award_basis: £7,500 injury to feelings plus £644 interest for victimisation, £1,387 loss of wages plus £70.22 interest, and £51.98 accrued holiday pay

deep.facts: Mr Markie, a 56-year-old Social Services/Support Worker with the Salvation Army, was dismissed for gross misconduct after he was heard to say of refugees 'send them all back on a fucking boat' during a discussion about housing shortages, which he admitted saying but claimed was flippant and not racist. He claimed unfair dismissal and direct sex discrimination/harassment, alleging his manager Miss Young had made a sexist comment to him; he withdrew his religion/belief claim. The respondent's witnesses said the offending sexist comment in fact originated from the claimant, not his manager.
issues: Was the dismissal for the refugee comment outside the band of reasonable responses and therefore unfair?
Was the claimant subjected to direct sex discrimination under s.13 Equality Act 2010?
Was he subjected to harassment under s.26 Equality Act 2010 on the grounds of sex (and age)?
deep.legal_test: Band of reasonable responses for conduct dismissal (applying Vaultex UK Ltd v Bialas on state of mind and reckless/thoughtless conduct); direct sex discrimination s.13 and harassment s.26 Equality Act 2010
deep.evidence_weighing: The investigatory, disciplinary and appeal minutes were not disputed and corroborated that the claimant made the comment; the judge rejected the claimant's evidence that the comment was spontaneous and harmless, and found Miss Young's denial that she originated the alleged sexist comment was corroborated by other evidence, the claimant having only raised it at the appeal stage to deflect from his own misconduct.
deep.reasoning: The employer genuinely believed the comment expressed racist views and was entitled to treat it as serious and substantial; dismissal was not for a trivial reason and fell within the band of reasonable responses, so unfair dismissal failed. On the discrimination/harassment claims, the offending comment originated from the claimant himself rather than his manager, his evidence could not be relied upon, and the factual basis for the claims was not made out, so they too were dismissed.

reasoning_profile.disposition_summary: Kemp A is a precise, doctrinally rigorous judge who decides on the strict legal framework rather than broad fairness, frequently splitting outcomes (many partly_upheld) and awarding claimants discrete, well-evidenced wins (unauthorised deductions, reasonable adjustments, disability status) while dismissing unproven discrimination heads. He is balanced overall, generous to claimants on clearly authorised/quantified contractual and deduction points but exacting on discrimination causation. He decides confidently once the legal question is correctly framed.
reasoning_profile.procedural_vs_substantive: balanced - he engages fully with substantive Equality Act and deduction merits, but readily disposes of cases on threshold points too (time limits, strike-out under Rule 38, employee/disability status).
reasoning_profile.evidence_approach: He weighs witness credibility candidly and draws adverse inferences from a respondent's failure to produce documents or to challenge a figure, preferring clear, consistent and contemporaneous evidence; he will find a claim made out 'just' on thin evidence where the legal test is met, and accepts conceded credibility on both sides.
recurring_themes: deductions are about legal authorisation, not fairness (s.13 ERA)
adverse inference from a respondent's missing documents or unchallenged figures
careful 'related to'/contextual analysis on harassment (Warby v Wunda)
two-stage burden of proof and 'something more' on discrimination (Madarassy)
strict on disability definition and constructive knowledge (s.6, A Ltd v Z)
high threshold for strike-out and res judicata/abuse of process
common_legal_tests: s.13 ERA unauthorised deductions and authorisation by contract/written consent
ss.20/21 reasonable adjustments and ss.13/15/26/27 Equality Act 2010
s.136 burden of proof (Igen v Wong, Hewage, Madarassy)
s.6 disability definition (substantial, long-term, Schedule 1)
s.111 ERA / s.123 EqA time-limit tests
Rule 38 strike-out (Ezsias, Twist DX) and overriding objective
reasoning_profile.deliberation_guidance: Frame each claim against its exact statutory provision and ask first whether the legal precondition is satisfied - was a deduction actually authorised in writing, is the person disabled within s.6, did the respondent have knowledge? Resist deciding on what feels fair; decide on what the contract, statute and authorities permit. On discrimination, require the claimant to show 'something more' than difference in treatment before shifting the burden, and analyse harassment contextually. Where a respondent fails to produce documents or challenge a quantified figure, be ready to draw an adverse inference and find for the claimant on that point.

deep.facts: Mrs Puri, an Indian female Public Enquiry Support Assistant for the Scottish Police Authority with a foot/ankle disability (bilateral planovalgus) causing pain from prolonged standing, brought claims of direct race discrimination, failure to make reasonable adjustments, harassment related to race and sex, and victimisation. The key disability issue concerned the height of the counter at Stonehaven Police Station public office, which caused her pain when standing. The respondent admitted disability and knowledge but denied all claims, with a partial time-bar point taken.
issues: Did the respondent fail to make reasonable adjustments (ss.20/21) regarding the counter height and other matters?
Was the claimant subjected to direct race discrimination under s.13?
Was she subjected to harassment related to race and sex under s.26?
Was she victimised under s.27?
Were any claims time-barred?
deep.legal_test: Reasonable adjustments duty ss.20/21 Equality Act 2010; direct discrimination s.13; harassment s.26 ('related to' protected characteristic - Warby v Wunda); victimisation s.27; burden of proof s.136 (Igen v Wong, Hewage); Vento bands (as updated by Da'Bell, De Souza) for remedy
deep.evidence_weighing: On the counter, the Tribunal accepted that the practice put the disabled claimant at a substantial disadvantage and that lowering the counter was a reasonable step the respondent failed to take; on the harassment and race claims, the conduct was found to relate to work disputes rather than to the protected characteristics (applying Warby contextual analysis).
deep.reasoning: Applying ss.20/21, the Tribunal unanimously found one reasonable adjustment had not been made - taking steps to lower the Stonehaven counter - and awarded compensation for that breach. All the remaining claims (direct race discrimination, harassment, victimisation) were not established on the evidence and were dismissed, the conduct complained of not being shown to be related to or because of the protected characteristics.
deep.award_basis: compensation for failure to make a reasonable adjustment (counter height) under ss.20/21 Equality Act 2010

deep.facts: Mr Williamson was recruited as a Business Development Manager by PTS Services Group Ltd, taking a salary cut from £58,000 to £50,000 on the strength of a 'Monthly bonus scheme' set out in a letter of offer handed to him at a meeting on 6 October 2023. The respondent later claimed it had given him a written contract of employment making the bonus discretionary, which superseded the offer letter. The claimant denied ever receiving such a contract and claimed the unpaid bonus as a breach of contract.
issues: Was the respondent in breach of contract in not paying bonus to the claimant?
If so, what sum should be awarded?
deep.legal_test: Breach of contract under the Employment Tribunals (Extension of Jurisdiction)(Scotland) Order 1994; contractual interpretation (HFD Glasgow 3 Ltd v Student Loans Co)
deep.evidence_weighing: The judge preferred the claimant's clear and consistent evidence (including his unchallenged higher prior salary) over Mr Ord's, and drew an adverse inference from the respondent's failure to produce any written evidence to challenge the £6,000 bonus figure despite holding the relevant financial figures, and from the lack of cross-examination on the amount.
deep.reasoning: The judge found the claimant credible and reliable and did not accept that the respondent had given him the written contract it relied on, so the non-discretionary bonus terms in the offer letter governed. Given the absence of any contrary evidence on quantum, the judge accepted the claimant's figure and held the respondent in breach for non-payment, awarding £6,000 gross subject to statutory deductions.
deep.award_basis: breach of contract for unpaid monthly bonus due under the letter of offer

deep.facts: Mr Allan, an ad hoc taxi driver for Central Taxis (North East) Ltd, damaged a company vehicle in the early hours of 1 June 2025 by reversing into a wall, causing £2,416.72 of damage; he accepted fault. The respondent deducted £500 (its insurance excess) from his wages, relying on a notice posted on a company app on 20 February 2025 stating drivers would pay for damage up to £500. The claimant had never been given a written contract or statement of particulars, had not read the notice, and had not consented in writing to the deduction.
issues: Did the respondent make an unauthorised deduction from the claimant's wages contrary to s.13 ERA 1996?
deep.legal_test: s.13 ERA 1996 - deduction must be authorised by a relevant contractual provision or prior written consent; incorporation of terms by notice (Kerr v Sweater Shop) and by custom/practice ('reasonable, notorious and certain' - Garratt, Park Cakes v Shumba, Quinn v Calder)
deep.evidence_weighing: Both witnesses were found credible and candid; Mr Anderson conceded he could not recall raising any deduction term when the claimant joined, so did not challenge the claimant's evidence that it was never raised, and there was no written contract or signed consent.
deep.reasoning: The judge held this was not a question of fairness but of legal authorisation: with no written contract, no signed consent, and a notice that (per Kerr) could not amount to a contractual term, the respondent had to but could not establish a contractual right to deduct. The custom-and-practice argument failed (the respondent itself was introducing a new consent form), and the hire-vehicle analogy was rejected because s.13 qualifies the common-law position; the £500 deduction was therefore unauthorised and awarded to the claimant.
deep.award_basis: unauthorised deduction from wages (insurance excess) under s.13 ERA 1996

cases.respondent: The Highland Laundry Room Ltd and Mr N Forbes

deep.facts: Ms Ozga, a Polish part-time Laundry Assistant for The Highland Laundry Room Ltd, was never given a written statement of particulars (the respondent told her 'you don't get a contract when you're part-time') and resigned on 26 July 2024, asking that accrued holiday pay be added to her final pay. She brought claims for failure to provide a statement of particulars (ss.1-4 ERA), failure to provide payslips (s.8 ERA), and unauthorised deductions from wages (s.13 ERA, including unpaid holiday pay); her direct race discrimination claim and the claim against the second respondent were withdrawn.
issues: Did the respondent fail to provide a statement of particulars under ss.1-4 ERA 1996?
Did the respondent fail to provide payslips under s.8 ERA 1996?
Did the respondent make unauthorised deductions from wages under s.13 ERA 1996 (including holiday pay)?
What remedy, if any?
deep.legal_test: ss.1-4 ERA 1996 statement of particulars (remedy via s.38 Employment Act 2002, contingent on a Schedule 5 jurisdiction such as s.23); s.8 ERA payslips; s.13 ERA unauthorised deductions; holiday pay under Working Time Regulations 1998 reg.14
deep.evidence_weighing: Both the claimant, her witness Ms Anuska, and Mr Forbes were found to be honest; the respondent had deliberately but wrongly taken the position that part-time/probationary staff get no statement of particulars and had not paid the holiday pay timeously despite it being specifically requested on 17 and 26 July 2024.
deep.reasoning: The judge dismissed the s.8 payslip claim and the withdrawn discrimination claims, but upheld the statement-of-particulars claim and granted a declaration of unlawful deductions, finding the respondent in serious breach including failing to pay accrued holiday pay. Compensation comprised the unpaid holiday pay plus a small (£50) award for financial loss from late payment (overdraft charges/loss of use of funds), with the s.38 uplift available because the s.23 deductions claim was engaged, totalling £806.92.
deep.award_basis: unpaid holiday pay/unlawful deductions plus £50 for late-payment financial loss, with statement-of-particulars breach declared

deep.facts: Miss Coutts, a Site Co-ordinator with Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease, was made redundant by Sky Subscriber Services Ltd effective 26 September 2024. She brought an unfair dismissal claim and disability discrimination claims (ss.15 and 20/21 Equality Act). Her claim form was presented on 4 March 2025, nine days after the 23 February 2025 deadline; she had contacted ACAS for redundancy advice but was not advised about tribunal time-limits, and her foot operation was repeatedly cancelled and postponed to April 2025.
issues: Was it not reasonably practicable to present the unfair dismissal claim in time under s.111 ERA 1996, and if so was it presented within a reasonable further period?
Was it just and equitable to extend time for the disability discrimination claims under s.123 Equality Act 2010?
deep.legal_test: s.111 ERA 1996 'not reasonably practicable' (Palmer v Southend - 'reasonably feasible'); s.123 Equality Act 2010 'just and equitable' discretion (Robertson, as qualified by Jones v Secretary of State for Health [2025] EAT 76); burden of proof considerations
deep.evidence_weighing: The claimant was found generally credible and reliable but produced no medical evidence to support her position; the judge accepted the dismissal and her condition affected her mental health, but noted she could work, looked after her child, looked for jobs and managed her symptoms.
deep.reasoning: On unfair dismissal, the burden was on the claimant to show it was not reasonably practicable to present in time, and despite accepting the impact on her mental health, the judge found she had not discharged that burden, so that claim was dismissed for want of jurisdiction. On the discrimination claims, however, the judge exercised the wider just-and-equitable discretion in her favour, holding it just and equitable to extend time, so those claims were allowed to proceed; the case management directions show liability/remedy on the substantive discrimination claims was left to a future final hearing.

deep.facts: Mr Smith joined Highland Fuels Ltd in January 2025 and the respondent paid for HGV fuel-driver training (CPC and ADR qualifications) involving flights and hotels. He soon attended interviews with other companies and resigned, and on 10 March 2025 had used another employee's passcode to obtain fuel without authority. The respondent deducted £2,509.80 from his final wages, relying on a contractual clause (clause 9) allowing recovery of monies the company is vicariously liable for; the claimant brought an unauthorised deduction claim and the amount was effectively undisputed.
issues: Did the respondent make an unauthorised deduction from the claimant's wages under s.13 ERA 1996?
If so, what sum should be awarded?
deep.legal_test: s.13 ERA 1996 - whether the deduction was authorised by a relevant written contractual provision; construction of the contractual deduction clause in the context of s.13
deep.evidence_weighing: The respondent's argument that the claimant always intended to leave (a form of fraudulent misrepresentation) failed on the facts - the claimant's evidence that he only sought new work after an issue with another driver and realising overtime was less than understood was accepted, and the new job did not even use the funded qualifications.
deep.reasoning: Construing the contract (clause 9 covered vicarious liability to third parties, not recovery of training costs) in the context of s.13, the judge concluded the deduction was not authorised by any relevant contractual provision. The respondent's misrepresentation argument was both legally incompetent as a defence to a s.13 claim and failed on the facts, so the full deducted sum of £2,509.80 was awarded to the claimant.
deep.award_basis: unauthorised deduction from wages under s.13 ERA 1996

cases.respondent: Mid and East Lothian Drugs SCIO

deep.facts: Ms Carter, a Recovery Worker employed by Mid and East Lothian Drugs SCIO, brought Equality Act claims and a preliminary hearing was held solely to determine whether she was a disabled person under s.6. She had suffered childhood abuse and time in care, attempted suicide twice, suffered a stillbirth, and was diagnosed with PTSD (later CPTSD), depression (2011) and anxiety (2018), with ongoing therapy and medication. Her disability impact statement was thin on detail about effects on day-to-day activities, but she described hypervigilance/difficulty leaving the house, poor sleep with nightmares/flashbacks, concentration and interaction problems at work, and difficulty with personal care.
issues: Was the claimant a disabled person within s.6 Equality Act 2010 at the material times - i.e. did she have a physical or mental impairment with a substantial and long-term adverse effect on her ability to carry out normal day-to-day activities?
deep.legal_test: s.6 Equality Act 2010 disability definition - impairment with a substantial (more than minor or trivial, s.212) and long-term (Schedule 1, lasting/likely 12+ months) adverse effect on normal day-to-day activities; deduced effects/medical treatment provisions in Schedule 1
deep.evidence_weighing: The judge accepted there was a CPTSD diagnosis in the medical records with specialist therapy, plus diagnosed depression and anxiety with medication, distinguishing this from a normal reaction to life events; despite the thin impact statement and limited oral evidence, the described effects were held, 'just', sufficient to meet the day-to-day activities and substantiality limbs.
deep.reasoning: The judge found the mental impairment (CPTSD/depression/anxiety) established and not merely normal reactions to life events, and although the evidence on adverse effect was lacking in detail, the hypervigilance, sleep problems, concentration/interaction difficulties and personal-care difficulties were normal day-to-day activities affected to a more than minor degree. He held the effect was long-term, ongoing since the 1997 PTSD diagnosis and fluctuating but persisting, and therefore concluded the claimant was a disabled person at all material times.

deep.facts: EF, a black Retentions Adviser with ADHD employed by McQueens Dairies Ltd, was dismissed during her probation and brought Equality Act claims of direct discrimination (s.13), discrimination arising from disability (s.15), failure to make reasonable adjustments (ss.20/21) and victimisation (s.27), naming an actual comparator. The respondent admitted disability status but not knowledge, and said the dismissal was because of concerns over absence and lateness, culminating in her notifying on 27 September 2023 that she would be late again by about three hours without a reason. The case involved numerous preliminary disputes over documents, comparators and a bias allegation against a tribunal member.
issues: Did the respondent know or could it reasonably have been expected to know of the disability?
Was there direct race or disability discrimination under s.13?
Was there discrimination arising from disability under s.15, and if so was it justified?
Did the respondent fail to make reasonable adjustments under ss.20/21?
Was the claimant victimised under s.27 (had a protected act occurred and was any detriment because of it)?
deep.legal_test: ss.13, 15, 20/21 and 27 Equality Act 2010; constructive knowledge (A Ltd v Z); 'unfavourable treatment' s.15 (Williams v Swansea University); objective justification (Hardys & Hansons v Lax, Hensman v MoD); comparator analysis (North Bristol NHS Trust v Harrold)
deep.evidence_weighing: The Tribunal preferred the respondent's witnesses, accepting Ms McLaughlin's evidence that she had not shouted at the claimant and rejecting the claimant's account; it found no sufficient evidence of a causal link between any alleged protected act and any detriment, noting the probation was extended on 13 September 2023 after the alleged disclosures.
deep.reasoning: The Tribunal found the reason for the documentation increase and dismissal was the claimant's absence and lateness, culminating in the unexplained late notification on 27 September 2023, and in no way because of any protected characteristic or protected act. Even if a protected act had been established, there was no adequate evidence the detriments were because of it, so the victimisation claim would fail on that separate basis; all the Equality Act claims were unanimously dismissed and the question of remedy did not arise.

deep.facts: Mr Brown was employed by the respondent in a security role on its ferries from around August 2017 and was suspended in December 2023 over allegations, then dismissed for gross misconduct, with his appeal refused on 1 March 2024 (the dismissal letter being dated 8 February 2024). He had earlier withdrawn an automatic unfair dismissal/whistleblowing claim and pursued only ordinary unfair dismissal. He commenced early conciliation on 20 June 2024 and presented his claim on 24 July 2024, asserting a termination date of 24 March 2024 to argue the claim was in time; his mental health deteriorated badly after dismissal.
issues: What was the effective date of termination?
If the claim was presented late, was it not reasonably practicable to present it in time?
If so, was the claim presented within a reasonable period thereafter?
deep.legal_test: Time-bar under s.111 ERA 1996: the effective date of termination, whether it was reasonably practicable to present the claim in time, and whether presentation followed within a reasonable further period (references to Inchcape Retail Ltd v Shelton and Chourafi v London United Bus).
deep.evidence_weighing: The judge found the claimant's evidence unreliable on key matters, treating his reliance on a 24 March 2024 termination date as an artificial vehicle to argue timeliness; he gave little weight to Ms Allison's comments on medical matters given her lack of relevant qualifications.
deep.reasoning: The judge rejected 24 March 2024 as the termination date as having no evidential basis. Even taking the claimant's case at its most favourable, after legal advice and early conciliation commenced on 20 June 2024 it was reasonable to present the claim within a few days, yet the claimant delayed a further unexplained three weeks until 24 July 2024, beyond a reasonable period given the short three-month limit had already long expired. The claim was therefore out of time, the Tribunal had no jurisdiction under s.111, and it was dismissed.

deep.facts: The claimant, a party litigant, had previously pursued (and lost/had struck out) an employment claim against his former employer myCare Tayside Ltd. He then brought this fresh claim against the solicitor (employed by Croner Consulting Ltd) who had represented that employer in the original case, complaining about a 'date listing letter' he said was his intellectual property and that it had been abused because of his religion. He sought reinstatement, arguing the solicitor could instruct the employer to reinstate him. The respondent solicitor applied to strike out the claim as vexatious and having no reasonable prospects.
issues: Whether the claim should be struck out as vexatious, conducted vexatiously, and/or as having no reasonable prospects of success under Rule 38
Whether the claim was an abuse of process / barred by res judicata given the determination of the original claim
Whether the Tribunal had jurisdiction over a claim against the employer's solicitor (who was not the employer)
Whether the claimant should be awarded the expenses of the transfer from Nottingham to Scotland
deep.legal_test: Strike out under Rule 38 (and Rule 3 overriding objective) of the Employment Tribunal Procedure Rules 2024 for vexatious conduct / no reasonable prospects of success, applying authorities such as Ezsias, Tayside v Reilly and Twist DX v Armes on the high threshold for striking out, together with the Scottish concept of res judicata / abuse of process (McCluskey, British Airways v Boyce)
deep.evidence_weighing: When repeatedly asked to articulate the legal basis of his claims, the claimant could not set out any claim the judge was able to understand; the respondent solicitor was visibly stressed and the proceedings imposed a clear mental toll, which the judge weighed in favour of strike out.
deep.reasoning: The judge found the claim had no legal basis: the respondent was the opposing party's solicitor, not the employer, so the Tribunal had no jurisdiction and reinstatement could not be ordered through her. The grievance about the date listing letter could and should have been raised within the original claim, making this re-litigation an abuse of process and vexatious. As the claimant could not articulate any coherent claim even when invited to, and further amendment would only increase expense and harm to the respondent, strike out (rather than a lesser step) accorded with the overriding objective; the expenses application was refused because the transfer was a proper, judge-granted step and nothing the respondent did was unreasonable.

deep.facts: The claimant, a dispenser employed by the respondent pharmacy from 2019, had a poor relationship with two basement-level colleagues (Ms McArthur and Ms Henderson). She raised a grievance which was partially upheld, then overturned on the colleague's appeal and re-investigated. She reduced her hours to Saturdays only to avoid the colleagues, then resigned, claiming constructive unfair dismissal, failure to make reasonable adjustments (prescriptions placed on low shelves she struggled to reach due to disability) and disability-related harassment.
issues: Whether the claimant was constructively dismissed under s.95(1)(c) ERA 1996 by reason of a fundamental breach of contract (failure to address the difficult working relationship)
Whether the respondent failed in the duty to make reasonable adjustments under s.21 Equality Act 2010 regarding prescriptions on low shelves
Whether the claimant was subjected to harassment related to disability under s.26 Equality Act 2010
Whether the harassment complaints were brought in time / part of conduct extending over a period
deep.legal_test: Constructive dismissal under s.95(1)(c) ERA 1996 (fundamental breach of contract); reasonable adjustments duty under ss.20/21 Equality Act 2010; harassment 'related to' a protected characteristic under s.26 EqA, applying Warby v Wunda (context) and EAT guidance that there must be a feature of the factual matrix linking the conduct to the characteristic
deep.evidence_weighing: The Tribunal generally accepted the respondent's witnesses and found the various meeting and interview notes to be reasonably accurate records; the claimant had not raised any adjustment issue at the May 2024 health review and had agreed there had been no bullying, undermining her account.
deep.reasoning: The Tribunal found no fundamental breach of contract: the respondent had handled the grievance, appeal and re-investigation reasonably, so there was no constructive dismissal. It found no failure to make reasonable adjustments. On harassment, the impugned acts were either out of time (and not just and equitable to extend, not being conduct extending over a period) or, in any event, not related to the claimant's disability (e.g. the HighFive message was handled properly and was not disability-related). All claims accordingly failed and the claim was dismissed.

deep.facts: The claimant, aged 16 and in her first job, was employed by the respondent fish-and-chip restaurant/takeaway from around August 2024. She was moved from the restaurant to the takeaway after being considered not to have performed well, and was dismissed (told by email) following a phone call in which she said she had not been trained on issues that arose; the directors believed she had muted the call, which she denied. She claimed direct age discrimination, relying on the respondent's use of age-related terms ('child workers', 'young workers') and failure to provide a statement of particulars. A breach of contract claim was withdrawn after notice and holiday pay were paid.
issues: Whether the respondent directly discriminated against the claimant because of age under s.13 Equality Act 2010 by (a) failing to provide a statement of particulars of employment and/or (b) dismissing her
If discrimination established, what remedy (injury to feelings and losses) was appropriate
deep.legal_test: Direct age discrimination under s.13 Equality Act 2010 with the two-stage burden of proof under s.136 (Igen v Wong, Madarassy, Ayodele), requiring the claimant first to establish primary facts from which discrimination could be inferred (Chapman v Simon; Bahl), the burden then shifting to the respondent
deep.evidence_weighing: The judge accepted Ms Buchan's evidence that the claimant had been moved due to performance concerns and that Ms Buchan was genuinely concerned about the claimant's conduct on the phone call (which she believed was not investigated but genuine); the use of age-labelling terms and the lack of any process were noted but found not to indicate age was a factor.
deep.reasoning: Although the respondent's conduct (no procedure, dismissing a 16-year-old by email, age-labelling terminology) was surprising and showed a lack of consideration, the judge found these did not show age itself operated on the decision-makers' minds. The respondent discharged the onus under s.136, establishing that age played no part whatsoever in either the failure to provide a statement of particulars or the dismissal, which were driven by genuine (if poorly handled) performance and conduct concerns. The s.13 claim therefore did not succeed; the breach of contract claim was withdrawn; and the claim was dismissed.

cases.respondent: Fife Health Board and Dr B Upton

deep.facts: The claimant, a long-serving nurse with gender critical beliefs, and the second respondent, a trans woman junior doctor permitted to use the female staff changing room, both worked for the first respondent NHS health board. Central to the case was an encounter between them in the changing room over Christmas Eve/Christmas Day 2023 and the first respondent's handling of a subsequent complaint by the second respondent against the claimant. The claimant brought a range of Equality Act claims: direct discrimination, indirect discrimination, harassment (s.26(1),(2),(3)) and victimisation, on grounds of sex and belief.
issues: Whether the first respondent harassed the claimant under s.26(1) Equality Act 2010 (including by permitting the second respondent to use the female changing room, delay in investigating, raising patient-care allegations, and a restrictive instruction)
Whether there was sexual harassment under s.26(2) or harassment by rejection/submission under s.26(3)
Whether there was direct discrimination under s.13 because of sex or belief
Whether there was indirect discrimination under s.19 in respect of sex or belief
Whether there was victimisation under s.27
Whether any claim succeeded against the second respondent personally
deep.legal_test: Liability under the Equality Act 2010 - harassment under s.26(1)/(2)/(3), direct discrimination s.13, indirect discrimination s.19, victimisation s.27 - applying For Women Scotland Ltd v Scottish Ministers [2025] ICR 899 on the meaning of sex/woman under the EA 2010
deep.evidence_weighing: The judgment text provided does not set out the detailed credibility/evidence findings (the trimmed text cuts to ECtHR authority on Article 10), but the Tribunal made specific findings that certain conduct by the first respondent (failure to revoke changing-room permission, an unreasonably long investigation exceeding six months, reference to patient-care allegations, and a discussion instruction) amounted to harassment.
deep.reasoning: The Tribunal upheld the s.26(1) harassment claim against the first respondent in four specific respects (failing to revoke the second respondent's changing-room permission until rota changes, taking an unreasonable time to investigate, referencing patient-care allegations on 28 March 2024, and the 5 July 2024 instruction not to discuss the case). All other harassment allegations and the s.26(2) and (3) claims failed, as did the direct discrimination (s.13), indirect discrimination (s.19) and victimisation (s.27) claims. The claims against the second respondent personally were dismissed. Liability only was decided, with remedy to be fixed at a separate hearing.

reasoning_profile.disposition_summary: Ayre is a balanced, structured judge who splits outcomes frequently, willing to make strong findings of discrimination where a decision-maker's conduct is unreliable and unexplained on any non-discriminatory basis, yet dismissing discrimination claims where the claimant cannot point to a comparator or facts shifting the burden. He applies the band of reasonable responses and material-factor/justification defences rigorously, and is firm on time-limit jurisdiction and on disability status as a gateway. He decides on a careful, issue-by-issue basis.
reasoning_profile.procedural_vs_substantive: balanced - he resolves many claims on substantive merits (discrimination inference, equal pay, capability) but also disposes of cases on reasonably-practicable time limits, disability status and interim-relief thresholds.
reasoning_profile.evidence_approach: He infers discrimination from a decision-maker's unreliable, inconsistent or unexplained conduct (e.g. interviewing only one racial group, relying on absent witnesses) but otherwise requires the claimant to identify a real comparator and prove facts; he tests 'unwanted' conduct against the claimant's contemporaneous demeanour and weighs medical evidence carefully on disability and capability.
recurring_themes: inference of discrimination from unreliable/unexplained decision-maker conduct
requires comparator and facts to shift the s.136 burden
band of reasonable responses and material-factor/justification defences
strict reasonably-practicable time-limit jurisdiction (Palmer, Dedman)
disability status under s.6 as a threshold (jurisdiction over adjustments)
context-sensitive 'unwanted conduct' test for harassment
common_legal_tests: s.13/s.26 EqA, s.23 comparator (Shamoon) and s.136 burden (Igen, Barton)
s.98(1)/(2)/(4) ERA band of reasonable responses (Beatt on reason)
equal pay - like work s.65 and material factor defence s.69 EqA
s.6 EqA disability definition (Goodwin/Rugamer effect-focused)
s.111/s.23 ERA reasonably-practicable time limits (Palmer, Dedman)
ss.128-129 ERA interim relief 'likely' threshold
reasoning_profile.deliberation_guidance: Work through the agreed list of issues methodically. On discrimination, first ask whether the claimant has proved primary facts and identified a genuine comparator; do not let the burden shift on bare difference in treatment, but be prepared to infer discrimination where a decision-maker's conduct is unreliable, inconsistent and unexplained on any non-discriminatory basis. Test harassment by whether the conduct was genuinely 'unwanted' in context, including the claimant's contemporaneous demeanour. Treat disability status and time limits as jurisdictional gateways and apply the reasonably-practicable test strictly. On unfair dismissal apply the band of reasonable responses, and on equal pay require the respondent to prove a non-sex material factor for the whole differential.

deep.facts: The claimant was employed as an Engineering Administrator in the Low Risk Engineering Department from April 2017 until 31 July 2024, when she was made redundant after the business lost a significant volume of work. She brought claims of unfair (redundancy) dismissal and equal pay, naming Tony Burke (a High Risk Engineering Administrator) as her comparator and contending she was paid less for like work because of sex. The respondent said the pay difference was due to service and Mr Burke's additional duties.
issues: What was the reason or principal reason for dismissal and whether redundancy dismissal was within the band of reasonable responses (selection pool and selection)
Whether the claimant's work was the same or broadly similar (like work) to that of comparator Tony Burke, and from what date
Whether the difference in pay was wholly attributable to a material factor other than sex under s.69 Equality Act 2010
What compensation/arrears were payable, and the correct arrears date under s.132 Equality Act 2010
deep.legal_test: Unfair dismissal: potentially fair reason under s.98(1)/(2) ERA and band of reasonable responses under s.98(4) (Beatt on reason for dismissal). Equal pay: like work under s.65(1) Equality Act 2010 and the material factor defence under s.69; arrears date under s.132(4) EqA
deep.evidence_weighing: The Tribunal accepted the redundancy reason and that the selection process fell within the range of reasonable responses; on equal pay it found the differences between the claimant's and Mr Burke's work were not of practical importance (like work) and the respondent failed to prove the whole pay difference was due to non-sex material factors (service/additional duties).
deep.reasoning: On unfair dismissal, the respondent showed redundancy as the reason and acted within the band of reasonable responses in its pool and selection, so that claim was dismissed. On equal pay, the claimant's work was like Mr Burke's under s.65(1) and the respondent did not establish a material factor other than sex under s.69, so the sex equality clause modified her pay terms. On its own initiative under Rule 71 the Tribunal corrected an error on the arrears date, limiting arrears to the six years before proceedings (from 17 November 2018 rather than 2018 employment-start). It awarded agreed arrears of £16,808.48 plus £4,829.79 interest, totalling £21,638.27.
deep.award_basis: equal pay arrears (£16,808.48) plus statutory interest (£4,829.79); unfair dismissal claim dismissed

deep.facts: The claimant, a Senior Fire Extinguisher Sales and Service Engineer employed since 2016, was dismissed for gross misconduct after, on 9 February 2024, he repeatedly punched and kicked another driver (Mr Bonner) following a parking dispute at a customer's premises while in a company van and branded clothing. The incident was captured on CCTV. He failed to attend reconvened disciplinary hearings, saying he had 'had enough'. He claimed unfair dismissal and unpaid February 2024 commission (as unlawful deduction and, alternatively, breach of contract); two further wage claims were withdrawn.
issues: Whether the dismissal for conduct was fair under s.98 ERA 1996 (reason and band of reasonable responses)
Whether the non-payment of February 2024 commission was an unauthorised deduction from wages under the ERA
Whether non-payment of the commission was a breach of contract
deep.legal_test: Unfair dismissal: potentially fair reason under s.98(1)/(2) ERA and reasonableness under s.98(4), band of reasonable responses (with Beatt on reason for dismissal); unauthorised deduction from wages under the ERA, construed against the contractual Performance Related Pay scheme rules
deep.evidence_weighing: The Tribunal viewed CCTV of the assault and heard a recording of the disciplinary hearing; it found the claimant a good performer but accepted he had committed the assault and had refused to attend reconvened hearings, and that the PRP scheme rules forfeited commission entitlement in his circumstances.
deep.reasoning: The conduct (a serious physical assault while representing the employer) was a fair reason and dismissal fell within the band of reasonable responses, so the unfair dismissal claim failed. On commission, the PRP/commission scheme rules in the handbook (which the contract incorporated subject to such conditions as the respondent decided) provided no entitlement to payment where an employee is suspended pending or found guilty of a disciplinary offence, so there was no sum properly payable and thus no unlawful deduction. For the same contractual reason the breach of contract claim failed. The withdrawn wage claims were dismissed on withdrawal.

deep.facts: The claimant, a Romanian warehouse operative who transferred to the respondent online retailer under TUPE, was dismissed on 20 December 2023 for conduct (alleged misconduct relating to consuming/handling product). He brought claims of unfair dismissal, wrongful dismissal (notice pay) and direct race discrimination, naming several British, Polish and Latvian colleagues as comparators and arguing they behaved similarly but were not disciplined. The respondent did not provide him a hard-copy bundle and the documents were in English (not his first language); he twice declined a postponement.
issues: Whether the dismissal for conduct was fair (genuine belief, reasonable grounds, reasonable investigation, procedural fairness, band of reasonable responses) under s.98 ERA
Whether the dismissal was unfair due to inconsistency of treatment
Whether the claimant was paid notice / guilty of gross misconduct (wrongful dismissal)
Whether the dismissal was less favourable treatment because of race (direct race discrimination) compared with named comparators
deep.legal_test: Unfair dismissal: reason under s.98(1)/(2) ERA and band of reasonable responses under s.98(4) (Burchell-type approach - genuine belief, reasonable grounds, reasonable investigation); wrongful dismissal: whether gross misconduct entitling summary dismissal without notice; direct race discrimination under s.13 Equality Act 2010 with two-stage burden of proof under s.136
deep.evidence_weighing: The Tribunal heard from the claimant and several former-colleague/witnesses plus the appeal officer, and admitted a disputed 'Toolbox Talk' record (which the claimant's witnesses said postdated his dismissal); findings on the unfair dismissal claim turned on shortcomings in the respondent's process, while the discrimination claim failed for lack of facts supporting an inference of race being the reason.
deep.reasoning: The Tribunal found the dismissal unfair (the unfair dismissal claim succeeded) and that the respondent breached contract by not giving notice or pay in lieu, so the notice pay claim succeeded. The direct race discrimination claim failed and was dismissed, the claimant not having proved facts from which race discrimination could be inferred. Remedy for unfair dismissal (beyond Polkey/contribution) was left to a separate Remedy Hearing. A later reconsideration application by the claimant was rejected as having no reasonable prospect of success, the correct route for any error of law being appeal.

deep.facts: The claimant, a white British Facilities Manager employed from August 2023 to November 2024, carried out PAT testing and, on 5 August 2024, picked up and put down (allegedly flung 'in contempt') an extension lead at the workstation of Mr Bashir Omar, a black South African colleague, without speaking to him. Mr Omar complained. The claimant brought claims of direct race discrimination (failure to investigate his own grievance; less favourable treatment than Mr Omar) and harassment related to race (alleging HR adviser Samantha Gaunt told him Mr Omar had a protected characteristic but he did not). The respondent later sought £20,000 costs.
issues: Whether the respondent failed to investigate the claimant's grievance and treated him less favourably than comparator Bashir Omar because of race (direct race discrimination)
Whether the claimant was subjected to harassment related to race (alleged comment by Samantha Gaunt)
Whether the respondent's application for costs of £20,000 should be granted
deep.legal_test: Direct race discrimination under s.13 Equality Act 2010 (less favourable treatment, comparator under s.23 - Shamoon) with two-stage burden of proof under s.136 (Igen v Wong, Barton); harassment related to race under s.26 EqA; costs under the Tribunal rules (exception not the rule - Yerrakalva, Power v Panasonic)
deep.evidence_weighing: The evidence showed the claimant's grievance was investigated promptly (a meeting six days after he raised it, with a written outcome); differences between the two investigations were carried out by different people and there was no evidence from which to infer they were because of race.
deep.reasoning: The Tribunal found the claimant had not proved facts from which race discrimination could be inferred: his grievance was in fact promptly and properly investigated, and the differences between the two investigations were not shown to be race-related, so the direct discrimination claim failed. The harassment claim also failed and was dismissed. On costs, the Tribunal held costs are the exception, the claim was not without reasonable prospects and the claimant had not acted unreasonably, so the respondent's £20,000 costs application was refused.

deep.facts: The claimant, disabled by bipolar disorder, brought disability discrimination claims against his former employer (now in creditors' voluntary liquidation), which did not respond or attend. He had not complied with case management orders (no witness statement, schedule of loss or documents) but elected to proceed, giving evidence orally. His complaints related to being excluded from meetings (the employer believing he had resigned), cancellation of his Westfield Health mental health support, and a manager (Mr Brewster) telling him in late July 2023 'no one likes you; no one respects you, you're crazy'.
issues: Whether the claims were brought within the time limit in s.123 Equality Act 2010 (and whether to extend time on a just and equitable basis)
Whether the claimant was disabled within s.6 Equality Act 2010 (bipolar disorder)
Whether there was discrimination arising from disability
Whether there was a failure to make reasonable adjustments
Whether the claimant was subjected to disability-related harassment
deep.legal_test: Disability status under s.6 Equality Act 2010; discrimination arising from disability (s.15); reasonable adjustments duty (ss.20/21); harassment related to disability under s.26 EqA; time limits and just-and-equitable extension under s.123 EqA
deep.evidence_weighing: With the claim undefended and only the claimant's oral evidence (no documents or statement), the Tribunal accepted he was disabled by bipolar disorder and accepted his account of Mr Brewster's 'you're crazy' comment as a specific act of disability-related harassment, while finding the other matters did not make out the other heads of claim.
deep.reasoning: The Tribunal held the claimant was a disabled person under s.6. The discrimination arising from disability and reasonable adjustments claims failed and were dismissed. The disability-related harassment claim succeeded only in respect of Mr Brewster's late-July 2023 remark ('no one likes you, no one respects you, you're crazy'), with other harassment complaints dismissed. The Tribunal awarded £2,000 for injury to feelings, noting recovery was unlikely given the respondent was in liquidation.
deep.award_basis: injury to feelings for disability-related harassment

deep.facts: The claimant, who had ulcerative colitis, had presented a first claim (constructive unfair dismissal) while still employed, then presented this second claim alleging automatic unfair dismissal for whistleblowing and applying for interim relief. He alleged multiple protected disclosures between November 2024 and August 2025 about occupational health recommendations, health and safety, holiday pay and data protection. The respondent said he was dismissed due to an irretrievable breakdown in the working relationship. The hearing also dealt with the claimant's applications to exclude the respondent's witness statement and to proceed on the papers.
issues: Whether the witness statement of Wendy Stroud should be excluded or given minimal weight
Whether it is 'likely' that at the final hearing the Tribunal would find the reason or principal reason for dismissal was the making of protected disclosures (the interim relief test)
Whether the disclosures relied upon were in the public interest / adequately particularised
Whether to grant interim relief
deep.legal_test: Interim relief under ss.128-129 Employment Rights Act 1996 - whether it is 'likely' (a higher threshold, generally pretty good chance) that the Tribunal at the final hearing will find the dismissal was for a protected disclosure (s.103A), making a broad assessment on the available material
deep.evidence_weighing: The judge admitted Wendy Stroud's (the dismissing decision-maker's) statement, since both sides served evidence at short notice and excluding the decision-maker's evidence would be unfair; no oral evidence was given. The claim form did not particularise the disclosures, did not explain why they were in the public interest, and did not identify whose interest was engaged.
deep.reasoning: Making a broad assessment for interim relief, the judge found the claimant had not discharged the burden of showing it was 'likely' the final Tribunal would find the dismissal was for protected disclosures: the claim form failed to particularise the disclosures or address the public interest element at all, and the occupational-health point relied on a general 'stress-free workplace' suggestion (removal of a colleague) rather than identified refused recommendations. The application for interim relief therefore failed and was dismissed; ancillary disclosure/witness applications were refused as premature.

deep.facts: The claimant, a Black African nurse employed at the respondent's complex-needs care home since 2015, was accused of sleeping on duty on 9/10 March 2023 (gross misconduct under the respondent's policy). Only white nursing staff on shift were interviewed during the process; she received a final written warning on 20 July 2023, and her appeal failed. She submitted a video showing a white nurse (Angela Briggs) sleeping at work, which was not taken into account. She brought direct race discrimination claims about the investigation, disciplinary process, the final written warning and the appeal, and later resigned.
issues: Whether the respondent failed to carry out a full and fair investigation (14 March-17 April 2023) by only speaking to white staff - and whether that was race discrimination
Whether the disciplinary process was conducted unfairly by only speaking to white staff because of race
Whether giving the final written warning on 20 July 2023 was race discrimination
Whether the appeal process failed to consider the claimant's position (failing to rectify earlier failings and to consider the video of a white nurse sleeping) because of race
Whether the treatment was less favourable than her comparator (Angela Briggs) / a hypothetical comparator and amounted to a detriment
deep.legal_test: Direct race discrimination under s.13 Equality Act 2010 - less favourable treatment, comparator under s.23 (Shamoon) - with the two-stage burden of proof under s.136 (Igen v Wong, Barton); injury-to-feelings assessment per Vento bands at the remedy stage
deep.evidence_weighing: The Tribunal found the dismissing manager Ms Payne's findings unreliable - she said no one had seen the claimant working when the disciplinary notes recorded otherwise, relied on a statement from a team leader not even working that night, took into account matters never put to the claimant, and failed to address the investigation's shortcomings - which led the Tribunal to infer race discrimination given only white staff were interviewed.
deep.reasoning: The Tribunal unanimously found the respondent discriminated against the claimant because of race in the disciplinary process (only speaking to white staff), in giving the final written warning, and in the appeal (failing to rectify earlier failings and to consider the video of a white nurse sleeping). The flawed and inconsistent conduct of Ms Payne, unexplained on any non-discriminatory basis, supported the inference of race discrimination. The single allegation about the initial investigation (14 March-17 April 2023) failed and was dismissed. Remedy was dealt with at a separate hearing applying Vento principles (specific quantum not stated in the provided text).
deep.award_basis: compensation for race discrimination including injury to feelings (Vento); quantum not stated in provided text

deep.facts: The claimant, an apprentice joiner employed from 31 May 2023 to 26 February 2024, was paid the apprentice rate (£7 then £7.35/hour) when, being 27 years old and without a valid apprenticeship agreement in place until 23 October 2023, he believed he should have received the National Minimum Wage for his age (£10.42/hour). He claimed unauthorised deduction from wages for the underpayment for 31 May to 22 October 2023. He raised it repeatedly with HR from late October 2023 but did not start ACAS early conciliation until 17 April 2024.
issues: Whether the Tribunal had jurisdiction, given the claim appeared to be presented outside the three-month time limit for unauthorised deduction from wages claims
Whether it was reasonably practicable for the claimant to present the claim in time
If not, whether it was presented within a reasonable further period
deep.legal_test: Time limit for unauthorised deduction from wages under s.23(2)-(4) ERA 1996 - whether it was 'not reasonably practicable' to present in time and, if so, presentation within a reasonable further period; time limits go to jurisdiction (Rodgers, Radakovits) and 'reasonably practicable' means reasonably feasible (Palmer v Southend)
deep.evidence_weighing: On the claimant's own evidence he knew of the alleged underpayment and that the respondent would not back-pay from his first conversation with HR (Sam Sutcliffe) in late October/November 2023, and he had access to and consulted trade union representatives, showing he was aware of and able to enforce his rights.
deep.reasoning: The last relevant pay date was 27 October 2023, so the ACAS time limit expired on 26 January 2024, but conciliation was not started until 17 April 2024 - almost three months late, a significant delay. As the claimant had all necessary facts from 23 October 2023, knew the respondent would not pay, and was able to take advice and steps to enforce his rights, it was reasonably practicable to have presented in time; nor was the claim presented within a reasonable further period. The Tribunal therefore had no jurisdiction and the claim could not be heard.

deep.facts: Ms Mackenzie-Wintle, an Associate Lecturer at The Sheffield College with autism (an admitted disability), complained about conduct by her managers Ms Parr and Mrs Marshall-Preece. Among the allegations were comments Ms Parr made at a 31 March 2023 meeting about her and a colleague needing to work on their communication ('at least you are both looking at each other now'), discussion of her reasonable adjustments with others, and the reassignment of a responsibility to a colleague after she raised a grievance. She brought claims of harassment related to disability and victimisation.
issues: Were the discrimination complaints brought within the time limit in s.123 Equality Act 2010, or was there conduct extending over a period / should time be extended on a just and equitable basis?
Did the alleged acts (e.g. Ms Parr's comments on 31 March 2023, discussion of the claimant's RAP) amount to unwanted conduct related to disability constituting harassment under the Equality Act 2010?
